''' Motto:''' Fidelitas Urbis Salus Regis
'' In the town's loyalty lies the King's safety'' {{cite web |url=http://www.civicheraldry.co.uk/severn_valley_marches.html |title=Civic Heraldry Of England And Wales-Severn Valley And The Marches |publisher=Civicheraldry.co.uk |access-date=29 May 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120504102005/http://www.civicheraldry.co.uk/severn_valley_marches.html |archive-date=4 May 2012 |url-status=dead }} |population = 12,079 |population_ref = (2011){{cite web |url=http://www.neighbourhood.statistics.gov.uk/dissemination/LeadKeyFigures.do?a=7&b=11121171&c=Bridgnorth&d=16&e=62&g=6460202&i=1001x1003x1032x1004&m=0&r=1&s=1448289485484&enc=1 |title=Bridgnorth (Parish): Key Figures for 2011 Census |work=Neighbourhood Statistics |publisher=Office for National Statistics |access-date=23 November 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304131038/http://www.neighbourhood.statistics.gov.uk/dissemination/LeadKeyFigures.do?a=7&b=11121171&c=Bridgnorth&d=16&e=62&g=6460202&i=1001x1003x1032x1004&m=0&r=1&s=1448289485484&enc=1 |archive-date=4 March 2016 |url-status=dead }} |unitary_england = [[Shropshire (district)|Shropshire]] |lieutenancy_england = [[Shropshire]] |region = West Midlands |constituency_westminster= [[South Shropshire (UK Parliament constituency)|South Shropshire]] |post_town = BRIDGNORTH |postcode_district = WV15, WV16 |postcode_area = WV |dial_code = 01746 |os_grid_reference = SO716927 }} '''Bridgnorth''' is a [[market town]] and [[civil parish]] in [[Shropshire]], England, named after a bridge over the [[River Severn]]. The river divides the town into High Town and Low Town, the upper town on its right bank and the lower on its left bank. The population at the [[United Kingdom Census 2011|2011 Census]] was 12,079. ==History== [[File:Bridgnorth castle ruins.jpg|thumb|The ruins of [[Bridgnorth Castle]]]] Bridgnorth is named after a bridge over the River Severn, which was built further north than an earlier bridge at [[Quatford]].{{Cite book |title=A Guide to Shropshire |last=Raven |first=Michael |page=32 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Txby6_Lrm0cC |year=2005 |isbn=0-906114-34-9 |publisher=Michael Raven |access-date=14 May 2008 }}{{Dead link|date=October 2023 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }} The earliest historical reference to the town is in 895, when it is recorded that the [[Danes (Germanic tribe)|Danes]] created a camp at ''Cwatbridge'';{{cite web|url=http://www3.shropshire-cc.gov.uk/roots/places/bridgnorth/bridgnorth.htm |title=Bridgnorth |work=Shropshire Routes to Roots |access-date=14 May 2008 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080908013227/http://www3.shropshire-cc.gov.uk/roots/places/bridgnorth/bridgnorth.htm |archive-date=8 September 2008 |df=dmy }} subsequently in 912, [[Æthelflæd]] constructed a mound on the west bank of the [[River Severn]], or possibly on the site of [[Bridgnorth Castle]], as part of an offensive against the Danes.{{EB1911|wstitle=Bridgnorth|volume=4|pages=559–560 |inline=1}} Earliest names for Bridgnorth include Brigge, Brug and Bruges, all referring to its position on the Severn.{{cite web |url=http://www.genuki.org.uk/big/eng/SAL/Bridgnorth/ |title=Bridgnorth, Shropshire |work=The National Gazetteer of Great Britain and Ireland 1868 transcribed by Colin Hinson ©2012 |publisher=GENUKI UK and Ireland Genealogy |access-date=27 June 2013}} After the [[Norman conquest of England|Norman conquest]], [[William the Conqueror|William I]] granted the [[manorialism|manor]] of Bridgnorth to [[Roger de Montgomerie, 1st Earl of Shrewsbury|Roger de Montgomerie]]. The town itself was not created until 1101, when [[Robert of Bellême, 3rd Earl of Shrewsbury]], the son of Roger de Montgomerie, moved from Quatford, constructing a [[Bridgnorth Castle|castle]] and a [[church (building)|church]] on the site of the modern-day town. The town became a royal borough on Robert Bellême's [[attainder]] in 1102. The castle's purpose was to defend against attacks from [[Wales]]. The town was attacked and burnt by [[Roger Mortimer, 1st Earl of March]] during the [[Despenser War]] in 1322.{{Citation |title= Parliamentary Writs Alphabetical Digest | volume=II | year=1834 | location=London | publisher= National Archives}} A small Jewish community was established in the town in 1267, but was expelled in 1274; one of the community was arrested in a campaign against alleged Jewish coin clipping, a prelude towards [[Edward I of England|Edward I]]'s [[Edict of Expulsion]] in 1290.{{cite book |last1=Hillaby |first1=Joe |last2=Hillaby |first2=Caroline |title=The Palgrave Dictionary of Medieval Anglo-Jewish History |year=2013 |publisher=Palgrave Macmillan |location=Basingstoke |isbn=9780230278165 |pages=59–60, 103–110}} Bridgnorth's [[town wall]]s were initially constructed in timber between 1216 and 1223; [[murage]] grants allowed them to be upgraded to stone between the 13th and 15th centuries.{{cite web |url=http://www.discovershropshire.org.uk/html/search/verb/GetRecord/CCS:MSA278 |title=Fragment of Town Walls (listed section), rear of 93 Cartway (E and N side), SMRNO00374 |work=Discovering Shropshire's History |access-date=22 October 2011 |archive-date=11 May 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120511221207/http://www.discovershropshire.org.uk/html/search/verb/GetRecord/CCS:MSA278 |url-status=dead }} By the 16th century, the [[antiquarian]] [[John Leland (antiquarian)|John Leland]] reported them in ruins and of the five gates, only one survives today.{{Citation needed|date=July 2019}} [[File:Bridgnorth 1646 inscription.JPG|thumb|Inscription on Bridgnorth Museum, commemorating the deliberate destruction of the town by royalist forces, commanded by [[Wolryche Baronets|Sir Thomas Wolryche]] of [[Dudmaston Hall]]]] It is probable that [[Henry I of England|Henry I]] granted the [[burgess (title)|burgesses]] certain privileges, for [[Henry II of England|Henry II]] confirmed to them all the franchises and customs which they had had in the time of Henry I.{{cite web |url=http://www.genuki.org.uk/big/eng/SAL/Bridgnorth/Gaz1868.html |title=BRIDGNORTH, Shropshire – Extract from National Gazetteer, 1868 |work=GENUKI |access-date=14 May 2008 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060127070011/http://www.genuki.org.uk/big/eng/SAL/Bridgnorth/Gaz1868.html |archive-date=27 January 2006 |df=dmy }} King [[John, King of England|John]] in 1215 granted them freedom from toll throughout England except the city of London, and in 1227 [[Henry III of England|Henry III]] conferred several new rights and liberties, among which were a [[gild merchant]] with a [[hanse]]. These early charters were confirmed by several succeeding kings, [[Henry VI of England|Henry VI]] granting in addition [[Assize of Bread and Ale]] and other privileges. The burgesses were additionally granted two fairs: a yearly fair on the feast of the Translation of [[Leonard of Noblac|St Leonard]] and the three following days was granted in 1359, and in 1630 [[Charles I of England|Charles I]] granted them licence to hold another fair on the Thursday before the first week in [[Lent]] and two following days. The burgesses returned two members to parliament in 1295,{{cite web |url=http://www.election.demon.co.uk/prereform.html |title=Parliamentary Constituencies in the unreformed House |access-date=14 May 2008 |archive-date=5 November 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071105102205/http://www.election.demon.co.uk/prereform.html |url-status=dead }} and continued to do so until 1867, when they were assigned only one member. The town was disfranchised in 1885. During the [[English Civil War|Civil War]], Bridgnorth was one of the Midlands' main Royalist strongholds, and in 1642 many Royalist troops were garrisoned there. In 1646, Cromwell's Roundheads arrived with orders to take Bridgnorth for the Parliamentarians from the garrison led by [[Robert Howard (Royalist)|Sir Robert Howard]].{{DNB Cite|wstitle=Howard, Robert (1585-1653)}} After a three-week siege, Cromwell was successful and he ordered that the castle be demolished. Bridgnorth had an ironworks in Low Town run by [[Hazledine and Company]] which in 1808 built the locomotive ''[[Catch Me Who Can]]'' designed and promoted by [[Richard Trevithick]]. A plaque on the foundry's site commemorates this association.{{cite news|title=Marking a milestone in locomotive history|work=Shropshire Star|date=24 April 2021}}Report by Rory Smith on unveiling of plaque. By 1824, the [[List of hundreds of England|borough and liberties of Bridgnorth]] were well defined.{{cite book|author=Shropshire gazetteer|title=The Shropshire gazetteer|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=5e8HAAAAQAAJ&pg=PA862|year=1824|pages=862 |access-date=10 June 2020}} The population of the municipal borough in 1841 was 6,198, and that of the town was 5,770.The National Cyclopaedia of Useful Knowledge, Vol III, (1847), London, Charles Knight, p.804 More than 255 men from the Bridgnorth area volunteered in the first months of the [[First World War]]. Their names were published in the ''Bridgnorth Journal'' on 26 December 1914 and those killed in action are remembered on the war memorial, sculpted by [[Adrian Jones (sculptor)|Adrian Jones]], in the castle grounds.{{cite book|last=Francis|first=Peter|title=Shropshire War Memorials, Sites of Remembrance|year=2013|publisher=YouCaxton|pages=108–109|isbn=978-1-909644-11-3}} Until 1961 the [[Royal Air Force]]'s initial recruit training unit was at [[RAF Bridgnorth]], a station opened in 1939. During the [[Second World War]], two women were killed in a German air raid in August 1940 when bombs hit neighbouring houses in High Town. In 2005, unverified German papers dating from 1941 were found, outlining new details about [[Operation Sea Lion]], the [[military plan]]s of [[Nazi Germany]] for an invasion of Britain. Two quiet Shropshire towns were mentioned in the documentation: [[Ludlow]] and Bridgnorth. Some experts believe that it was [[Adolf Hitler|Hitler's]] intention to make Bridgnorth his personal [[headquarters]] in Britain, due to its central position in the UK, rural location, rail connections and [[airfield]].{{cite news|url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/england/shropshire/4461879.stm|title=Hitler's secret Shropshire plans|publisher=BBC | date=19 April 2005| access-date=2 January 2010}}. The airfield was mentioned in 2005 by an auctioneer's consultant, unaware that nearby [[RAF Bridgnorth]], created in 1939 as a recruit training depot, never had an airfield; but German war planners might have assumed all major RAF depots had airfields.{{cite video| url= https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/av/uk-england-20592917 | title=Adolf Hitler's plans for British base in Shropshire | publisher=BBC Inside Out | date=10 December 2012 | access-date=10 December 2012 | people= Richie Woodall (presenter)}} In 1978, Bridgnorth was twinned with the French town of [[Thiers, Puy-de-Dôme|Thiers]], and in 1992 it also twinned with the [[Bavaria]]n town of [[Schrobenhausen]], Germany{{cite web|url=http://www.bridgnorth-dc.gov.uk/static/page1051.htm |title=Twin Towns |work=Bridgnorth District Council |access-date=14 May 2008 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081121031734/http://www.bridgnorth-dc.gov.uk/static/page1051.htm |archive-date=21 November 2008 |df=dmy }} that had already twinned with Thiers a few years earlier. On 21 August 2003 Bridgnorth was granted [[Fairtrade Town]] status.{{cite web |url=http://www.aboutbridgnorth.com/about.htm |title=History Of Bridgnorth, Shropshire |work=About Bridgnorth |access-date=14 May 2008 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080430164709/http://www.aboutbridgnorth.com/about.htm |archive-date=30 April 2008 |df=dmy }} ==Geography== The town is in the [[Severn Valley]], where the river passes through a relatively narrow valley with largely-wooded slopes. High Town, the part of the town sited on the west side of the Severn, is built on a notable [[promontory]], at the southern end of which the castle was constructed, and is known as Castle Hill. Low Town is on lower-lying ground on the banks of the river. High Town is at an elevation of 65–68 metres (213–223 feet) above sea level, whilst Low Town is at 32–33 metres (105 feet).[[Ordnance Survey]] mapping The lie of the land of Low Town is less hilly but then rises steeply to its immediate east. The [[West Midlands Green Belt]] covers the countryside to the east of the Severn and the settlement. The [[civil parish]] includes [[Danesford]], [[Oldbury, Shropshire|Oldbury]] and [[Quatford]].[https://www.bridgnorthtowncouncil.gov.uk/council-information/ward-map/ Bridgnorth Town Council] Ward map ==Landmarks== {{See also|Listed buildings in Bridgnorth}} [[File:Bridgnorth - Old Market Hall - geograph.org.uk - 1323006.jpg|thumb|Bridgnorth High Street with [[Bridgnorth Town Hall|town hall]] (built 1652)]] Bridgnorth is home to a [[funicular]] railway that links the High and Low towns, the [[Bridgnorth Cliff Railway|Castle Hill Railway]], which is the steepest and only inland railway of its type in England.{{cite web |url= http://www.bbc.co.uk/shropshire/content/articles/2005/03/22/bridgnorth_town_guide_feature.shtml |title=Bridgnorth Town Guide |work=BBC Shropshire |access-date=14 May 2008}} Additionally, within the High Town is [[Bridgnorth railway station]] on the [[Severn Valley Railway]], which runs southwards to [[Kidderminster]]. The ruins of [[Bridgnorth Castle]], built in 1101, are present in the town. Due to damage caused during the English Civil War, the castle is inclined at an angle of 15 degrees.{{cite web |url=http://www.visitbritain.co.kr/things-to-see-and-do/attractions-and-events/detail.aspx?TowPosCd=%25ube0c%25ub9ac%25uc9c0%25ub178%25uc2a4(Bridgnorth)&Sec=Events%2CAttraction&advsrch=1&display=list&Lat=52.53825069&Lon=-2.420245828&Rad=5&Caption=%25ube0c%25ub9ac%25uc9c0%25ub178%25uc2a4(Bridgnorth)&Pid=126791 |title=Bridgnorth Castle |work=Visit Britain |access-date=14 May 2008}} High Town has two prominent [[Church of England]] churches. [[Church of St. Mary Magdalene, Bridgnorth]], a [[church (building)|church]] built in the classic style of the late 18th century, was designed by [[Thomas Telford]];{{cite web|url=http://www.engineering-timelines.com/scripts/engineeringItem.asp?id=565 |title=St Mary Magdalene, Bridgnorth |work=Engineering Timelines |access-date=14 May 2008 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061110120548/http://www.engineering-timelines.com/scripts/engineeringItem.asp?id=565 |archive-date=10 November 2006 |df=dmy }} and is still used for worship. [[St Leonard's Church, Bridgnorth|St. Leonard's]] was formerly collegiate, and Bridgnorth was a [[Royal Peculiar]] until 1856. It was subsequently largely rebuilt{{Cite book |title=Shropshire |page=161 |last=Newman |first=John |author2=Pevsner, Nikolaus |year=2006 |publisher=Yale University Press |isbn=0-300-12083-4 |access-date=14 May 2008 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=3Zqbit3opjQC}} but is no longer used for regular worship. It has many community uses and is in the care of the [[Churches Conservation Trust]]. [[File:Bridgnorth Bridge - geograph.org.uk - 1146188.jpg|right|thumb|View from Low Town towards High Town and St Mary Magdalene's]] Bishop Percy's House on the Cartway was built in 1580 by Richard Forster and has been a Grade I listed building since 18 July 1949. It was one of the few properties of its type to survive the great fire of Bridgnorth in April 1646, and was the birthplace of [[Thomas Percy (Bishop of Dromore)]], author of 'Reliques of Ancient English Poetry'.{{cite web|url=http://www.bishoppercyshouse.co.uk |title=Bishop Percys House, bridgnorth |access-date=16 April 2011 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110907181948/http://www.bishoppercyshouse.co.uk/ |archive-date=7 September 2011 }}{{cite web |url=http://www.aboutbridgnorth.com/bishop-percys-house/ |title=Bishop Percys House |date=4 May 2013 |publisher=Bridgnorth Tourist Information Guide & Business Directory |access-date=19 October 2015}} Other notable buildings in the town are the 17th century [[Bridgnorth Town Hall]], a [[Timber framing|half-timbered]] building,{{NHLE|desc= Town Hall|num=1053998|access-date=23 December 2020}} and a surviving town gate the Northgate which houses the museum.{{NHLE|desc= North Gate |num= 1374846|access-date=23 December 2020}} [[Daniel's Mill]], a well known [[watermill]] is situated a short distance along the [[River Severn]] from Bridgnorth. The remains of an old [[Hermitage (religious retreat)|hermitage]] can be seen from the high town, they are commonly called The Queens Parlor by locals. One local legend tells of its occupation in AD 925 by a hermit called Ethelred or Ethelwald, a grandson to [[Alfred the Great]]. This may not be such an unlikely story as Bridgnorth was founded in 912 by Alfred the Great's daughter Aethelflaed. {{Further|Ropewalk Dingle}} ==Education== [[File:Bridgnorth Grammar School - New Northgate Building.JPG|thumb|[[Bridgnorth Endowed School]]'s Northgate building was once home to the town's grammar school]] There are a number of [[primary schools]] in Bridgnorth, including: Castlefields County Primary School, two [[Church of England]] schools, St Mary's and St Leonard's; the [[Roman Catholic]] St John's school; and, in addition, the Morville and Brown Clee schools.{{cite web |url=http://www.shropshire.gov.uk/schools.nsf/open/042EA20A25E7FBDC80256D560031DD1B |work=Shropshire County Council |title=Shropshire County Council maintained schools in Bridgnorth |access-date=2 July 2008}} The town has two [[secondary schools]]: [[Oldbury Wells School]] and [[Bridgnorth Endowed School]] (previously named [[Bridgnorth Grammar School]]). These serve the town and its outlying villages, including [[Alveley]] and [[Highley]]. There is a [[Sixth form college|sixth form]] in Bridgnorth, [http://bridgnorthsixthform.com/ Bridgnorth Sixth Form], which is run within Oldbury Wells School. A consultation was published which outlines consideration of no new student intake in September 2024 and potential closure in September 2025.{{Cite web |title=Bridgnorth 6th Form Consultation |url=http://bridgnorthsixthform.com/bridgnorth-6th-form-consultation |access-date=2023-11-14 |website=bridgnorthsixthform.com |language=en}} In September 2023, [[Telford College]] made a deal with both Bridgnorth secondary schools.{{Cite web |last=Williams |first=Richard |date=2023-10-27 |title=College deal could see sixth form saved in Bridgnorth |url=https://www.shropshirestar.com/news/local-hubs/bridgnorth/2023/10/27/college-deal-could-see-sixth-form-saved-in-bridgnorth/ |access-date=2023-11-14 |website=www.shropshirestar.com |language=en}} {{Clear}} ==Culture== [[File:Majestic Cinema, Bridgnorth.jpg|right|thumb|The town's art-deco [[Majestic Cinema, Bridgnorth|Majestic Cinema]]]] There is a theatre, the ''Theatre on the Steps'', and a 1930s cinema, the [[Majestic Cinema, Bridgnorth|Majestic]]. The Northgate Museum contains many artefacts connected with the town and surrounding area. It was the first independent museum in Shropshire to be accredited by the [[Museums, Libraries and Archives Council]].{{cite web|url=http://www.bridgnorthmuseum.org.uk |title=Bridgnorth's Northgate Museum |publisher=Bridgnorthmuseum.org.uk |date=1 November 2007 |access-date=29 July 2015}} The town has an orchestra, Bridgnorth Sinfonia, which performers regular concerts in St Mary's Church in East Castle Street.{{cite web|url=https://www.bridgnorthsinfonia.com|title=Bridgnorth Sinfonia}} ===Sport and clubs=== [[File:Bridgnorth town centre in the summer sunshine - geograph.org.uk - 1453399.jpg|upright|thumb|The [[New Market Hall, Bridgnorth|New Market Hall building]] at the top of Bridgnorth's High Street]] [[Bridgnorth Town F.C.]] was the football club based in Bridgnorth. They joined the [[Midland Football Combination|Worcestershire Combination]] in 1938 and twice reached the 5th round of the [[FA Vase]]. They won the championship of the [[West Midlands (Regional) League]] Premier Division in 2008. Affiliated to the club was the junior section known as "Bridgnorth Town Juniors". The teams ranged from under 8s to under 16s and competed in the Telford Junior League. After folding in 2013, the club was effectively replaced by "phoenix club" [[A.F.C. Bridgnorth]]. Bridgnorth Spartans Juniors Football Club run junior and adult teams. These teams include boys' teams, ranging from Under-8s to Under-15s, girls' teams and women's teams. Home games are played at Oldbury Wells School.{{Citation needed|date=May 2019}} The [[Bridgnorth and District Football League]] was played in the area from 1925 to 2001. Bridgnorth Rowing Club occupies 'The Maltings' building on the edge of Severn Park, which was purchased by the club in 1983. Work to convert the malting building into the boat house started in 1993. It competes in events in the local region and further afield, including attending the annual Head of the River Race on the [[River Thames|Thames]] in London, and hosts an annual regatta with racing along the length of the Severn Park.{{Citation needed|date=May 2019}} [[File:Bridgnorth Golf Course - geograph.org.uk - 692401.jpg|right|thumb|Bridgnorth Golf Club is home to an 18-hole course]] Bridgnorth Army Cadets is the oldest Army Cadet detachment in Shropshire.{{Citation needed|date=April 2019}} The [[Army Cadet Force]] (ACF) in 2010 celebrated 150 years. In 2007, Bridgnorth hosted the UK Downhill Street Race in cycling. In January 2010, the Kidderminster branch of Stagecoach Theatre Arts expanded to Bridgnorth, providing the town with a part-time performing arts school for people of ages between 6 and 18. The Kidderminster School is now named "Stagecoach Kidderminster & Bridgnorth".{{Citation needed|date=May 2019}} ===Media=== Local news and television programmes are provided by [[BBC West Midlands]] and [[ITV Central]]. Television signals are received from the [[The Wrekin transmitting station|Wrekin]]{{cite web|url=https://ukfree.tv/transmitters/tv/The_Wrekin|title=Full Freeview on the The[sic] Wrekin (Telford and Wrekin, England) transmitter|date=1 May 2004|website=UK Free TV|accessdate=19 November 2023}} and the local relay TV transmitters.{{cite web|url=https://ukfree.tv/transmitters/tv/Bridgnorth|title=Freeview Light on the Bridgnorth (Shropshire, England) transmitter|date=1 May 2004|website=UK Free TV|accessdate=19 November 2023}} Local radio stations are [[BBC Radio Shropshire]], [[Heart West Midlands]], [[Capital North West and Wales]], [[Smooth West Midlands]], [[Hits Radio Black Country & Shropshire]], [[Greatest Hits Radio Black Country & Shropshire]], and Severnvalley Radio, a community based station.{{Cite web |url=https://severnvalleyradio.co.uk/|title=Severnvalley Radio |access-date=19 November 2023}} The town is served by the local newspaper, [[Shropshire Star]] (formerly Bridgnorth Journal).{{cite web|url=https://www.britishpapers.co.uk/england-wmids/bridgnorth-journal/|title=Bridgnorth Journal|date=21 April 2014|website=British Papers|accessdate=19 November 2023}} ==Transport== [[File:436 bus in the High Street - geograph.org.uk - 1453392 cropped.jpg|right|thumb|The [[Arriva Midlands]] 436 bus service to Shrewsbury enters Bridgnorth through Northgate]] ===Roads=== Bridgnorth grew initially as a [[market town]] at the centre of a system of local radial roads linking it with more rural, smaller settlements. Many of these roads crossed Bridgnorth at the point on the High Street where the town hall now stands. The River Severn historically also played a major role as a trading connection for the town, but is no longer generally navigable this far upstream.{{Citation needed|date=May 2019}} Bridgnorth is connected to [[Shrewsbury]] and [[Stourbridge]] by the [[A458 road]], [[Telford]] and [[Kidderminster]] by the [[A442 road]], and [[Wolverhampton]] via the [[A454 road]]. The town is {{convert|11|mi|km}} from the [[M54 motorway|M54]] motorway, at Telford. The A458 passes to the south of the town centre on a by-pass, construction of which was started in 1982 and now serves to relieve the town centre of the congestion that once plagued it. The bypass also provided a second bridge across the Severn at Bridgnorth, which remains the only local alternative to the historic bridge that connects Low and High towns. ===Buses=== The town is served by buses to and from Telford, Shrewsbury, Wolverhampton, [[Much Wenlock]], [[Ironbridge]], [[Shifnal]] and Kidderminster. These are operated by [[Arriva Midlands]], Select Bus Services, and [[Diamond West Midlands|Diamond Bus]]. ===Railway=== {{Main|Severn Valley Railway|Bridgnorth railway station}} [[File:Bridgnorth railway station MMB 09.jpg|left|thumb|[[Bridgnorth railway station|Bridgnorth station]] is the current northern terminus of the [[Severn Valley Railway]].]] Currently the closest towns with active railway stations on the [[National Rail]] network are Telford and Wolverhampton. However, Bridgnorth does still have a station on an active heritage line, the [[Severn Valley Railway]]. Bridgnorth station was not the northern terminus of this line when built, but the main intermediate station, being 18{{frac|1|4}} miles from [[Hartlebury]] and 22{{frac|1|2}} miles from [[Shrewsbury]]. The station, which was opened to the public by the SVR on 1 February 1862, was passed to [[Great Western Railway]] (GWR) and then eventually to [[British Rail]]ways in 1948. It closed to passengers after 101 years of service on 8 September 1963 and to freight traffic on 30 November 1963. Although thought by some to have been closed as part of the [[Beeching cuts]], its planned closure pre-dated his report. The neo-Jacobean station is the only listed railway station on the Severn Valley Railway. Necessitating that, any future plans to enhance visitor facilities will need to be carefully designed to be in keeping with the railway station's architecture and historic character. The line now ends just north of the modern-day station, where the line formerly bridged Hollybush Road and passed through Bridgnorth Tunnel and on to the next station on the line, [[Linley Halt railway station|Linley]]. There exists an ongoing debate whether the railway should [[Severn Valley Railway#Northwards|extend]] beyond its current limits north of Bridgnorth.{{cite web |url=http://forum.svra.org.uk/viewtopic.php?t=214 |title=SVR-Online Forum :: View topic – North of B'north |publisher=Forum.svra.org.uk |access-date=29 May 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140512220232/http://forum.svra.org.uk/viewtopic.php?t=214 |archive-date=12 May 2014 |url-status=usurped |df=dmy-all }} {{Clear}} ===Cliff railway=== {{Main|Bridgnorth Cliff Railway}} [[File:BridgnorthCliffRailway-looking-down.jpg|thumb|right|Bridgnorth's [[Bridgnorth Cliff Railway|Castle Hill Railway]]]] The Bridgnorth Cliff Railway, also known as the Bridgnorth Funicular Railway or Castle Hill Railway, is a [[funicular|funicular railway]] which has operated in Bridgnorth for over 100 years. The line links the lower part of High Town to the upper part. The bottom entrance is adjacent to the [[River Severn]] while the top is adjacent to the ruins of [[Bridgnorth Castle]]. Opened on 7 July 1892 to great fanfare and the proclamation of a public holiday, the line is one of four funicular railways in the [[United Kingdom|UK]] built to the same basic design - the others were the [[Clifton Rocks Railway]] in Bristol; the [[Lynton and Lynmouth Cliff Railway]] in Devon; and the [[Aberystwyth Electric Cliff Railway|Constitution Hill Railway]] in Aberystwyth, Wales. It is one of the steepest railways in the country and at least one source (the information panel outside the top station) claims it is both the steepest and shortest. It is the only functional inland funicular railway in England - there are about 15 more at English seaside towns.{{cite web | url= https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-england-shropshire-12617870 |title= Bridgnorth Cliff Railway put up for sale |date= 2 March 2011 |publisher= BCC News |access-date=2 March 2011}} Originally, the railway was powered by a simple system using water and gravity, but was converted in 1943–44 to run on electricity. Then, in 1955, new cars were installed on the railway; these were able to carry 18 passengers each and are still in use today. As of {{As of|2024|alt=April 2024}} return tickets cost £2.00 with discounts available for groups of 15 or more.{{cite web | url= https://www.bridgnorthcliffrailway.co.uk/ |title=Welcome to Bridgnorth Cliff Railway |publisher=bridgnorthcliffrailway.co.uk/ |access-date=30 March 2024}} Single tickets are not available. The railway allows pedestrians to easily get between the High Town and Low Town as the only other ways between the two are via 200 steps, or by using roads which drastically increase the journey time and distance. The terminals at the upper and lower part of the railway are currently used as tea-rooms and guest houses.{{cn|date=January 2026}} The railway was temporarily closed in December 2022 due to damage to a retaining wall and further damage was discovered during repairs. The railway reopened on 4 March 2024.{{cite web |url=https://www.bridgnorthcliffrailway.co.uk/passenger-service-resumed/ |title=Passenger Service Resumed and Cards Accepted |publisher=bridgnorthcliffrailway.co.uk/ |date=4 March 2024 |access-date=30 March 2024}} ===Walking and cycling=== [[File:Steps to high town - panoramio.jpg|thumb|right|Stoneway Steps: one of the long flights of steps that lead up to High Town]] Bridgnorth being split between High and Low Towns is connected by at least a dozen steps — for which the place is noted — from the north, going clockwise: *innominate steps from Love Lane to Bramble Ridge *'''Moat St Steps''' from St Leonard's Close to Moat Street *'''Granary Steps''' from St Leonard's Close to Friars' Street *'''St Leonard's Steps''' from St Leonard's Close to Cartway *'''Friars' Loade / Friary Steps''' from Friars' Street to Riverside *'''Bank Steps''' from Cartway to Riverside *'''Stoneway Steps''' from Waterloo Terrace to Underhill Street *'''St Mary's Steps''' from East Castle Street to Underhill Street *'''Library Steps''' from Castle Walk to Underhill Street *'''Cannon Steps''' from Castle Walk to Hollybush Road *'''Folly Hole''' from New Road to Hollybush Road *'''Ebenezer / Railway Steps''' from New Road to Hollybush Road The town is on National Route 45 of the Sustrans National Cycle Network, which is named the [[Mercian Way]]. The long-distance trail called the [[Geopark Way]] begins in the town. Every year since 1967, a sponsored walk has been held in Bridgnorth.{{cite web |url=http://www.bridgnorthwalk.org |title=The Bridgnorth Walk and Marathon |work=Bridgnorth Lions |access-date=22 January 2012}} Since 2017 this has been organised by the Bridgnorth Lions Club. ==Economy== On the eastern side of the town is a large [[aluminium]] works, founded in the 1950s.[https://www.bridgnorthaluminium.co.uk/ Bridgnorth Aluminium] ==Governance== The [[Town councils in England|town council]] has sixteen members, with four elected from each of the four [[Wards and electoral divisions in the United Kingdom|wards]] that cover the civil parish (named Castle, Morfe, East, and West).{{cite web |url=https://www.bridgnorthtowncouncil.gov.uk/council-information/about-us/ |work=Bridgnorth Town Council |title=About us |access-date=31 March 2021 }} Castle ward includes Oldbury, while Morfe ward includes Danesford and Quatford. Local government and services are otherwise provided by [[Shropshire Council]] and the town [[2017 Shropshire Council election#Bridgnorth East and Astley Abbotts|elects four of its members]] — one electoral division comprises East and Morfe wards together with [[Astley Abbotts]], and the other comprises West and Castle wards together with [[Tasley, Shropshire|Tasley]].[https://www.ordnancesurvey.co.uk/election-maps/gb/ Ordnance Survey] Election maps GB From 1974 until 2009, there was also [[Bridgnorth (district)|Bridgnorth District Council]], a 966714.title: Attingham Park
966714.extract:
Attingham Park  is an English country house and estate in Shropshire located near the village of Atcham, on the B4380 Shrewsbury to Wellington road. It is owned by the National Trust and is a Grade I listed building.
Attingham Park was built in 1785 for Noel Hill, 1st Baron Berwick, replacing a house on the site called Tern Hall. With money he inherited, along with his title, he commissioned the architect George Steuart to design a new and grander house to be built around the original hall. The new country house encapsulated the old property entirely, and once completed it was given the new name "Attingham Hall".
The estate comprises roughly 4,000 acres (1,600 ha), and the extensive 640 acres (260 ha) of parkland and gardens of Attingham have Grade II* listed status. Over 560,000 people visited in 2022/23, placing it as the most popular National Trust property.
Across the parkland there are five Grade II* listed buildings, including the stable block, the Tern Lodge toll house which can be seen on the B4380, and two bridges that span the River Tern. There are also 12 Grade II listed structures including the retaining walls of the estate, the bee house, the ice house, the walled garden, the ha-ha, which can be seen in the front of the mansion, and the Home Farm.

[[File:Attingham Park - geograph.org.uk - 370372.jpg|thumb|The garden front]]
'''Attingham Park''' {{IPAc-en|'|æ|t|ɪ|ŋ|əm|}} is an [[English country house]] and estate in [[Shropshire]] located near the village of [[Atcham]], on the B4380 [[Shrewsbury]] to [[Wellington, Shropshire|Wellington]] road. It is owned by the [[National Trust]] and is a Grade I [[listed building]].

Attingham Park was built in 1785 for [[Noel Hill, 1st Baron Berwick]], replacing a house on the site called '''Tern Hall'''. With money he inherited, along with his title, he commissioned the architect [[George Steuart (architect)|George Steuart]] to design a new and grander house to be built around the original hall. The new country house encapsulated the old property entirely, and once completed it was given the new name "Attingham Hall".

The estate comprises roughly {{convert|4,000|acres}}, and the extensive {{convert|640|acres}} of parkland and gardens of Attingham have Grade II* listed status. Over 560,000 people visited in 2022/23, placing it as the most popular National Trust property.<ref>[https://nt.global.ssl.fastly.net/binaries/content/assets/website/national/pdf/national-trust-annual-report-2021-2022.pdf National Trust Annual Report 2021-2022]</ref>

Across the parkland there are five Grade II* listed buildings, including the [[stable]] block, the Tern Lodge [[toll house]] which can be seen on the B4380, and two bridges that span the [[River Tern]]. There are also 12 Grade II listed structures including the retaining walls of the estate, the bee house, the ice house, the walled garden, the [[ha-ha]], which can be seen in the front of the mansion, and the [[Home farm (agriculture)|Home Farm]].

==History==
===Pre-history, Roman and Early Medieval===
The archaeology of Attingham Park is diverse covering many different periods of history and human habitation. People have lived around the area of the estate for around 4,000 years since the [[Bronze Age]], utilising the rich [[alluvial]] soils for agriculture. There are seven scheduled ancient monuments across the wider estate including an [[Iron Age]] settlement, Roman forts and a significant portion of the fourth largest [[civitas]] in [[Roman Britain]], [[Viroconium]], on the site of the nearby village of [[Wroxeter]].<ref>Douglas, p.38</ref> A recent large scale magnetometer survey has revealed the existence of two Roman villas and a cemetery along with evidence of some Iron Age or [[Romano-British]] farms. There are also traces of several [[Roman roads]] to the west of Wroxeter.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Price |first1=Richard |title=Evidence of Roman villas found in survey |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3gd548jem3o |website=BBC News |access-date=4 July 2024}}</ref>

There are also the archeological remains of Anglo-Saxon palaces in form of two rare 25m-long timber halls dating to around 650 AD, highlighting a significant and well-resourced Anglo-Saxon community in the region.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Neal |first=Toby |date=2018-02-07 |title=Rare Saxon hall find at Attingham excites the experts |url=https://www.shropshirestar.com/news/2018/02/08/rare-saxon-hall-find-excites-the-experts/ |access-date=2025-03-31 |website=www.shropshirestar.com |language=en}}</ref> 

By the mediaeval period, a village, '''Berwick Maviston''', is recorded. This has not survived, but today the remains of a [[moat]] and fish ponds from the old manor can still be seen. The manor and the village dated back to the [[Norman Conquest]], being mentioned in the 1086 [[Domesday Book]]. This original manor fell into disrepair in mediaeval times: by 1324 it was in ruins.<ref name=bw /> It was replaced with another house known as 'Grant's Mansion' was recorded on the site in 1790. The village was occupied until the 1780s when the newly created [[Baron Berwick]] built Attingham and removed the village from his land. The title of Baron Berwick comes from the name of this village.<ref name=bw>{{National Heritage List for England |num=1020281 |accessdate=3 April 2015}}</ref>

===The arrival of the Hill family===
[[File:British (English) School - Sir Rowland Hill (1492–1561) - 1298284 - National Trust.jpg|alt=A Tudor statesman in his chains of office and gown|thumb|207x207px|Sir Rowland Hill of Soulton; this portrait is in the National Trust Collection]]
The associations of the Hill family with the area of the Park can be traced to a civic benefaction of the Tudor statesman Sir [[Rowland Hill (MP)|Rowland Hill]] of [[Soulton]], convenor of the [[Geneva Bible]] translation, who built the first stone bridge over the river here:<ref>{{Cite book |last=Camden |first=Theophilus |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=5adJ1fJE-zQC&dq=sir+rowland+hill+lord+mayor+of+london&pg=PA311 |title=The History of the Present War in Spain and Portugal: From Its Commencement to the Battle of Vittoria ... : to which Will be Added, Memoirs of the Life of Lord Wellington ... |date=1813 |publisher=W. Stratford |language=en}}</ref> this was part of his wider civic projects across London and Shropshire and a portrait of him is still displayed in the mansion.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Trigg |first=Keri |title=Portrait of the past is restored at Attingham Park |url=https://www.shropshirestar.com/entertainment/attractions/2019/10/26/portrait-of-the-past-is-restored-at-attingham-park/ |access-date=2023-04-16 |website=www.shropshirestar.com |language=en}}</ref>  [[File:British (English) School - The Reverend and Right Honourable Richard Hill of Hawkstone (1654–1727) - 1298214 - National Trust.jpg|thumb|Richard Hill, "the Great Hill" tutor to the [[Richard Boyle, 1st Earl of Burlington|Boyle]] family owned Tern Hall that predated the current mansion and was encased within it
.|189x189px]]
Prior to the construction of the current mansion, a building called Tern Hall existed on the site which had been built to his own designs by a relative of [[Richard Hill of Hawkstone]], a relative of 'Old Sir Rowland'.<ref name=":022">Jenkins, 638</ref><ref name=":122">Douglas, p.4</ref>

===The Hills, Barons of Berwick===
Attingham, including [[Cronkhill]], was the seat of the [[Barons Berwick]] from the 1780s until that title became extinct in 1953. On the death of Thomas Henry Noel-Hill, 8th Baron Berwick (1877–1947), who died childless, the Attingham Estate, comprising the mansion and some {{convert|4,000|acres}}, was gifted to the National Trust.<ref name="Douglas, p.13">Douglas, p.13</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=The wider Attingham Estate |url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/attingham-park/features/the-wider-attingham-estate |access-date=2022-08-30 |website=National Trust |language=en}}</ref>

Attingham Park was designed by [[George Steuart (architect)|George Steuart]], a follower of [[James Wyatt]] and encapsulated Tern Hall. It is the only remaining example of a country house by Steuart; he later designed [[St Chad's Church, Shrewsbury]].<ref name=":022"/> It was built from 1782 to 1785 for [[Noel Hill, 1st Baron Berwick]]. Lord Berwick, a former MP for [[Shropshire (UK Parliament constituency)|Shropshire]], received his title in 1784 during the premiership of [[William Pitt the Younger]], during which he had been instrumental in the [[Pitt's India Act|reorganisation of the East India Company]].<ref name=":122">Douglas, p.4</ref> The proportions have been criticised: for [[Simon Jenkins]] "The façade is uncomfortably tall, almost barracks-like, the portico columns painfully thin".<ref name=":022">Jenkins, 638</ref> There is a large entrance court, with an imposing gatehouse, and two single storey wings stretch out to either side of the main block. The main reception rooms were divided into a male and female set on either side of the house.

[[File:Attingham Park - stained glass inner skylight by Nash.jpg|thumb|Stained glass inner skylight dome above the Nash staircase]]

[[File:Baron Berwick coa.png|thumb|Arms of 1st Baron Berwick]]

In 1789, the 1st Lord Berwick died, and his son, [[Thomas Noel Hill, 2nd Baron Berwick]], succeeded him. Thomas was a collector and patron of the arts, who commissioned improvements to the house and extensions of the estate.<ref name=":2">Douglas, p.6</ref> This included commissioning [[John Nash (architect)|John Nash]] in 1805 to add the picture gallery, a project that was flawed from the beginning as it suffered from leaks. Constructed using cast iron and curved glass to give the effect of [[molding (decorative)|coving]], it throws light into the gallery below.<ref>Douglas, p.50</ref> In 2013 work began on building a new protective roof above the delicate Nash roof, replacing one installed in the 1970s with a new one which will stop leakage and reduce natural weather wear. The new roof has temperature control, blinds, and UV resistant glass.<ref>{{cite web|title=Attingham Park restoration work starts.|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-england-shropshire-21012019|work=BBC News|accessdate=16 March 2013}}</ref>

[[File:William Noel-Hill, 3rd Baron Berwick.jpg|thumb|upright|3rd Baron Berwick]]
The 2nd Lord Berwick reached financial ruin, and all the contents of the house were auctioned in 1827 and in 1829; some were purchased by his two brothers.<ref name=":022"/> He died in Italy in 1832, and his brother, [[William Noel-Hill, 3rd Baron Berwick]] inherited the estate.<ref name=":2" /> William was a diplomat, who was posted in Italy for 28 years; described by [[Lord Byron]] as 'the only one of the diplomatists whom I ever knew who really is Excellent’, his collection of Italian art and furniture became part of Attingham's collection upon his inheritance. This included the tableware by silversmith [[Paul Storr]].<ref>Douglas, 8-9</ref> William died in 1842, and his younger brother, [[Richard Noel-Hill, 4th Baron Berwick]] inherited; as the youngest son and a clergyman, he had not expected to inherit. His son, [[Richard Noel Noel-Hill, 5th Baron Berwick]], inherited in 1848, and was a careful steward, introducing agricultural modernisations and clearing many of the estate's debts that had been accrued by his father and uncles.<ref name="Douglas, 10-11">Douglas, 10-11</ref> He lived at [[Cronkhill]] on the estate and whilst there invented to eponymous [[Cronkhill rifle]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Williams |first=Gareth |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=tEI3EAAAQBAJ&dq=cronkhill+rifle&pg=PA201 |title=The Country Houses of Shropshire |date=2021 |publisher=Boydell & Brewer |isbn=978-1-78327-539-7 |pages=201 |language=en}}</ref>

Richard was succeeded by his brother, [[William Noel-Hill, 6th Baron Berwick]], in 1861, who was a colonel in the army, and chose to not live at Attingham. William died in 1882 and his nephew [[Richard Henry Noel-Hill, 7th Baron Berwick]], inherited the estate. The 7th Baron had financial problems and sold family heirlooms to pay off debts.<ref name="Douglas, 10-11"/> He died in 1897.

===20th century===
[[Thomas Henry Noel-Hill, 8th Baron Berwick]] (nephew of the 7th baron) inherited the estate. A diplomat, who worked in France, he added French decorative arts to the Attingham collection. He also had electricity installed in the house, and made improvements to the estate.<ref name=":3">Douglas, 12-13</ref>
 
[[File:Kitchen at Attingham.jpg|thumb|Kitchen at Attingham, whose contents are listed in a 1913 inventory.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Eveleigh |first=David |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=dTU7AwAAQBAJ&dq=attingham+kitchen&pg=PT23 |title=A History of the Kitchen |date=2011-09-16 |publisher=The History Press |isbn=978-0-7524-7055-9 |language=en}}</ref>]]During the [[First World War]], Attingham was owned by the 8th Lord Berwick who let the property to the Dutch-American [[Harry Van Bergen|Van Bergen]] family who encouraged the establishment of a hospital for wounded soldiers at Attingham. The hospital opened in October 1914 and by 1918 had 60 beds and an operating theatre. During the War, the 8th Lord Berwick served with the [[Shropshire Yeomanry]] and as a diplomat in Paris. Throughout the war years he corresponded with Teresa Hulton, daughter of the artist [[William Stokes Hulton]], whom he married in June 1919. During the war, Teresa Hulton had worked with Belgian refugees in London and as a Red Cross nurse in Italy.<ref>{{cite web|title=Attingham WWI Stories|url=http://attinghamww1stories.wordpress.com/|accessdate=1 August 2014}}</ref> The couple dedicated themselves to the renovation of the house, with Hulton taking on responsibility for the conservation of historic textiles.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Ponsonby |first=Margaret |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=2TsHDAAAQBAJ&dq=attingham+conservation&pg=PA143 |title=Faded and Threadbare Historic Textiles and their Role in Houses Open to the Public |date=2016-04-15 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1-317-13690-3 |pages=143 |language=en}}</ref> During the [[Second World War]], Edgbaston Church of England Girls' School was evacuated and lived in part of the house; it later hosted the [[Women's Auxiliary Air Force]].<ref name=":3" />

===Transfer to the National Trust===
In 1937, negotiations started with the National Trust, and it was donated to them in 1947 as a bequest in the will of the 8th Lord Berwick. His wishes stated that the house and estate should be curated as "a good example of Eighteenth Century Architecture with such contents in the principal rooms as a nobleman of that period would have had".<ref name="Douglas, p.13"/>

==Management under the National Trust==

===Attingham Trust and country house studies===
[[File:Attingham Park, inner courtyard.JPG|thumb|upright=0.75|The internal courtyard]]

Between 1948 and 1976, the [[Shropshire Adult Education College]] occupied the hall, run by [[Sir George Trevelyan, 4th Baronet|Sir George Trevelyan]].

In 1952, the [[Attingham Trust]] was set up by George Trevelyan and Helen Lowenthal, the purpose of the Attingham Trust being to offer American curators the opportunity to learn about British country houses. A summer school has been run by the Attingham Trust every year since 1952 and now takes in a diverse array of country houses around the United Kingdom including some National Trust properties. The Attingham name has since been used worldwide with the American Friends of the Attingham Trust being founded in 1962 in [[New York City]], and the Attingham Society being founded in 1985. The Attingham Society covers the whole world and alongside the American Friends its purpose is to keep its members in touch and the continued education and interest of British country houses.<ref>{{cite web|title=The Attingham Trust: About us|url=http://www.attinghamtrust.org/about-us//|work=The Attingham Trust|accessdate=28 April 2013}}</ref>

===Restoration and conservation===
Until the 1990s, most of Attingham was closed to the public and visitors could only enter a small number of rooms. From 2000 to 2016, the National Trust ran a research and conservation programme entitled ''Attingham Re-discovered'', where conservators worked in view of the public and rooms were re-displayed. Major projects as part of the restoration included replacement of the Picture Gallery's carpet, and the replacement of a secondary roof in 2012.<ref>Douglas, p.48-50</ref> In 2014, visitors were invited to participate in identifying outstanding conservation needs in the house.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Dillon |first1=C. |last2=Golfomitsou |first2=S. |last3=Storey |first3=C. |last4=Lithgow |first4=K. |date=2019-03-04 |title=A clear view: crowdsourcing conservation needs in historic houses using visitor-led photo surveys |url=https://doi.org/10.1080/09647775.2018.1520642 |journal=Museum Management and Curatorship |volume=34 |issue=2 |pages=144–165 |doi=10.1080/09647775.2018.1520642 |s2cid=149798868 |issn=0964-7775|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>Dillon, C. ''et al''., [https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Catherine-Dillon-2/publication/319376838_A_clean_sheet_A_bottom-up_and_mixed_methods_approach_to_understanding_visitors'_perceptions_of_dust_dirt_and_cleaning/links/5a54caf2a6fdcc51a61a5a91/A-clean-sheet-A-bottom-up-and-mixed-methods-approach-to-understanding-visitors-perceptions-of-dust-dirt-and-cleaning.pdf "Bottom‑up and Mixed‑Methods Approach to Understanding Visi‑tors’ Perceptions of Dust, Dirt and Cleaning"], ''ICOM‑CC 18th Triennial Conference Preprints (Copenhagen, 2017). Paris: International Council of Museums''. 2017.</ref>

==Estate buildings==
The estate has a [[walled garden]] and an [[orchard]], which grows fresh produce which is used on the estate in the tearooms, and sold to visitors. The walled garden is a rare Georgian survival; a restoration programme began in the 1990s, which led to a return to cultivation of 25% of the garden by 2008. The orchard contains 37 varieties of fruit trees.<ref>Douglas, p.32</ref>

Attingham is also the location of one of the two surviving [[Regency era|Regency]] bee houses in the country.<ref>Douglas, p.27</ref> The [[Attingham bee house]] dates to 1805, has a slate roof to keep the hives dry, and lattice work to enable bees to freely fly in and out.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Foy |first=Karen |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-vtsBQAAQBAJ&dq=attingham+kitchen&pg=PA32 |title=Life in the Victorian Kitchen: Culinary Secrets and Servants' Stories |date=2014-09-30 |publisher=Pen and Sword |isbn=978-1-78303-639-4 |pages=32 |language=en}}</ref>
[[File:Stable_block,_Attingham_Park_-_geograph.org.uk_-_1604643.jpg|thumb|Stable block, Attingham Park - looking towards driveway]]
Attingham's stables were purpose-built for the first Lord Berwick at the same time as the house. Designed by Steuart, they have pyramidal ornamentation and were purposefully sited on the approach to the house, as a demonstration of taste and wealth.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Newman |first1=John |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=3Zqbit3opjQC&dq=attingham+stables&pg=PA52 |title=Shropshire |last2=Pevsner |first2=Nikolaus |last3=Watson |first3=Gavin |date=2006-01-01 |publisher=Yale University Press |isbn=978-0-300-12083-7 |pages=52 |language=en}}</ref>

==Parkland==
The Estate comprises roughly {{convert|4,000|acres}}, but during the early 1800s extended to twice that amount at {{convert|8,000|acres}}.<ref>Douglas, p.40</ref> The extensive {{convert|640|acres}} of parkland and gardens at Attingham have a Grade II* Listed status.

The park was landscaped by [[Humphry Repton]] and includes [[woodland]]s and a [[Medieval deer park|deer park]]. As of 2018, around 180 [[fallow deer]] lived in the park, with number maintained through an annual cull.<ref>Douglas, p.44</ref>

[[File:Tern seen from the Weir - geograph.org.uk - 26738.jpg|thumb|Tern seen from the Weir]]The [[River Tern]], which flows through the centre of the estate, joins the larger [[River Severn]] at the confluence just south of the Tern Bridge.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Black |first=Jeremy |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=HSgPEAAAQBAJ&dq=attingham+weir+repton&pg=PA53 |title=England in the Age of Austen |date=2021 |publisher=Indiana University Press |isbn=978-0-253-05194-3 |pages=53 |language=en}}</ref> The rivers were also used by the estate, with ironworks on the Tern that enhanced family fortune in the 1700s.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Rowley |first=Trevor |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=hAMhAAAAMAAJ&q=attingham+ironworks |title=The Landscape of the Welsh Marches |date=1986 |publisher=M. Joseph |isbn=978-0-7181-2347-5 |language=en}}</ref> Fish from the rivers were an important resource, both for food and for recreation.<ref>Douglas, p.41</ref>

The park is a designated [[Site of Special Scientific Interest]] (SSSI) due to it being home to many rare species of [[invertebrates]]. There are seven units of SSSI around the park totalling to {{convert|470|acres}}, nearly three-quarters of the entire estate. The amount of deadwood left by fallen trees around the parkland makes it the perfect habitat for a variety of different species, primarily beetles. Several of these beetle species are adapted to the ecology of ancient trees, including the flat bark beetle, ''[[Notolaemus unifasciatus]],'' and the silken fungus beetle, ''[[Atomaria barani]].''<ref>{{cite web|title=Site of Special Scientific Interest information|url=https://necmsi.esdm.co.uk/PDFsForWeb/Citation/2000402.pdf|work=Natural England|access-date=14 March 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170316024230/https://necmsi.esdm.co.uk/PDFsForWeb/Citation/2000402.pdf|archive-date=16 March 2017|url-status=dead}}</ref> In 2005 a survey of the flora of the park was undertaken by Shropshire Botanical Society, which identified 68 species in the park, that had not been recorded on the last survey undertaken 1969–72. Drainage of the site had an impact on several species, with the loss of ''[[Alopecurus aequalis]]'', ''[[Rumex maritimus]]'' and ''[[Veronica scutellata]],'' as well as the additions of dry heathland species such as ''[[Veronica officinalis]]'' and ''[[Ulex europaeus]].<ref>Whild, Sarah, et al. [http://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/viewdoc/download?doi=10.1.1.662.2814&rep=rep1&type=pdf "New Flora of Attingham Park."] (2005).</ref>''

==Cronkhill==
{{main|Cronkhill}}
The nearby Italianate villa of Cronkhill on the estate is an important pioneer of this style in England and was designed by the architect, John Nash. It was designed for the 2nd Lord Berwick, around the same time as the Picture Gallery, and the first person to live in it was his land agent, Francis Walford.<ref>"A generous gesture for a friend" according to the National Trust; other sources imply that Walford was Nash's patron in this project.</ref> Cronkhill is located on the wider estate, on a hillside overlooking the River Severn valley and the Wrekin hill. The villa is owned by the National Trust and is privately tenanted. It is open to visitors a few days of the year.<ref>{{cite web |title=Attingham Park Estate Cronkhill |url=http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/attingham-park-cronkhill/ |work=National Trust |accessdate=17 March 2013}}</ref>

2486352.title: Benthall Hall
2486352.extract:
Benthall Hall is a 16th-century English country house in Benthall in the town of Broseley, Shropshire, England, and a few miles from the historic Ironbridge Gorge. It retains much of its fine oak interior, and an elaborate 17th-century staircase. It is still occupied by the Benthall family, but has been owned by the National Trust since 1958, and is open to the public every Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Saturday, Sunday and Bank Holiday Monday (February – October).
The Hall was built around 1580, probably on the site of an earlier 12th-century medieval manor and manor house. During the Civil War it was garrisoned, and was a site of several skirmishes.
The garden is largely the product of two tenants. George Maw (1832–1912), local pottery manufacturer and crocus enthusiast developed the garden from around 1865 onwards. Subsequently, the Victorian era Romantic painter and sculptor Robert Bateman (1842–1922), who was the son of a famous horticulturalist, added the rockeries and terraces of the current garden.
The Restoration era church of St. Bartholomew, built 1667–68, stands close by the Hall. The Shropshire Way, a waymarked long-distance footpath, passes through the extensive woodland that lies to the north, between the estate and the River Severn.
In the film Enola Holmes, Benthall Hall was used for the exterior shots of the Holmes' family estate.

6304981.title: Cronkhill
6304981.extract:
Cronkhill, Atcham, Shropshire, designed by John Nash, is "the earliest Italianate villa in England".
Drawing on influences from the Italian Campagna and the Picturesque, including the art of Claude Lorrain, it began an architectural style that was hugely influential in England in the first half of the nineteenth century. Major examples include Trentham Park and Osborne House. Nash's "most original building", it is Grade I listed.

'''Cronkhill''', [[Atcham]], [[Shropshire]], designed by [[John Nash (architect)|John Nash]], is "the earliest [[Italianate architecture|Italianate]] villa in England".<ref name=NHLE>{{NHLE|num=1176915|desc=Cronkhill|access-date=12 March 2017|mode=cs2}}</ref>

Drawing on influences from the [[Roman Campagna|Italian Campagna]] and the [[Picturesque]], including the art of [[Claude Lorrain]], it began an architectural style that was hugely influential in England in the first half of the nineteenth century. Major examples include [[Trentham Estate|Trentham Park]] and [[Osborne House]]. Nash's "most original building",{{sfn|Greeves|p=111}} it is [[Listed building#England and Wales|Grade I listed]].<ref name=NHLE/>

==History==
The house was designed by [[John Nash (architect)|John Nash]] in 1802<ref>A design was exhibited at the [[Royal Academy]], 1802, as a "house near Shrewsbury" (Howard Colvin).</ref> for Francis Walford.{{sfn|Newman & Pevsner|p=240-1}} Walford was a friend of [[Thomas Noel Hill, 2nd Baron Berwick]], of nearby [[Attingham Park]], and the agent for Berwick's Attingham estates.{{sfn|Newman & Pevsner|p=240-1}} Michael Mansbridge considers that the design was "almost certainly inspired" by [[Claude Lorrain]]'s painting "Landscape near Rome with a View of the [[Ponte Molle]]".{{Sfn|Mansbridge|p=101}} Lord Berwick was the owner of two Claude landscapes.{{sfn|Greeves|p=111}}  Walford lived at Cronkhill, managing Lord Berwick's Attingham interests, until their relationship ended acrimoniously in 1828, when Walford left the house.<ref name="nationaltrust1">{{cite web|url=http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/attingham-park-estate-cronkhill/features/delve-into-the-history-of-cronkhill-on-the-attingham-estate |title=Delve into the history of Cronkhill on the Attingham estate |publisher=National Trust |accessdate=2016-07-11}}</ref> It was then occupied by members of the Berwick family, often when Attingham Park was let, until their final return to Attingham in the 1920s.<ref name="nationaltrust1"/> Cronkhill, along with Attingham Park, was gifted to the [[National Trust]] in the post-war period.{{sfn|Newman & Pevsner|p=240-1}} As a tenanted property, it is only open to the public on a limited number of days each year.<ref>National Trust, [https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/visit/shropshire-staffordshire/attingham-park-estate-cronkhill/visiting-cronkhill Visiting Cronkhill], accessed on 26 January 2026</ref>

==Architecture==
The body of the house is a rectangular two-storey block,{{sfn|Newman & Pevsner|p=240-1}} with a circular, three-storey, tower to the north and a square, three-storey, tower to the west.<ref name=NHLE/> A [[loggia]] links the two towers.<ref name=NHLE/> The walls are now white [[stucco]],{{sfn|Newman & Pevsner|p=240-1}} although the colour may originally have been designed to imitate [[ashlar]].{{sfn|Newman & Pevsner|p=240-1}} Internally, the main reception rooms are simply decorated, comprising a drawing room in the round tower, a library in the square tower and a dining room in the body of the house.{{sfn|Greeves|p=111}} Although influential, the house, as with much of Nash's work, was subject to criticism, Davis describing the round tower as "merely a dramatic architectural trick, (containing neither) a circular staircase, nor even one circular room".{{sfn|Davis|p=23}} In 2016, the National Trust undertook a major restoration of the house to "restore Cronkhill's appearance back to Nash's original design."<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/attingham-park-estate-cronkhill/features/open-days-at-cronkhill |title=Open days at Cronkhill |publisher=National Trust |accessdate=2016-07-11}}</ref>

14893052.title: Morville Hall
14893052.extract:
Morville Hall is a grade I listed country house and gardens in the care of the National Trust in the county of Shropshire, England, United Kingdom.
Morville Hall is located at the junction of the A458 road and the B4368 road, three miles outside the market town of Bridgnorth.
It is a large grey stone mansion with projecting wings, originally built in  two storeys in the 16th-century but increased to three as part of an 18th-century enlargement. Once part of the Aldenham estate, the house stands on the site of the abandoned Morville Priory. 
Morville Hall was originally an Elizabethan country house dating from 1546, at the time the site was acquired by Roger Smyth, who married into the local Cressett family. It was enlarged and expanded around 1750 by Arthur Weaver, MP for Bridgnorth.
The gardens incorporate the Dower house Gardens and features such as a Cloister garden and an Elizabethan knot garden. The gardens project was a 15-year project for Katherine Swift who wanted to show how gardens have developed and evolved throughout history. Each section of her garden relates to a previous occupant of the Hall, from the Elizabethan Smyths through to the 18th century Weavers, and finally to the seven Victorian age Warren sisters who lived on in the house long after the death of their father, the last one, Juliana, dying in the 1920s.

[[File:Morville Hall - geograph.org.uk - 21434.jpg|thumb|Morville Hall]]{{More citations needed|date=July 2022}}
'''Morville Hall''' is a grade I listed [[English country house|country house]] and gardens in the care of the [[National Trust]] in the county of [[Shropshire]], England, United Kingdom.

Morville Hall is located at the junction of the [[A458 road]] and the B4368 road, three miles outside the [[market town]] of [[Bridgnorth]].

It is a large grey stone mansion with projecting wings, originally built in  two storeys in the 16th-century but increased to three as part of an 18th-century enlargement. Once part of the [[Aldenham Park, Morville|Aldenham]] estate, the house stands on the site of the abandoned [[Morville Priory]]. <ref> {{cite web|url = http://www.britishlistedbuildings.co.uk/en-254759-morville-hall-morville-| title= Morville Hall, Morville|publisher= British Listed Buildings|accessdate= 27 January 2014}} </ref>

Morville Hall was originally an [[Elizabethan]] country house dating from 1546, at the time the site was acquired by Roger Smyth, who married into the local Cressett family. It was enlarged and expanded around 1750 by [[Arthur Weaver (MP)|Arthur Weaver]], MP for [[Bridgnorth (UK Parliament constituency)|Bridgnorth]].

The gardens incorporate the [[Dower house]] Gardens and features such as a Cloister garden and an Elizabethan [[knot garden]]. The gardens project was a 15-year project for Katherine Swift who wanted to show how gardens have developed and evolved throughout history. Each section of her garden relates to a previous occupant of the Hall, from the Elizabethan Smyths through to the 18th century Weavers, and finally to the seven Victorian age Warren sisters who lived on in the house long after the death of their father, the last one, Juliana, dying in the 1920s. 

==National Trust and closure to the public==

The property has belonged to the [[National Trust]] since 1965.<ref>{{cite web|url = http://www.parksandgardens.org/places-and-people/site/5978?preview=1|title= Morville Hall, Morville, Shropshire, England-Record Id: 5978|publisher= ParksandGardens.org|accessdate = 27 January 2014}} </ref> From 2017, it was leased to a private tenant who was forced to leave the lease early due to two major water tank leaks. The tenant documented the troubles on an Instagram account called The Tenants of Morville Hall, a play on the title of the Bronte novel, The Tenant of Wildfell Hall. The house and adjoining apartments have been empty for some time. The building remains closed and unused as of 2025.<ref>{{cite web|url = https://www.britainexpress.com/attractions.htm?attraction=3666 | title=Morville Hall | History & Visiting Information }}</ref> It has not been open to the public since the [[COVID-19 pandemic|global pandemic of 2019]].  Two barn conversions on the Morville estate, also managed by the National Trust, are available to rent as accommodation.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/holidays/shropshire-staffordshire/1-morville-barn |title=1 Morville Barn Shropshire }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/holidays/shropshire-staffordshire/2-morville-barn |title=2 Morville Barn Shropshire }}</ref>

14893354.extract:

Dudmaston Hall is located near the village of Quatt, a few miles south of the market town of Bridgnorth, just off the A442 road.
