({{IPAc-en|audio=en-uk-shrewsbury-rp.ogg|ˈ|ʃ|r|oʊ|z|b|r|i}} {{respell|SHROHZ|bree}}, {{IPAc-en|also|audio=en-uk-shrewsbury.ogg|ˈ|ʃ|r|uː|z|-}} {{respell|SHROOZ|-}}){{cite book |last=Room |first=Adrian |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=M1JIPAN-eJ4C&q=Origin%20of%20the%20name%20Shrewsbury&pg=PA345 |title=Placenames of the World: Origins And Meanings of the Names for 6,600 Countries, Cities, Territories, Natural Features And Historic Sites |publisher=[[McFarland & Company|McFarland]] |year=2006 |isbn=0786422483 |location=[[Stamford, Lincolnshire|Stamford]] |page=345}}{{cite book |title=Oxford Dictionary of English |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=0-19-861057-2 |edition=2nd edition (revised) |at=loc. 647563 of 801946}} is a [[market town]] and [[civil parish]] in [[Shropshire (district)|Shropshire]], England. It is sited on the [[River Severn]], {{convert|33|miles|km}} northwest of [[Wolverhampton]], {{convert|15|miles|km}} west of [[Telford]], {{convert|31|miles|km}} southeast of [[Wrexham]] and {{convert|53|miles|km}} north of [[Hereford]]. At the [[2021–2022 United Kingdom censuses|2021 census]], the parish had a population of 76,782.{{cite web |title=Shrewsbury Parish in West Midlands |url=https://www.citypopulation.de/en/uk/westmidlands/admin/shropshire/E04011358__shrewsbury/ |access-date=24 December 2022 |publisher=City Population}} It is the [[county town]] of the ceremonial county of [[Shropshire]]. Shrewsbury has [[Anglo-Saxon]] roots and institutions whose foundations, dating from that time, represent a cultural continuity possibly going back as far as the 8th century.{{Cite web |title=Colleges of secular canons: Shrewsbury {{!}} British History Online |url=https://www.british-history.ac.uk/vch/salop/vol2/pp114-123#fnn18 |access-date=2023-07-16 |website=british-history.ac.uk}}{{Harvnb|Newman|Pevsner|Watson|2006|p=526}} The centre has a largely undisturbed [[medieval]] street plan and over 660 [[Listed buildings in Shrewsbury|listed buildings]],{{Cite web |title=About Shrewsbury {{!}} Original Shrewsbury |url=https://originalshrewsbury.co.uk/about |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071101010837/https://originalshrewsbury.co.uk/about |archive-date=1 November 2007 |access-date=14 June 2018 |publisher=Enjoy England |df=dmy-all}} including several examples of [[timber framing]] from the 15th and 16th centuries. [[Shrewsbury Castle]], a red [[sandstone]] fortification, and [[Shrewsbury Abbey]], were founded in 1074 and 1083 respectively by the [[Normans|Norman]] [[Earl of Shrewsbury]], [[Roger de Montgomery]]. The town is the birthplace of the naturalist [[Charles Darwin]].{{Cite web |title=Charles Darwin: His Life, Work and Shrewsbury {{!}} Original Shrewsbury |url=https://originalshrewsbury.co.uk/birthplace-charles-darwin-shrewsbury |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180614144322/https://originalshrewsbury.co.uk/birthplace-charles-darwin-shrewsbury |archive-date=14 June 2018 |access-date=2018-06-14 |website=originalshrewsbury.co.uk |language=en}} It has had a role in nurturing aspects of English culture, including [[drama]],{{Cite web |title="Nigel Hinton Nigel's Notes on Shrewsbury Mystery Plays". |url=http://www.nigelhinton.co.uk |access-date=11 August 2020}} [[ballet]], [[dance]]{{Cite web |title=John Weaver {{!}} British dancer {{!}} Encyclopædia Britannica |url=https://www.britannica.com/biography/John-Weaver |access-date=2023-03-11 |website=britannica.com |language=en}} and [[pantomime]]. Located {{convert|9|mi}} east of the [[England–Wales border]], Shrewsbury serves as the commercial centre for Shropshire and parts of mid-Wales, with a retail output of over £299 million per year and light industry and distribution centres, such as [[Battlefield Enterprise Park]], on the outskirts. The [[A5 road (Great Britain)|A5]] and [[A49 road|A49]] [[trunk road]]s come together as the town's by-pass and five railway lines meet at [[Shrewsbury railway station]]. == Toponymy == The name comes from [[Old English]] ''{{lang|ang|Scrobbesburh}}'' ([[dative]] ''{{lang|ang|Scrobbesbyrig}}''), meaning either "Scrobb's fort" or "the fortified place of the scrubland". The surrounding county was known as {{lang|ang|Scrobbesbyrigscir}} or simply {{lang|ang|Scrobscir}}, a name that later became ''Shropshire''. The [[Anglo-Normans|Normans]], who had trouble pronouncing the initial consonant cluster, referred to the town as ''Salopesberie'' and the county as ''Salopescira'', hence the abbreviation ''Salop''.{{cite book|last=Ekwall|first=Eilert|title=The Concise Oxford Dictionary of English Place-Names|date=1947|edition=3rd|location=Oxford|publisher=Clarendon Press|pages=400 f|url=https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.184064/page/n446}}{{cite book|title=The Cambridge Dictionary of English Place-Names|date=2010|editor-last=Watts|editor-first=Victor|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-0-521-16855-7|pages=548 f|url=https://archive.org/details/cambridgediction0000unse_y6u4/page/548}} The town's name can be pronounced as either {{IPAc-en|audio=en-uk-shrewsbury-rp.ogg|ˈ|ʃ|r|oʊ|z|b|ər|i}} ({{respell|SHROHZ|bər|ee}}) or {{IPAc-en|audio=en-uk-shrewsbury.ogg|ˈ|ʃ|r|uː|z|b|ər|i}} ({{respell|SHROOZ|bər|ee}}), the correct pronunciation being a matter of longstanding debate.{{cite news |url= https://www.shropshirestar.com/pictures/2008/02/06/shroosbury-v-shrowsbury/|title='Shroosbury' v 'Shrowsbury' |publisher= [[MNA Media]] |date= 6 February 2008 |newspaper=[[Shropshire Star]] |access-date=6 March 2013 |location=Shrewsbury |page=1}}{{cite web |title=Shrowsbury or Shroosbury - the results are in |url=https://www.shropshirestar.com/news/2015/06/27/shrowsbury-or-shroosbury-the-results-are-in/ |publisher=Shropshire Star |access-date=25 December 2022 |date=27 June 2015}} ==History== ===Prehistory=== {{main|History of Shrewsbury}} Evidence of [[Neolithic]] occupation of a religious form dating back before 2,000 BC, was discovered in 2017 in the grounds of the medieval Church of the Holy Fathers in [[Sutton Farm]], making it Britain's oldest place of worship.{{Cite web |date=18 May 2017 |title=Shropshire church found to be UK's oldest sacred site still in use |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2017/05/18/shropshire-church-found-uks-oldest-sacred-site/ |publisher=The Telegraph}} An Early [[Bronze Age]] urned burial was excavated at Crowmeole in 2015.{{Cite journal |last1=Bradley |first1=R. |last2=Evans |first2=J. |last3=Quinn |first3=P. |date=2019 |title=An Early Bronze Age Urned Burial from Crowmeole, Shrewsbury, Shropshire |url=https://shropshirearchaeologyhistory.org/publications/transactions-2/ |journal=Transactions of the Shropshire Archaeological and Historical Society |volume=94 |pages=77–96}} An [[Iron Age]] double [[ring ditch]] has been excavated at [[Meole Brace]]. Amongst other finds, parts of an Iron Age sword and scabbard were recovered.{{Cite web |title=Library |url=https://archaeologydataservice.ac.uk/library/browse/issue.xhtml?recordId=1130009&recordType=GreyLitSeries |access-date=2023-04-20 |website=archaeologydataservice.ac.uk |language=en}}{{Cite journal |last=Bain |first=Kate |title=A Late Iron Age and Early Romano-British Enclosure at Meole Brace, Shrewsbury |url=https://www.academia.edu/6100814 |journal=Transactions of the Shropshire Historical and Archaeological Society}} === Roman and Saxon === At Meole Brace, an extensive roadside settlement along the line of the Roman military road connecting [[Viroconium Cornoviorum]] and [[Caersws]] was uncovered,{{cite web |last1=Bain |first1=Kate |title=Meole Brace, Shrewsbury Archaeological Investigations 2005-6 Post-Excavation Assessment |url=https://archaeologydataservice.ac.uk/archiveDS/archiveDownload?t=arch-502-1/dissemination/pdf/birmingh2-49879_1.pdf |website=Archaeology Data Service|date=March 2007 |access-date=1 September 2023}} with evidence of trading of [[amphora]]e and [[mortaria]].{{Cite web |title=ASPROM: Wroxeter and its hinterland, by R. H. White |url=http://www.asprom.org/resources/Wroxeter/WroxeterRHW.html |access-date=2023-04-20 |website=Asprom.org}} A major discovery was the finding of the [[Shrewsbury Hoard]] of more than 9000 Roman coins in a field near the town in 2009.{{Cite web |last=Pett |first=Daniel |date=2009-09-07 |title=Recent discovery of a Roman Coin Hoard in the Shrewsbury Area |url=http://finds.org.uk/blogs/centralunit/2009/09/07/recent-discovery-of-a-roman-coin-hoard-in-the-shrewsbury-area/ |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120306021611/http://finds.org.uk/blogs/centralunit/2009/09/07/recent-discovery-of-a-roman-coin-hoard-in-the-shrewsbury-area/ |archive-date=2012-03-06 |access-date=2010-07-09 |publisher=[[Portable Antiquities Scheme]]}}{{Cite web |last=Reavill |first=Peter |date=2011-10-25 |title=Inquest into largest coin hoard from Shropshire |url=https://finds.org.uk/news/story/220 |access-date=2017-02-12 |publisher=[[Portable Antiquities Scheme]]}} It is claimed that [[Pengwern]], sometime capital of the [[Kingdom of Powys]] (itself established by the 440s), was at Shrewsbury,{{Cite web |date=2023-11-12 |title=Shrewsbury {{!}} England, Map, & History {{!}} Britannica |url=https://www.britannica.com/place/Shrewsbury-England |access-date=2023-11-19 |website=Britannica.com |language=en}} and it has been said in Parliament that the town was founded by the late 600s,{{Cite web |title=Shrewsbury And Atcham Borough Council Bill Hl - Hansard - UK Parliament |url=https://hansard.parliament.uk/Lords/1982-02-25/debates/466a9a79-407f-46db-9466-3f55a3862f62/ShrewsburyAndAtchamBoroughCouncilBillHl?highlight=unprecedented |access-date=2025-02-23 |website=hansard.parliament.uk |language=en}} the basis for this likely the [[Anglo-Saxon Chronicle|Anglo-Saxon Chronicle's]] account of the 584 battle at Fethanleag, where [[Ceawlin]] defeated the Britons and captured numerous settlements including possibly Uriconium, which sets the historical context for the first likely textual mention of Shrewsbury in the poetry of the British prince [[Llywarch Hen]], who mourned the destruction of Uriconium. Llywarch Hen's presence at the court of Prince [[Cynddylan]] at Pengwern, understood as the British name for Shrewsbury, implies the town's existence during this period.{{Cite book |last=Auden |first=Thomas |url=https://archive.org/details/shrewsburyhistor00audeuoft/page/n23/mode/2up |title=Shrewsbury, a historical and topographical account of the town |date=1905 |publisher=London : Methuen |others=Robarts - University of Toronto}} There is consistent tradition that the town was "founded in the 5th century, on occasion of the decay of the Roman [[Uriconium]]." Historian John Wacher suggests that Shrewsbury may have been refortified by refugees fleeing an outbreak of a plague in Viroconium around this time.{{cite book |last1=Wacher |first1=John |title=The Towns of Roman Britain |date=1976 |publisher=BookClub Associates |location=London |page=374}} Context for the nature of early Medieval period life in the wider district can be found in archaeological evidence on the nearby [[Attingham Park|Attingham estate]], where foundations of two rare 25m-long Anglo-Saxon timber halls dating to around 650 AD have been discovered, highlighting a significant and well-resourced Anglo-Saxon community in the region.{{Cite web |last=Neal |first=Toby |date=2018-02-07 |title=Rare Saxon hall find at Attingham excites the experts |url=https://www.shropshirestar.com/news/2018/02/08/rare-saxon-hall-find-excites-the-experts/ |access-date=2025-03-31 |website=Shropshirestar.com |language=en}} The first attested association of Pengwern with Shrewsbury is mentioned by [[Giraldus Cambrensis]] in the 12th century. Alternative suggestions as to the location of Pengwern include [[Whittington Castle]] near [[Oswestry]],{{cite web|title=Whittington Castle|url=http://www.castlewales.com/whittng.html|publisher=Castle Wales}} and Berth, a hillfort near [[Baschurch]]. The ''Historia Divae Monacellae'', composed in the 14th or 15th century, says that [[Brochwel Ysgithrog]], the 6th-century king of Powis, had a palace at Shrewsbury that became the site of the foundation of St Chad.{{Cite web|title=History of St Monacella, in Montgomeryshire collections relating to Montgomeryshire and its borders. {{!}} Vol. 82 {{!}} 1994 {{!}} Welsh Journals - The National Library of Wales|url=https://journals.library.wales/view/1264487/1271085/44#?xywh=-3913%2C51%2C10843%2C4527|access-date=2023-08-06 |website=journals.library.wales |language=en}}[[File:Æthelflæd as depicted in the cartulary of Abingdon Abbey.png|thumb|upright|[[Æthelflæd]], 'Lady of the Mercians']] In the late 8th century, it is said that [[Offa]] took the town for the [[Mercia]]ns in 778,{{Cite book |last=Shipley |first=John |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=YZOSDwAAQBAJ&pg=PT18 |title=Secret Shrewsbury |publisher=Amberley Publishing |year=2019 |isbn=978-1445678450}}{{efn|the [[Annales Cambriae]] merely refers to "The devastation of the South Britons by Offa." in that year.{{cite web |last1=Ingram |first1=James |title=Annales Cambrae |url=https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Annals_of_Wales_A#cite_ref-17 |website=Wikisource |access-date=27 August 2023}}}} and he is associated by some sources with establishing the town's first church and dedicating it to [[St Chad's Church, Shrewsbury|St Chad]]. If so, then there may have been an ecclesiastical foundation in the town within a century of the death of [[Chad of Mercia]].{{Cite web |title=A History of the County of Shropshire {{!}} British History Online |url=https://www.british-history.ac.uk/vch/salop/vol2 |access-date=2023-08-06 |website=British-history.ac.uk}} Shrewsbury remained part of the Mercian kingdom until its incorporation into the larger realm of England under Egbert in the first half of the ninth century. During the subsequent Saxon period, historical records of the town are scarce.{{Cite book |last=Auden |first=Thomas |url=https://archive.org/details/shrewsburyhistor00audeuoft/page/n27/mode/2up |title=Shrewsbury, a historical and topographical account of the town |date=1905 |publisher=London : Methuen |others=Robarts - University of Toronto}} Early in the tenth century [[Athelstan]] made a law to secure uniformity of coinage throughout his dominion, and this enactment specified the number of moneyers in the principal towns. Shrewsbury possessed one such moneyer, proving that while it reached a certain point of importance it did not rank among towns of the first class (this number was later raised to three in the reign of [[Edward the Confessor]]; and all through the period from Athelstan to [[Henry III of England|Henry III]], the Shrewsbury mint was busy).{{cite book |last=Shipley |first=John |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=YZOSDwAAQBAJ&pg=PT18 |title=Secret Shrewsbury |publisher=Amberley Publishing |year=2019 |isbn=978-1445678450}}{{Cite web |last=Lambert |first=Tim |title=Saxon and Medieval Shrewsbury |url=http://www.localhistories.org/shrewsbury.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120315203401/http://www.localhistories.org/shrewsbury.html |archive-date=15 March 2012 |website=A Short History of Shrewsbury, Shropshire, England |publisher=A World History Encyclopaedia |df=dmy-all}} Viking raiders from the north were reaching as far south as [[Bridgnorth]] by 910, and in 914,{{sfnm|1a1=Costambeys|1y=2004a|2a1=Stenton|2y=1971|2pp=325–327}}{{efn|Tim Clarkson's biography has a detailed discussion of Æthelflæd' burhs.{{sfn|Clarkson|2018}} }} [[Æthelflæd]], daughter of [[Alfred the Great]] and known as the Lady of the Mercians, fortified Shrewsbury, along with [[Hereford]] and two other fortresses, at ''Scergeat'' (a currently unknown location) and ''Weardbyrig'' (thought to be [[Whitchurch, Shropshire|Whitchurch]],{{Cite book |last=Matthew Blake and Andrew Sargent |title='For the Protection of all the People': Æthelflæd and her Burhs in Northwest Mercia |publisher=Keele University |year=2018}} which would make sense given the strategic importance of the Roman Road link via the [[Via Devana]]). Recent excavations at Shrewsbury Castle, funded by the Castle Studies Trust, revealed a massive defensive ditch surrounding the Norman motte and evidence of fortified presence on the castle site, predating the Norman invasion.{{Cite web |date=2021-09-07 |title=Nigel Baker – Castle Studies Trust Blog |url=https://castlestudiestrust.org/blog/author/nigel-baker/ |access-date=2025-03-31 |language=en-GB}} [[File:St Alkmund sarcophagus .jpg|thumb|St Alkmund's sarcophagus, now at [[Derby Museum and Art Gallery]], almost certainly made as a shrine for the body of St. Alkmund soon after he was killed in AD 800. Pilgrims would have worshipped at it. The relics were in Shrewsbury from the early 900s CE to about 1145.]] Some time before 918,{{Cite journal |last=Bowen |first=James |date=2015 |title=Review of 'Victoria County History: Shropshire VI Shrewsbury' |journal=Reviews in History |doi=10.14296/rih/2014/1754 |doi-broken-date=18 July 2025 |issn=1749-8155|doi-access=free }} the relics of [[Alkmund of Derby|St Alkmund]] were translated to Shrewsbury and back to Shropshire from [[Derby]], this was probably the work of Æthelflæd.{{cite book |last=Meijns |first=Brigitte |title=England and the Continent in the Tenth Century |publisher=Brepols |year=2010 |isbn=9782503532080 |editor1-last=Rollason |editor1-first=David |location=Turnhout, Belgium |page=476 |chapter=The Policy on Relic Translations of Baldwin II of Flanders (879–918), Edward of Wessex (899–924), and Æthelflæd of Mercia (d.924): A Key to Anglo-Flemish Relations |author-link=Brigitte Meijns |editor2-last=Leyser |editor2-first=Conrad |editor3-last=Williams |editor3-first=Hannah}} This return to Shropshire move followed Alkmund's initial burial in Shropshire after his death in 800.{{Cite web |title=BBC - Derby - Faith - St Alkmund: Patron Saint of Derby |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/derby/content/articles/2006/05/25/stalkmund_feature.shtml |access-date=2025-03-31 |website=Bbc.co.uk}} Later, [[Edgar, King of England|King Edgar]] (957–75) established a collegiate church with a dean and 10 prebendaries at St Alkmund's Church, it was a [[Royal peculiar]], and subsequently, it became the property of [[Lilleshall Abbey]] in about 1145, when the relics were retranslated back to Derby.''Saint Alkmund, His Life, Murder and Cults'', Derek & Marion Taulbut, 1998 [[File:Ethelred the Unready.jpg|thumb|upright|Traditional accounts recount that during the devastating Danish invasion of 1006, King Æthelred II chose to withdraw to his royal seat in Shrewsbury.]] Following Æthelflæd's fortification of Shrewsbury, the town largely avoided the devastating wave of the Danish invasions that impacted other parts of England. This immunity, which extended across Shropshire, is notable despite evidence of Danish ships on the River Severn (suggested by the name Danesford near Bridgnorth) and a recorded [[Battle of Buttington|Danish defeat at Buttington]] (near Welshpool) in 894. The protection of the region is mainly attributed to [[Æthelred, Lord of the Mercians|Æthelred]], the ealdorman of Mercia appointed by Alfred, and Æthelflæd herself. Subsequently, during the tenth century, Shrewsbury appears to have experienced a period of relative stability.{{Cite book |last=Auden |first=Thomas |url=https://archive.org/details/shrewsburyhistor00audeuoft/page/n29/mode/2up |title=Shrewsbury, a historical and topographical account of the town |date=1905 |publisher=London : Methuen |others=Robarts - University of Toronto}} An historical narrative, well established in the nineteenth century, asserts that during the devastating Danish invasion of 1006, [[Æthelred the Unready]] withdrew to his royal seat in Shrewsbury. In this account, the King experienced "great perplexity," reflecting the collapse of the national defense. This strategic withdrawal preceded the disastrous decision to pay the immense sum of £30,000 [[Danegeld]] in 1007 to halt the Danish advance.{{Cite book |last=Rimmer |first=Alfred |title=A History of Shrewsbury School from the Blakeway MSS, and many other sources |publisher=Simpkin Marshall and Co. |year=1889 |publication-date=1889}}{{efn|Stenton's ''Anglo-Saxon England'' in the Oxford History of England, makes no mention of AÆthelred retreating to Shrewsbury at this time.}} ===Norman=== [[File:The Shropshire Regimental museum at Shrewsbury Castle - geograph.org.uk - 4129824.jpg|thumb|alt=Red stone built castle with turret on the left and flowers lining the approach road|[[Shrewsbury Castle]], built at around 1074 by Roger de Montgomery]] [[Roger de Montgomery]] was given the town as a gift from [[William the Conqueror]] and was created Earl of Shrewsbury. He built at [[Shrewsbury Castle]] at around 1074,{{Cite web |title=Shrewsbury Castle and Shropshire Regimental Museum {{!}} Original Shrewsbury |url=https://originalshrewsbury.co.uk/visit/shrewsbury-castle-shropshire-regimental-museum |access-date=2018-06-14 |website=originalshrewsbury.co.uk |language=en |archive-date=14 June 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180614144348/https://originalshrewsbury.co.uk/visit/shrewsbury-castle-shropshire-regimental-museum |url-status=dead }} though there is evidence the location may have been a fortified site in the time of the Anglo-Saxons.{{Cite web |date=2019-11-27 |title=Anglo-Saxon pottery identified from Shrewsbury Castle dig |url=https://newsroom.shropshire.gov.uk/2019/11/anglo-saxon-pottery/ |access-date=2023-07-20 |website=Shropshire Council Newsroom |language=en-GB}} This construction work destroyed 51 properties, and it is thought much of this hard labour was forced on local workers.{{Cite web |title=Shrewsbury's Favourite Lifestyle Magazine {{!}} My Shrewsbury |url=https://www.myshrewsbury.co.uk/index.php/ |access-date=2025-03-31 |website=Myshrewsbury.co.uk |language=en}} [[File:Shrewsbury Abbey Exterior, Shropshire, UK - Diliff.jpg|thumb|Shrewsbury Abbey, founded 1083]] He also founded [[Shrewsbury Abbey]] as a [[Benedictine]] [[monastery]] in 1083.{{Cite web |title=Shrewsbury Abbey {{!}} Original Shrewsbury |url=https://originalshrewsbury.co.uk/visit/shrewsbury-abbey |access-date=2018-06-14 |website=originalshrewsbury.co.uk |language=en}} The town's position just off Watling Street placed it within the [[Forest of Arden]], a thickly wooded area, unpenetrated by Roman roads and somewhat dangerous in medieval times, so that travellers would pray at [[Coughton, Warwickshire|Coughton]] before entering.{{Cite web |date=2012-02-08 |title=Forest of Arden |url=http://hearteng.110mb.com/arden.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120208130648/http://hearteng.110mb.com/arden.htm |archive-date=8 February 2012 |access-date=2023-07-08}} In 1102, [[Robert of Bellême, 3rd Earl of Shrewsbury]] was deposed and the title forfeited, as a consequence of him rebelling against [[Henry I of England|Henry I]] and joining the [[Robert Curthose|Duke of Normandy]]'s invasion of England in 1101. [[William Pantulf]], Lord of [[Wem]], assisted Henry in putting down the rebellion. To deal with the thickly wooded local forests, ideal for the concealment of archers, Pantulf brought in 6,000 foot soldiers to cut down trees and open up the roads.{{Cite book |last=Woodward |first=Iris |title=The Story of Wem |publisher=Wildings of Shrewsbury |year=1952 |pages=23–25}}{{Cite web |title=Imperial Gazetteer entry for Shrewsbury |url=http://www.visionofbritain.org.uk/descriptions/entry_page.jsp?text_id=934570&word=NULL |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121022153342/http://www.visionofbritain.org.uk/descriptions/entry_page.jsp?text_id=934570&word=NULL |archive-date=22 October 2012 |access-date=4 March 2008 |website=Visions of Britain |df=dmy-all}} Henry subsequently took the government of the town into his own hands and in 1116 the nobility of England did homage to [[William Adelin|William Ætheling]], Henry’s son, at Shrewsbury, and swore allegiance to his father.{{Cite web |title=The Stranger in Shrewsbury, by Thomas Howell |url=https://www.gutenberg.org/files/62274/62274-h/62274-h.htm |access-date=2023-07-20 |website=Gutenberg.org}} The early death of William Ætheling without issue led to the succession crisis, known in history as [[the Anarchy]], and during this period, in 1138, [[Stephen of England|King Stephen]] successfully besieged the town's castle held by [[William FitzAlan, Lord of Oswestry|William FitzAlan]] for the [[Empress Maud]].{{Cite web |title=Shrewsbury Castle|url=http://www.castlewales.com/shrwsbry.html |access-date=8 June 2018 |publisher=Castle Wales}} [[File:Prologue_life_of_St_Winifred.png|thumb|Part of the prologue of a life of St Winifred by [[Robert of Shrewsbury (died 1168)|Robert of Shrewsbury]] (Bodleian Mss. Laud c.94.)]] In 1138, the relics of [[St Winifred]] were brought to Shrewsbury from [[Gwytherin|Gwytheryn]],{{Cite web |last=Parsons |first=David |date=2016-09-19 |title=St Winifrede at Shrewsbury Cathedral – Seintiau |url=https://saints.wales/st-winifrede-at-shrewsbury-cathedral/ |access-date=2023-07-20 |language=en-US}} following their purchase by the [[Abbot of Shrewsbury]], the abbey being ready for consecration but having no relics prior to that time.{{Cite web |date=2021-04-02 |title=Saint Winefride (Gwenffrewi) |url=https://www.shrewsburyorthodox.com/local-saints/saint-winefride-gwenffrewi/ |access-date=2023-07-20 |website=Church of the 318 Holy Fathers}} The popularity of St Winifred grew in the 14th and 15th centuries and a new shrine for her relics was built in the late 1300s. Around this time the abbey illegally acquired the relics of [[St Beuno]], uncle of St Winifred, by stealing them. As a result the abbey was fined but allowed to keep the relics.{{Cite web |last=greencanticle.com |title=Green Canticle » St. Beuno |url=https://greencanticle.com/tag/st-beuno/ |access-date=2023-07-20 |website=greencanticle.com}} From 1155, during the reign of [[Henry II of England|Henry II]], there was a leper hospital dedicated to St Giles and associated with Shrewsbury Abbey. From the 1220s, there was also a general hospital dedicated to St John the Baptist.{{Cite web |title=Hospitals: Shrewsbury Pages 105-108 A History of the County of Shropshire: Volume 2. Originally published by Victoria County History, London, 1973. |url=https://www.british-history.ac.uk/vch/salop/vol2/pp105-108 |access-date=13 July 2020 |website=British History Online}} In January 1234, Prince [[Llywelyn ab Iorwerth]] of Wales and [[Richard Marshal, 3rd Earl of Pembroke]] burned down the town and laid siege to its castle.https://magnacarta800th.com/history-of-the-magna-carta/battles/restoring-royal-authority/. Retrieved 25 January 2024. [[File:Edward I - Westminster Abbey Sedilia.jpg|thumb|upright|Edward I summoned a Parliament to Shrewsbury]] In 1283, [[Edward I]] (whose military campaigns in Wales frequently brought him to Shropshire) summoned a parliament in Shrewsbury, later adjourned to [[Acton Burnell]],{{Cite web |title=Acton Burnell Castle |url=http://www.virtual-shropshire.co.uk/visitor_guide/acton_burnell_castle_guide.shtml |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071130164935/http://www.virtual-shropshire.co.uk/visitor_guide/acton_burnell_castle_guide.shtml |archive-date=30 November 2007 |access-date=28 November 2007 |publisher=Virtual Shropshire}} to try and condemn [[Dafydd ap Gruffydd]], last of the native Princes of Wales, to execution by hanging, drawing and quartering within the town after Dafydd was captured, ending his rebellion against the king.{{cite DWB| id=s-DAFY-APG-1283 |title=Dafydd ap Gruffydd (David III, died 1283), prince of Gwynedd |first= Thomas Jones|last=Pierce |date=1959}} It is thought this parliament met in the Abbey.{{Cite web |last=Leighton |first=W. A. (William Allport) |date=1850 |title=A guide, descriptive and historical, through the Town of Shrewsbury |url=https://www.gutenberg.org/files/62688/62688-h/62688-h.htm |access-date=2023-07-08 |language=en}} {{PD-notice}} This is often considered to be the first Parliament at which commoners were represented.{{Cite web |title=History of Acton Burnell Castle |url=https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/visit/places/acton-burnell-castle/history/ |access-date=2025-02-23 |website=English Heritage}} ===Middle Ages=== Shrewsbury was devastated by the [[Black Death]], which, records suggest, arrived in the spring of 1349.{{Cite book |last=Shipley |first=John |title=The A-Z of Curious Shropshire : Strange Stories of Mysteries, Crimes and Eccentrics. |date=2017 |publisher=The History Press |isbn=9780750983174 |quote="The Black Death arrives in Shropshire around the spring of 1349...."}} Examining the number of local church [[benefice]]s falling vacant due to death, 1349 alone saw twice as many vacancies as the previous ten years combined, suggesting a high death toll in Shrewsbury.{{Cite book |last=Gasquet |first=Francis A. |url=https://archive.org/details/blackdeathof1908gasq |title=The Black Death of 1348 and 1349 |date=1908 |publisher=George Bell & Sons |isbn=9781331933663 |edition=2nd |location=London |pages=[https://archive.org/details/blackdeathof1908gasq/page/166 166]–167}} "The Great Fire of Shrewsbury" took place in 1394: St Chad's church was consumed by an accidental fire, which spread to a great portion of the town, then chiefly consisting of timber houses with thatched roofs. The damage was so considerable that [[Richard II]] remitted the town's taxes for three years towards the repairs. [[File:The Westminster Portrait of Richard II of England (1390s).jpg|thumb|upright|[[Richard II]] also summoned a Parliament in the town]] In 1398, Richard II summoned a Great Parliament in the town, which is believed to have met in the Abbey; dubbed the "Revenge Parliament," it originally met in Westminster but was prorogued to Shrewsbury{{Cite web |title=Virtual Treasury |url=https://virtualtreasury.ie/archive-fever/in-search-of-the-mortimers |access-date=2025-02-23 |website=Virtual Treasury |language=en}} (he publicly proclaimed it an act of affection for the people of Shropshire). It was a turning point in Richard II's reign,{{Cite journal |last=EDWARDS |first=J. G. |date=1925 |title=The Parliamentary Committee of 1398 |url=https://doi.org/10.1093/ehr/xl.clix.321 |journal=The English Historical Review |volume=XL |issue=CLIX |pages=321–333 |doi=10.1093/ehr/xl.clix.321 |issn=0013-8266|url-access=subscription }} and sowed the seeds of his eventual downfall.{{Citation |last=Griffiths |first=John |title=S. R. Gardiner, a Student's History of England from the Earliest Times to 1885 (London: Longmans and Co., 1892), pp. 952–955. |date=2021-09-27 |work=Empire and Popular Culture |pages=176–178 |url=https://doi.org/10.4324/9781351024822-18 |access-date=2025-02-23 |place=London |publisher=Routledge |doi=10.4324/9781351024822-18 |isbn=978-1-351-02482-2|url-access=subscription }} This national drama played out against a backdrop of local controversy, as Shrewsbury itself grappled with its own internal power struggles and grievances against its ruling elite.{{Citation |last=Given-Wilson |first=Chris |title=Introduction |date=2013-01-01 |work=Chronicles of the Revolution, 1397–1400 |pages=1–52 |url=https://www.manchesterhive.com/display/9781526112859/9781526112859.00011.xml |access-date=2025-02-23 |publisher=Manchester University Press |language=en-US |isbn=978-1-5261-1285-9}} In 1403, the [[Battle of Shrewsbury]] was fought at [[Battlefield, Shropshire|Battlefield]], a few miles north of the town centre, between King [[Henry IV of England|Henry IV]] and [[Henry Percy (Hotspur)]], with the king emerging victorious.{{Cite web |title=Battle of Shrewsbury – Henry VI at Shrewsbury |url=http://militaryhistory.about.com/od/battleswars14011600/p/Shrewsbury.htm |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080504094134/http://militaryhistory.about.com/od/battleswars14011600/p/Shrewsbury.htm |archive-date=4 May 2008 |access-date=23 February 2008 |publisher=About.com |df=dmy-all}} Hotspur's body was taken by [[Baron Furnivall|Thomas Neville]], to [[Whitchurch, Shropshire|Whitchurch]], for burial. However, when rumours circulated that Percy was still alive, the king "had the corpse exhumed and displayed it, propped upright between two millstones, in the market place at Shrewsbury".{{Harvnb|Walker|2004}}. That being done, Percy was subjected to [[posthumous execution]].{{Cite book |title = The Complete Peerage, edited by H.A. Doubleday|last = Cokayne|first = George Edward |publisher = St. Catherine Press|location = London|year = 1936|volume = IX|page=714}} [[File:The Princes in the Tower by John Everett Millais (1878).png|thumb|upright|''[[The Princes in the Tower (painting)|The Two Princes Edward and Richard in the Tower, 1483]]'' by Sir [[John Everett Millais]]]] One of the [[Princes in the Tower]], [[Richard of Shrewsbury]], was born in the town around 17 August 1473,{{Cite web |title=Richard of Shrewsbury, Duke of York |url=https://www.warsoftheroses.com/people/richard-of-shrewsbury-duke-of-york/ |access-date=2023-12-30 |website=Wars of the Roses |language=en-GB}} the second son of [[King Edward IV]] of England and [[Elizabeth Woodville]]. In 1480, [[Edward V]], then [[Prince of Wales]] (and the other prince of the Princes in the Tower), was resident in Shrewsbury. On 11 May Edward V confirmed the composition of the town's [[Worshipful Company of Mercers|Mercer's Company]], which had merged with the guilds of the [[Worshipful Company of Ironmongers|Ironmongers]] and [[Worshipful Company of Goldsmiths|Goldsmiths]]. This fraternity were patrons of the Altar of St Michael in St Chad's Church and they kept a Mercers Hall on the site of the [[sacristy|Sextry]] of Old [[St Chad's Church, Shrewsbury|St Chads]].[[File:71, 72 & 73, Wyle Cop 3.JPG|thumb|The building Henry Tudor stayed in before the [[Battle of Bosworth Field|Battle of Bosworth]]]] In 1485, ahead of the [[Battle of Bosworth Field]], [[Henry VII of England|Henry Tudor]], while not yet king, marched his forces on a route that lay through Shrewsbury. He was initially denied access to the town, but on intervention by a member of the Stanley family he was admitted.{{Cite web |title=The Battle of Bosworth Field |url=https://www.historic-uk.com/HistoryMagazine/DestinationsUK/The-Battle-of-Bosworth-Field/ |access-date=2023-04-20 |website=Historic UK |language=en-GB}}{{Cite web |date=2015-04-13 |title=The Road to Bosworth by Sarah Bryson - The Tudor Society |url=https://www.tudorsociety.com/the-road-to-bosworth-by-sarah-bryson/ |access-date=2023-04-20 |website=Tudorsociety.com |language=en-gb}} Thomas Mytton, the Bailiff of the town, a supporter of [[Richard III of England|Richard III]], had vowed that the only way he would get through was "over his dead body". Thomas then lay down and allowed Henry to step over him, to free himself from his oath.{{Cite news |date=30 May 2022 |title=Sunrise on Wyle Cop in Shrewsbury, looking as if very little has changed over the centuries. |url=https://www.shropshireandbeyond.com/blog/timeless-scene-on-historic-wyle-cop |access-date=2023-04-20 |website=Shropshire and Beyond |language=en-GB}} Henry was accommodated in the building now known as Henry Tudor House on Wyle Cop.{{Cite web |title=Home - Discover Henry Tudor House A Restaurant, Bar & Events Space |url=https://henrytudorhouse.com/ |access-date=2023-04-20 |website=Henry Tudor House}} In 1490, Henry VII, accompanied by his [[Elizabeth of York|queen]] and his son, [[Arthur, Prince of Wales|Prince Arthur]], celebrated the feast of St George in the town. The town is recorded as having entertained Henry again in 1496, with attendants lodged in the Sextry of Old St Chads; more generally it is said of Henry VII's relations with the town that:
The intercourse which had begun thus favourably was kept up in after years by Henry, who, with his queen and son, frequently visited this town, upon which occasions they were feasted by the Bailiffs in a most royal and hospitable manner.
=== Reformation === Shrewsbury's monastic institutions were disbanded with the [[Dissolution of the Monasteries]] and the Abbey was closed in 1540. [[Henry VIII]] intended to make Shrewsbury one of his 13 new [[bishoprics]] (serving Shropshire and [[Staffordshire]]) and hence a cathedral city, after the formation of the [[Church of England]] but the citizens of the town declined the offer, which is the point of origin of the term "Proud Salopians": the town leadership preferring to be the most senior town in the country and not the most junior city.{{efn|This story is also attributed to Charles II}} As a consequence of the dissolution, the monastic hospitals were closed and the incomes from their endowments were transferred to secular owners. St Giles's leper hospital passed to the Prince family, who were succeeded by their descendants the [[Earls of Tankerville]]. St John the Baptist hospital passed to the Wood family and became almshouses. At this time the shrine and relics of St Winifred were destroyed. === Council of Wales and the Marches === {{multiple image | width = 120 | image1 = British (English) School - Sir Rowland Hill (1492^–1561) - 609006 - National Trust.jpg | alt1 = Sir Rowland Hill | image2 = Henry Sidney.jpg | alt2 = | footer = Principal members of the Council of the Marches | align = | direction = | total_width = | caption1 = [[Rowland Hill (MP)|Sir Rowland Hill]] | caption2 = Sir Henry Sidney }} {{main|Council of Wales and the Marches}} The [[Council of Wales and the Marches]] was established during the 1470s by Edward IV with a headquarters in the town.{{Cite web |title=Council in the Marches of Wales |url=https://www.oxfordreference.com/display/10.1093/oi/authority.20110810104658259 |access-date=2023-07-08 |website=Oxford Reference |language=en |doi= }} Its buildings partly survive near the castle and were later adapted to be an episcopal palace,{{Cite web |title=THE OLD COUNCIL HOUSE, Shrewsbury - 1270996 {{!}} Historic England |url=https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1270996 |access-date=2023-07-08 |website=historicengland.org.uk |language=en}} the council also met at [[Ludlow Castle]]. Members of this council included [[John Dudley, Earl of Warwick]], [[Sir Henry Sidney]], [[William Herbert, 1st Earl of Pembroke (1551 creation)|William Herbert, 1st Earl of Pembroke]], and [[Rowland Hill (MP)|Sir Rowland Hill]], publisher of the [[Geneva Bible]] and potential inspiration for a hero in Shakespeare's ''[[As You Like It]]''.{{Cite web |last=Austin |first=Sue |date=2024-01-29 |title=Shakespeare's links with Shropshire unveiled - when and where you can hear about them |url=https://www.shropshirestar.com/news/local-hubs/north-shropshire/wem/2024/01/29/london-lecture-comes-to-shropshire-as-links-between-shakespeare-and-the-county-are-unveiled/ |access-date=2024-01-30 |website=Shropshirestar.com |language=en}} [[File:Council House & Gateway 02.JPG|thumb|upright|Gate house of the council headquarters in the town]] Its functions were interpreted widely. It was to hear all suits, civil and criminal, which were brought by individuals too poor to sue at common law; it was to try all cases of murder, felony, piracy, wrecking and such crimes as were likely to disturb the peace; it was to investigate charges of misgovernment by officials and the false verdicts of juries; it was to enforce the laws against livery and maintenance, to punish rumour mongers and adulterers, and to deal with disputes concerning enclosures, villein service and manorial questions; it heard appeals from the common law courts; and it was responsible for administering the legislation dealing with religion.{{Cite web|url=http://www.ngfl-cymru.org.uk/vtc/ngfl/history/wjec_unit_5/the_council_of_Wales_and_the_marches.doc|title=Domain Registered at Safenames|website=Ngfl-cymru.org.uk}} According to historian [[John Davies (historian)|John Davies]], at its peak in the mid-16th century, the Council:
represented a remarkable experiment in regional government. It administered the law cheaply and rapidly; it dealt with up to twenty cases a day and [[George Owen of Henllys|George Owen]] stated that the 'oppressed poor' flocked to it.John Davies, ''A History of Wales'', Penguin, 1993, {{ISBN|0-14-028475-3}}
[[File:John Caius G&C.jpg|thumb|upright|Dr John Caius]] In 1551, there was a notable outbreak of sweating sickness in the town, which [[John Caius|Dr John Caius]] was in the town to attend to at the command of the council.{{Cite web |title=The Sweating Sickness: A Boke or Counseill Against the Disease Commonly Called the Sweate or Sweatyng Sicknesse, by John Caius et al. {{!}} The Online Books Page |url=https://onlinebooks.library.upenn.edu/webbin/book/lookupid?key=olbp85998 |access-date=2023-07-08 |website=onlinebooks.library.upenn.edu}} The following year, after his return to London, Caius published ''A Boke or Counseill Against the Disease Commonly Called the Sweate, or Sweatyng Sicknesse''. The president of the council was the dedicatee of the book and the dedicatory epistle explains his appointment. This text became the main source of knowledge of this disease, now understood to be [[influenza]].{{Cite web |title=John Caius {{!}} British physician {{!}} Britannica |url=https://www.britannica.com/biography/John-Caius |access-date=2023-04-20 |website=Britannica.com |language=en}} In 1581, Sir Henry Sidney, celebrated the feast of St George, on 23 April, in this town, with great splendour: a solemn procession went from the Council House to St Chad’s Church, the choir of which was fitted up in imitation of [[St George's Chapel, Windsor Castle]] with the stalls decorated with the arms of the [[Knights of the Garter]]; on the conclusion of divine service Sir Henry devoted the afternoon to feasting the burgesses. === Early Modern === Shrewsbury thrived throughout the 16th and 17th centuries, a period when the town was at the height of its commercial importance. This success was largely due to the town's location, which allowed it to control the Welsh [[wool trade]], a major industry at the time, with the rest of Britain and Europe, with the River Severn and [[Watling Street]] acting as trading routes.{{Cite journal |last=Mitchell |first=Jean |date=March 1955 |title=Reviewed Work: ''The Shrewsbury Drapers and the Welsh Wool Trade in the XVI and XVII Centuries.'' by T. C. Mendenhall |department=Review |journal=The Economic Journal |publisher=Wiley |volume=65 |pages=147–149 |doi=10.2307/2227468 |jstor=2227468 |number=257}} This trade was dominated by the [[Shrewsbury Drapers Company]] for many years.{{Citation |title=History of Shrewsbury Drapers |url=http://shrewsburydrapers.org.uk/about/history |df=dmy-all |access-date=2 April 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160325094439/http://shrewsburydrapers.org.uk/about/history |url-status=live |publisher=Shrewsbury Drapers |archive-date=25 March 2016}} As a result, a number of grand edifices, including the Ireland's Mansion (built 1575) and Draper's Hall (1560), were constructed. It was in this period that [[Edward VI]] gave permission for the foundation of a free school, which was later to become [[Shrewsbury School]].{{Cite book |last1=Fisher |first1=George William |url=http://archive.org/details/annalsofshrewsbu00fishrich |title=Annals of Shrewsbury School |last2=Hill |first2=John Spencer |date=1899 |publisher=London : Methuen |others=University of California Libraries}} Later, [[William Camden]], in his ''Britannia'' (begun 1577), remarked of the town that "Shrewsbury is inhabited both by Welsh and English, who speak each other's language; and among other things greatly to their praise is the grammar school founded by them, the best filled in all England, whose flourishing state is owing to provision made by its head master, the excellent and worthy [[Thomas Ashton (schoolmaster)|Thomas Ashton]]", the school's first head master.{{cite book|title=Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, Volume 2|page=684}} Article on Thomas Ashton by Martin E. Speight. === Civil War === [[File:Gerrit van Honthorst (c.1590-1592-1656) - Prince Rupert of the Rhine (1619–1682), Count Palatine, Later Duke of Cumberland - 493057 - National Trust.jpg|alt=a young C17th noble soldier |thumb|upright|[[Prince Rupert]]]] {{main|Shropshire in the English Civil War}} During the [[English Civil War]], Shrewsbury was a [[Cavalier|Royalist]] stronghold, under the command of Sir [[Francis Ottley]].{{Cite ODNB|id=20940|title=Ottley, Sir Francis|first=Wright |last=Stephen}} In the autumn of 1642 [[Charles I of England|Charles I]] had a temporary base in the town.{{Cite web |title=English Civil War Battle of Edgehill |url=https://www.britishbattles.com/english-civil-war/the-battle-of-edgehill/ |access-date=2023-04-15 |website=Britishbattles.com}} [[Prince Rupert]] established his headquarters in the town on 18 February 1644, being welcomed by Shrewsbury's aldermen. He was billeted in a building then the home of the family of [[Thomas Jones (British justice)|Thomas Jones]]{{Cite web |title=JONES, Thomas I (1614-92), of Shrewsbury, Salop and Cerreghwfa, Mont. | History of Parliament Online |url=http://www.historyofparliamentonline.org/volume/1660-1690/member/jones-thomas-i-1614-92 |website=Historyofparliamentonline.org}} in the precincts of what is now the Prince Rupert Hotel.{{Cite web |title=A stroll into the history of Shrewsbury |url=https://www.shropshireandbeyond.com/blog/a-stroll-into-the-history-of-shrewsbury |access-date=2023-04-20 |website=Shropshire and Beyond |language=en-GB}} Shrewsbury only fell to Parliament forces after they were let in by a parliamentarian sympathiser at the St Mary's Water Gate (now also known as Traitor's Gate).{{cite web |title=Shrewsbury Medieval gateway visible again after facelift |url=https://www.shropshirestar.com/news/2016/03/26/shrewsbury-medieval-gateway-visible-again-after-facelift/ |website=Shropshire Star |date=26 March 2016 |access-date=30 August 2023}} After [[Thomas Mytton]] captured Shrewsbury in February 1645, in following with the [[Ordinance of no quarter to the Irish|ordnance of no quarter]], a dozen [[Irish people|Irish]] prisoners were selected to be killed after picking lots.{{harvnb|Carlton|1994|p=262}}.{{Cite news |date=29 January 2015 |title=Shrewsbury, the house at the Castle Gates and the hanged Irish mercenaries |publisher=Gwendda |url=http://www.witchphotographer.com/shop/shrewsbury/shrewsbury-the-house-at-the-castle-gates-and-the-hanged-irish-mercenaries/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161125084047/http://www.witchphotographer.com/shop/shrewsbury/shrewsbury-the-house-at-the-castle-gates-and-the-hanged-irish-mercenaries/ |archive-date=25 November 2016 |df=dmy-all}} This prompted Rupert to respond by executing Parliamentarian prisoners in [[Oswestry]].{{Cite book |last=Royle |first=Trevor |title=Civil War: The Wars of the Three Kingdoms 1638–1660 |publisher=Abacus |year=2004 |isbn=978-0-349-11564-1 |edition=2006 |page=277}} === Georgian and Victorian === By the 18th century, Shrewsbury had become an important market town and stopping point for stagecoaches travelling between London and [[Holyhead]] with passengers on their way to Ireland; this led to the establishment of a number of coaching inns, many of which, such as the Lion Hotel, are extant to this day. [[File:Town Hall Shrewsbury and the Old Market House, 1796.jpg|thumb|The former Shire Hall (since demolished) and Old Market Hall, 1796]] A town hall was built in the Market Place on the site of an ancient guildhall in 1730;{{Cite book |last=Lewis |first=Samuel |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=4-CzYeAyoIYC&pg=PT37 |title=A Topographical Dictionary of England: With Historical and Statistical Descriptions |publisher=S. Lewis & Co. |year=1833}} it was demolished and a new [[Old Shirehall, Shrewsbury|combined guildhall and shirehall]] was erected on the site in 1837.{{Cite book |last=Pidgeon |first=Henry |url=https://archive.org/details/memorialsshrews00pidggoog |title=Memorials of Shrewsbury: being a concise description of the town and its environs |year=1837 |page=[https://archive.org/details/memorialsshrews00pidggoog/page/n146 116] |quote=Old Shire Hall Shrewsbury Robert Smirke 1837.}} Local soldier and statesman [[Robert Clive]] served as the town's mayor in 1762 and was Shrewsbury's MP from 1762 until his death in 1774.{{Cite web |title=Former Mayors of Shrewsbury 1638 to present |url=http://www.shrewsburytowncouncil.gov.uk/live/welcome.asp?id=714 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141129042744/http://www.shrewsburytowncouncil.gov.uk/live/welcome.asp?id=714 |archive-date=29 November 2014 |access-date=19 November 2014 |publisher=Shrewsbury Town Council}} St Chad's Church collapsed in 1788 after attempts to expand the crypt compromised the structural integrity of the tower above. Now known as Old St Chad's, the remains of the church building and its churchyard are on the corner of Princess Street, College Hill and Belmont. A new [[St Chad's Church, Shrewsbury|St Chad's Church]] was built just four years after the collapse, but as a large neo-classical round church and in a different and more elevated location, at the top of Claremont Hill close to the Quarry. In the [[Industrial Revolution]] the [[Shrewsbury Canal]] opened in 1797, initially connecting the town to [[Trench, Shropshire|Trench]]. By 1835 it had been linked up to the [[Shropshire Canal]] and thence to the rest of the [[Canals of Great Britain|canal network]].{{Cite web |title=Thomas Telford in Shropshire |url=http://www.bbc.co.uk/shropshire/telford/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090531093521/http://www.bbc.co.uk/shropshire/telford/ |archive-date=31 May 2009 |access-date=4 March 2008 |publisher=BBC Shropshire |df=dmy-all}} In the period directly after [[Napoleon]]'s surrender after the [[Battle of Waterloo]], the town's own [[53rd (Shropshire) Regiment of Foot]] was sent to guard him in his exile on [[St Helena]]. A locket containing a lock of the emperor's hair, presented to an officer of the 53rd, remains to this day in the collections of the Soldiers of Shropshire Museum at Shrewsbury Castle.{{Cite web |date=7 January 2013 |title=Kings Shropshire Light Infantry |url=http://www.dlisouthshields.org.uk/kings_shropshire_light_infantry.php |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120508064451/http://www.dlisouthshields.org.uk/kings_shropshire_light_infantry.php |archive-date=8 May 2012 |publisher=Durham Light Infantry Association, South Shields |df=dmy-all}} [[File:Shrewsbury Prison 1796.png|thumb|Shrewsbury's Georgian prison]] [[HM Prison Shrewsbury]], when new in the Georgian period, was considered a national example of improved conditions and more enlightened penal policy. Times change and a 2005 report on prison population found that it was the most overcrowded in [[England and Wales]], despite a major expansion in Victorian times.{{Cite news |date=27 July 2005 |title=Jail most overcrowded in country |work=BBC News |url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/low/england/shropshire/4722157.stm |access-date=16 January 2008}} The prison, which was also known as the Dana because it was built near the site of the medieval Dana gaol, was closed in 2013 and then sold by the [[Ministry of Justice (United Kingdom)|Ministry of Justice]] to private property developers in 2014.[http://www.shropshirestar.com/news/2014/11/20/shrewsburys-dana-prison-to-become-homes-and-offices/ Shropshire Star] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150201021314/http://www.shropshirestar.com/news/2014/11/20/shrewsburys-dana-prison-to-become-homes-and-offices/ |date=1 February 2015 }} ''Sold: Shrewsbury's Dana prison to become homes and offices'' (20 November 2014) In 1821, the county purchased a building in College Hill which was adapted to become the judge's lodgings, providing accommodation for the judges and their retinue during their attendance at the [[Assizes]]. ===20th and 21st centuries=== [[File:BT Building - geograph.org.uk - 142496.jpg|thumb|BT Telephone Exchange, Town Walls (now demolished)]] The town suffered very little from air raids in the [[Second World War]]; the worst case was in 1940, when a woman and her two grandchildren were killed when a cottage was destroyed on Ellesmere Road, the only local air raid deaths.{{Cite book |last=Simcox |first=Kenneth |title=A Town at War, Shrewsbury 1939–45 |publisher=Shropshire Libraries |year=1983 |isbn=0-903802-25-2 |page=14}} Therefore, many of its ancient buildings remain intact and there was little redevelopment in the 1960s and 1970s. However, some historic buildings were demolished to make way for the [[brutalist]] architectural style of the 1960s, though the town was saved from a new inner ring road due to its challenging geography.{{Cite book |last=Rowley |first=Trevor |url=https://archive.org/details/englishlandscape0000rowl |title=The English Landscape in the Twentieth Century |publisher=A&C Black |year=2006 |isbn=9781852853884 |page=[https://archive.org/details/englishlandscape0000rowl/page/149 149] |quote=shrewsbury england redevelopment architecture 1960s 1970s. |access-date=13 April 2008 |url-access=registration |df=dmy-all}} A notable example of 1960s/70s construction in Shrewsbury was Telecom House on Smithfield Road, demolished in the 2000s.{{Cite web |title=Smithfield Cattle Market, Shrewsbury |url=http://search.shropshirehistory.org.uk/collections/getrecord/CCS_MSA17987/ |access-date=14 July 2020 |publisher=Discovering Shropshire's History |archive-date=14 July 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200714182714/http://search.shropshirehistory.org.uk/collections/getrecord/CCS_MSA17987/ |url-status=dead }} Between 1962 and 1992 there was a hardened [[nuclear bunker]], built for [[Royal Observer Corps#Restructuring and reconstruction|No 16 Group Royal Observer Corps Shrewsbury]], who provided the field force of the [[United Kingdom Warning and Monitoring Organisation]] and would have sounded the [[four-minute warning]] alarm in the event of war and warned the population of Shrewsbury in the event of approaching radioactive fallout.{{Cite web |title=UKWMO Group Controls |url=http://www.subbrit.org.uk/rsg/roc/group_hq.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071025003958/http://www.subbrit.org.uk/rsg/roc/group_hq.html |archive-date=25 October 2007 |access-date=17 March 2008 |publisher=Subbrit.org.uk |df=dmy-all}} The building was staffed by up to 120 volunteers who trained on a weekly basis. After the breakup of the communist bloc in 1989, the Royal Observer Corps was disbanded between September 1991 and December 1995. However, the nuclear bunker still stands just inside Holywell Street near the Abbey as a lasting reminder of the Cold War, but is now converted and used as a veterinary practice.{{Cite web |title=Shrewsbury ROC Group HQ – Subterranea Britannica |url=https://www.subbrit.org.uk/sites/shrewsbury-roc-group-hq/ |website=Subbrit.org.uk}} The town was targeted by the [[Provisional Irish Republican Army campaign|IRA]] in 1992. One bomb was detonated at Shrewsbury Castle, causing severe damage to the regimental museum of the [[Shropshire Light Infantry]],{{Cite news |last=Kirby |first=Terry |date=26 August 1992 |title=Firebomb attack at army museum linked to IRA |work=[[The Independent]]}} estimated to be in the region of £250,000 and many artefacts were lost. A second bomb, detonated in the [[Darwin Shopping Centre]], was put out by the sprinkler system before any major damage was caused. Finally, a third bomb was discovered elsewhere in the town centre but failed to do any serious damage.{{Cite web |title=Shropshire bombing |url=http://shropshirehistory.com/disasters/bomb.htm |access-date=19 June 2019 |website=Shropshire History |archive-date=19 June 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190619043436/http://shropshirehistory.com/disasters/bomb.htm |url-status=dead }} [[File:Shrewsbury Abbey from the west - geograph.org.uk - 56158.jpg|thumb|Flooding in Shrewsbury (2000)]] From the late 1990s, the town experienced [[Shrewsbury floods|severe flooding problems]] from the Severn and [[Rea Brook]]. In the autumn of 2000 large swathes of the town were underwater, notably [[Frankwell]], which flooded three times in six weeks.{{Cite web |title=Shrewsbury flood alleviation scheme |url=http://www.environment-agency.gov.uk/regions/midlands/567079/567090/893833/894284/202790/?lang=_e |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070110011902/http://www.environment-agency.gov.uk/regions/midlands/567079/567090/893833/894284/202790/?lang=_e |archive-date=10 January 2007 |access-date=24 February 2008 |publisher=Environment Agency}} The Frankwell flood defences were completed in 2003, along with the new offices of [[Shrewsbury and Atcham Borough Council]]. More recently, such as in 2005 and 2007 but not [[2019–20 United Kingdom floods|2020]], flooding has been less severe and the defences have generally held back floodwaters from the town centre areas. However, the town car parks are often left to be flooded in the winter, which reduces trade in the town, most evidenced in the run up to Christmas in 2007.{{Cite news |date=10 December 2007 |title=Flood watch continues on Severn |publisher=BBC Shropshire News |url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/england/shropshire/7135099.stm |url-status=live |access-date=24 February 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071213155630/http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/england/shropshire/7135099.stm |archive-date=13 December 2007 |df=dmy-all}} Shrewsbury won the ''[[West Midlands (region)|West Midlands]] Capital of Enterprise'' award in 2004.{{Cite web |title=Advantage WM |url=http://www.advantagewm.co.uk/news-media-events/news/2006/01/enterprise-capital-search-now-underway.aspx |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080621060912/http://www.advantagewm.co.uk/news-media-events/news/2006/01/enterprise-capital-search-now-underway.aspx |archive-date=21 June 2008 |access-date=18 September 2007}} The town has two large expanding business parks, [[Shrewsbury Business Park]] by the A5 in the southeast and [[Battlefield Enterprise Park]] in the north. There are many residential developments currently under construction in the town to cater for the increasing numbers of people wishing to live in the town, which is a popular place to commute to [[Telford]], [[Wolverhampton]] and [[Birmingham]] from.{{Cite web |title=Travel – A day on the Shrewsbury-Birmingham line |url=http://www.bbc.co.uk/shropshire/content/articles/2006/07/13/commuter_blog_feature.shtml |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070127042516/http://www.bbc.co.uk/shropshire/content/articles/2006/07/13/commuter_blog_feature.shtml |archive-date=27 January 2007 |access-date=13 April 2008 |website=BBC Shropshire |df=dmy-all}} In 2009 [[Shrewsbury Town Council]] was formed and the town's traditional coat of arms was returned to everyday use.{{Cite web |title=Case study on the experience of newly established local (parish and town) councils |url=https://www.nalc.gov.uk/library/our-work/create-a-council-resources/1367-shrewsbury-town-council-shropshire/file |access-date=14 July 2020 |publisher=National Association of Local Councils}} In 2021 the lost seal of the town, dating from 1425, was discovered.{{Cite journal |title=Supplementum Epigraphicum Graecum Phthiotic Thebes. Christian bronze seal. |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1163/1874-6772_seg_a43_308 |access-date=2023-07-08 |website=Supplementum Epigraphicum Graecum|date=2016 |doi=10.1163/1874-6772_seg_a43_308 |url-access=subscription }} ==Governance== [[File:Livesey House.jpg|thumb|Livesey House, 7 St John's Hill: Town Council's headquarters since 2023]] There are two tiers of local government covering Shrewsbury, at [[civil parish|parish]] (town) and [[Unitary authorities of England|unitary authority]] level: [[Shrewsbury Town Council]] and [[Shropshire Council]]. The town council is based at Livesey House on St John's Hill.{{cite news |last1=Humphreys |first1=Nick |title=New town council HQ 'will be cost effective and environmentally friendly' |url=https://www.shropshirestar.com/news/local-hubs/shrewsbury/2023/04/01/new-town-council-hq-will-be-cost-effective-and-environmentally-friendly/ |access-date=9 July 2025 |work=Shropshire Star |date=1 April 2023}} Shropshire Council is also based in the town, at the Guildhall on Frankwell Quay.{{cite news |last1=Jones |first1=Megan |title= Shropshire Council HQ at Shirehall officially closes its doors to the public |url=https://www.shropshirestar.com/news/2025/02/28/shropshire-council-hq-at-shirehall-officially-closes-its-doors-to-the-public/ |access-date=4 May 2025 |work=Shropshire Star |date=28 February 2025}} [[File:The Guildhall, Shrewsbury.jpg|thumb|The Guildhall, Frankwell Quay: Shropshire Council's headquarters since 2025]] Shrewsbury is in the [[Shrewsbury (constituency)|Shrewsbury constituency]] and is the only large settlement in the constituency. At the most recent general election, in [[2024 United Kingdom general election|2024]], [[Julia Buckley]] of the [[Labour Party (United Kingdom)|Labour Party]] was elected with a majority of 11,355.{{cite news|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/election/2024/uk/constituencies/E14001473 |title=Shrewsbury - General election results 2024 |publisher=BBC News|language=en-gb |access-date=5 July 2024}} The 19th-century Prime Minister, [[Benjamin Disraeli]], was MP for Shrewsbury.{{Cite web |title=Benjamin Disraeli (1804–1881) |url=http://www.victorianweb.org/history/pms/dizzy.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080214233216/http://www.victorianweb.org/history/pms/dizzy.html |archive-date=14 February 2008 |access-date=23 February 2008 |publisher=VictorianWeb.org |df=dmy-all}} ===Administrative history=== Shrewsbury was an [[ancient borough]]. It was described as a borough in the [[Domesday Book]] of 1086, and its earliest known [[municipal charter|charter]] was issued by [[Henry II of England|Henry II]] (reigned 1154–1189).{{cite book |title=Report of the Commissioners appointed to inquire into the Municipal Corporations in England and Wales: Appendix 3 |date=1835 |page=2011 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=N3FTAAAAcAAJ&pg=PA2011 |access-date=9 July 2025}} It was reformed to become a [[municipal borough]] in 1836 under the [[Municipal Corporations Act 1835]], which standardised how most boroughs operated across the country.{{cite book |title=Municipal Corporations Act |date=1835 |page=458 |url=https://archive.org/details/statutesunitedk35britgoog/page/458/mode/2up |access-date=9 July 2025}} The municipal borough of Shrewsbury was abolished in 1974. Its area merged with the surrounding Atcham Rural District to become a new [[non-metropolitan district]], which was initially called Shrewsbury,{{cite legislation UK|type=si|si=The English Non-metropolitan Districts (Names) Order 1973|year=1973|number=551|access-date=18 September 2022}} but was renamed [[Shrewsbury and Atcham]] later in 1974.{{cite web |title=Historical information on changes to electoral arrangements of Local authorities, Parliamentary areas and European Parliamentary boundaries |url=https://docs.os.uk/os-downloads/addressing-and-location/boundary-line/boundary-line-downloads |website=Boundary-Line Downloads |publisher=Ordnance Survey |access-date=25 August 2025}} (See downloadable [https://1897589978-files.gitbook.io/~/files/v0/b/gitbook-x-prod.appspot.com/o/spaces%2FcNpJpLP8RROUaWVQo5ea%2Fuploads%2FwKAeeIvHz0AhpuZU7aaJ%2Fboundary-legislation-changes-from-1973.xls?alt=media&token=791e9948-3e7e-4606-bc19-e082fb7aee0c boundary-legislation-changes-from-1973.xls] spreadsheet.) The new district was granted [[borough status]] from its creation.{{cite web|url=https://api.parliament.uk/historic-hansard/written-answers/1974/mar/28/district-councils-and-boroughs#S5CV0871P0_19740328_CWA_145|title=District Councils and Boroughs|date=28 March 1974|work=[[Hansard|Parliamentary Debates (Hansard)]]|access-date=16 January 2012}} Shrewsbury and Atcham Borough Council was abolished in 2009, when its functions were taken over by Shropshire County Council, which was renamed Shropshire Council.{{cite legislation UK|type=si|si=The Shropshire (Structural Change) Order 2008|year=2008|number=1866|access-date=18 September 2022}} The town of Shrewsbury had been an [[unparished area]] since the 1974 reforms. A new parish of Shrewsbury was established as part of the 2009 reforms, with the parish council adopting the name Shrewsbury Town Council.{{cite web |title=The Shrewsbury and Atcham (Parish) Order 2008 |url=https://webarchive.nationalarchives.gov.uk/ukgwa/20221202003347mp_/https://s3-eu-west-2.amazonaws.com/lgbce/__data/assets/pdf_file/0004/12685/the-shrewsbury-and-atcham-parish-order-2008.pdf |website=The National Archives |publisher=Local Government Boundary Commission for England |access-date=9 July 2025}} ====Coat of arms==== [[File:Coat of arms of Shrewsbury.png|thumb|upright|Coat of arms]] The coat of arms of the former Shrewsbury Borough Council and now of the Town Council, depicts three loggerheads (leopards), with the motto ''Floreat Salopia'', a Latin phrase that can be translated to "May Shrewsbury Flourish".{{Cite web |title=Origins of the name of Shrewsbury |url=http://www.shrewsbury.gov.uk/public/council/civictradition/shrewsburyname.htm |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070927222315/http://www.shrewsbury.gov.uk/public/council/civictradition/shrewsburyname.htm |archive-date=27 September 2007 |access-date=17 January 2008 |website=Shrewsbury and Atcham Borough Council |df=dmy-all}}{{Cite web |title=Shrewsbury and Atcham Borough Council |url=http://www.civicheraldry.co.uk/salop.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071120060932/http://www.civicheraldry.co.uk/salop.html |archive-date=20 November 2007 |access-date=5 April 2008 |publisher=civicheraldry.co.uk |df=dmy-all}} The coat of arms of the (now abolished) Shrewsbury and Atcham Borough Council was Shrewsbury's shield with the addition of [[Atcham]] Bridge running above the leopards. The [[flag of Shropshire]], and other county crests, also uses the three loggerheads. ===Affiliations=== Shrewsbury was twinned with [[Zutphen]], Netherlands from 1977{{Cite web |title=Culture and Arts – Zutphen on the Ijsel |url=http://www.bbc.co.uk/shropshire/culture/2002/08/zutphen.shtml |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20041215211836/http://www.bbc.co.uk/shropshire/culture/2002/08/zutphen.shtml |archive-date=15 December 2004 |access-date=18 September 2007 |publisher=BBC Shropshire |df=dmy-all}} until 2018.{{Cite news |last= Todman|first=Lucy |date=14 November 2018 |title=Historic link with Shrewsbury's twin town is axed |work=[[Shropshire Star]] |url=https://www.shropshirestar.com/news/local-hubs/shrewsbury/2018/11/13/twin-ties-severed-after-40-years/ |access-date=11 April 2020}} The [[Royal Navy]] submarine, {{HMS|Talent|S92|6}}, decommissioned in 2022, was affiliated with Shrewsbury.{{cite web |last1=Humprhries |first1=Hilary |title=HMS Talent Returns Freedom Rights to Shrewsbury |url=https://www.shrewsburytowncouncil.gov.uk/hms-talent-returns-freedom-rights-to-shrewsbury/ |website=Shrewsbury Town Council |access-date=23 April 2023 |date=27 October 2022}} ==Geography== [[File:English Bridge Shrewsbury - panoramio - PJMarriott.jpg|thumb|The River Severn at the English Bridge]] Shrewsbury is about {{convert|14|mi|km}} west of Telford, {{convert|43|mi|km}} west of [[Birmingham]] and the [[West Midlands conurbation]] and about {{convert|153|mi|km}} north-west of the capital, [[London]]. More locally, the town is to the east of [[Welshpool]], with [[Bridgnorth]] and [[Kidderminster]] to the south-east. The border with [[Wales]] is {{convert|9|mi}} to the west. The town centre is partially built on a hill whose elevation is, at its highest, {{convert|246|ft|m}} above sea level. The longest river in the United Kingdom, the [[River Severn]], flows through the town, forming a meander around its centre. The [[Rea Brook]] is a small river that has its confluence with the Severn at Shrewsbury, just upstream from the English Bridge, and much of the [[Rea Brook Valley]] within the town is a country park and local nature reserve, encompassing {{convert|36|ha|acre}}.[https://www.shrewsburytowncouncil.gov.uk/assets/rea-brook-valley-local-nature-reserve/ Shrewsbury Town Council] Rea Brook Valley Local Nature Reserve The town is subject to flooding from these rivers. {| class="toccolours" style="float:right; font-size:80%; margin-left:0px;" |+ '''Areas of Shrewsbury''' | style="padding-right:1em;" |
