|} {{Clear}} ===Geology=== The town lies to the west of [[Haughmond Hill]], a site where [[Precambrian]] rocks, some of the oldest rocks in the county can be found,{{Cite web |title=Haughmond Hill |url=http://www.shropshiregeology.org.uk/shropgeol/haughmond/haughmondmain.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071009002424/http://www.shropshiregeology.org.uk/shropgeol/haughmond/haughmondmain.html |archive-date=9 October 2007 |access-date=2 January 2008 |website=Shropshire Geology |df=dmy-all}} and the town itself is sited on an area of largely [[Carboniferous]] rocks.{{Cite web |title=Shropshire's Geological Trail |url=http://www.shropshirerocks.org/shropshiregeologicaltrail |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081119145001/http://www.shropshirerocks.org/shropshiregeologicaltrail |archive-date=19 November 2008 |access-date=2 January 2008 |website=Shropshire Rocks!}} A fault, the Hodnet Fault, starts approximately at the town and runs north-east into the [[Stoke-on-Trent]] area.{{cite web |last1=Smith |first1=N J P |last2=Kirby |first2=G A |last3=Pharoah |first3=TC |title=Structure and evolution of the south-west Pennine Basin and adjacent area |url=https://webapps.bgs.ac.uk/Memoirs/docs/B06160.html |website=British Geographical Society |access-date=30 August 2023}} ===Climate=== [[File:Shrewsbury Food Festival Crowds.jpg|thumb|[[The Quarry (park)|The Quarry]] is often busy during spring and summer.]] The [[climate]] of Shrewsbury is similar to that of the rest of Shropshire, generally moderate. Rainfall averages {{convert|76|to|100|cm|in|abbr=on}}, influenced by being in the [[rainshadow]] of the [[Cambrian Mountains]] from warm, moist [[Precipitation (meteorology)#Frontal activity|frontal systems]] of the [[Atlantic Ocean]], which bring generally light precipitation in autumn and spring.{{Cite web |title=Shropshire |url=http://uk.encarta.msn.com/encyclopedia_781530177/Shrewsbury.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080718233554/https://uk.encarta.msn.com/encyclopedia_781530177/Shrewsbury.html |archive-date=18 July 2008 |access-date=24 February 2008 |publisher=MSN Encarta}} The nearest weather station is at [[Shawbury]], about {{convert|6.5|mi}} north-east of Shrewsbury town centre. The local topography, being that of a low-lying plain surrounded by higher ground to the west, south and east gives the Shrewsbury area its own microclimate – the absolute maximum at Shawbury of {{convert|34.9|°C|°F|abbr=on}} and absolute minimum of {{convert|-25.2|°C|°F|abbr=on}} represents the largest temperature range of any individual weather station in the British Isles – although the maximum range of average temperatures tends to peak to the south-east of the Shrewsbury area, particularly in the south-east midlands, inland East Anglia and inland south-east England. In an average year, the warmest day is {{convert|28.4|°C|°F|abbr=on}},{{Cite web |title=1971-00 average warmest day |url=http://eca.knmi.nl/utils/calcdetail.php?seasonid=0&periodid=1971-2000&indexid=TXx&stationid=1633 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120611101444/http://eca.knmi.nl/utils/calcdetail.php?seasonid=0&periodid=1971-2000&indexid=TXx&stationid=1633 |archive-date=11 June 2012 |access-date=3 March 2011 |df=dmy-all}} giving a total of 8.9 days{{Cite web |title=1971-00 >25c days average |url=http://eca.knmi.nl/utils/calcdetail.php?seasonid=0&periodid=1971-2000&indexid=SU&stationid=1633 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120611101450/http://eca.knmi.nl/utils/calcdetail.php?seasonid=0&periodid=1971-2000&indexid=SU&stationid=1633 |archive-date=11 June 2012 |access-date=3 March 2011 |df=dmy-all}} of {{convert|25.1|°C|°F|abbr=on}} or above. The absolute maximum of {{convert|34.9|°C|°F|abbr=on}}{{Cite web |title=1990 Maximum |url=http://eca.knmi.nl/utils/monitordetail.php?seasonid=14&year=1990&indexid=TXx&stationid=1633 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120611101455/http://eca.knmi.nl/utils/monitordetail.php?seasonid=14&year=1990&indexid=TXx&stationid=1633 |archive-date=11 June 2012 |access-date=3 March 2011 |df=dmy-all}} was recorded in August 1990. Conversely, the coldest night of the year typically falls to {{convert|-9.6|°C|°F|abbr=on}}{{Cite web |title=1971-00 average coldest day |url=http://eca.knmi.nl/utils/calcdetail.php?seasonid=0&periodid=1971-2000&indexid=TNn&stationid=1633 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120611101501/http://eca.knmi.nl/utils/calcdetail.php?seasonid=0&periodid=1971-2000&indexid=TNn&stationid=1633 |archive-date=11 June 2012 |access-date=3 March 2011 |df=dmy-all}} – in total 61.7 air frosts are recorded in an average year. The absolute minimum of {{convert|-25.2|°C|°F|abbr=on}}{{Cite web |title=1981 December |url=http://www.torro.org.uk/site/lowtempsyear.php |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110119082325/http://www.torro.org.uk/site/lowtempsyear.php |archive-date=19 January 2011 |access-date=3 March 2011 |df=dmy-all}} was recorded in 1981. Annual average rainfall averages around {{convert|650|mm}}, with over {{convert|1|mm|2}} falling on 124 days of the year. {{Shawbury weatherbox}} ==Demography== In 2021, the town of Shrewsbury had a population of 76,782. This represents an increase of 0.69% since 2011. The ethnic distribution was as follows: White – 72,975; Asian – 1755; Black – 348; Arab – 122; Mixed – 1,267; Other – 308.{{cite web |title=Shrewsbury |url=https://www.citypopulation.de/en/uk/westmidlands/admin/shropshire/E04011358__shrewsbury/ |website=City Population |access-date=28 August 2023}} Religious affiliations were as follows: Christian – 52.7%; Muslim – 0.5%; Sikh – 0.5%; Buddhist – 0.3%; Hindu – 0.2%; Jewish – 0.1%; Other – 0.1%; No religion – 39.1%; No answer – 6.4%.{{cite web |title=Shrewsbury Census 2021 |url=https://www.plumplot.co.uk/Shrewsbury-census-2021.html#:~:text=96.9%25%20people%20are%20white%2C%201.3,%25%20households%20have%203%2B%20cars. |website=Plumpot |access-date=1 September 2023}} ==Economy== [[File:Pride Hill Shrewsbury_2016.jpg|thumb|Pride Hill, one of the town's main shopping streets, in 2016]] Throughout the medieval period, Shrewsbury was a centre for the wool trade,{{Cite web |title=The Shrewsbury Drapers Guild |url=http://www.shrewsburydrapers.org.uk/guild |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081120121522/http://www.shrewsburydrapers.org.uk/guild |archive-date=20 November 2008 |access-date=4 April 2008 |website=shrewsburydrapers.org.uk |df=dmy-all}} and later used its position on the River Severn to transport goods across England via the canal system. By the early 1900s, the town became focused on transport services and the general service and professional sector, owing to its position on the [[A5 road (Great Britain)|A5]], part of the strategic route to [[North Wales]].{{Cite web |title=Shrewsbury, Shropshire Industry Statistics |url=http://www.visionofbritain.org.uk/data_cube_table_page.jsp?data_theme=T_IND&data_cube=N_OCC_ORD1921&u_id=10023750&c_id=10001043&add=Y |access-date=9 March 2008 |publisher=A Vision of Britain}} Unlike many other towns in this period, Shrewsbury never became a major centre for heavy industry though, in 1915, the [[Sentinel Waggon Works]] at Shrewsbury was opened for the building of steam rail and road locomotives. Later it converted to the production of diesel locomotives before being taken over, in 1958, by [[Rolls-Royce Limited]] for the manufacture of their range of diesel industrial engines, so that the [[Derby]] facility could concentrate on aero engines.{{Cite book |last=Robotham |first=William Arthur |title=Silver Ghosts and Silver Dawn |publisher=Constable |year=1970 |location=London |pages=160, 161}} The town is the location of both town and county councils and a number of [[retail]] complexes, both in and out of the town centre. These provide significant employment. Shrewsbury is home to a high number of independent businesses, including shops, cafes and restaurants. Wyle Cop in Shrewsbury is said to have the 'longest uninterrupted row of independent shops'.{{Cite web |title=Wyle Cop {{!}} Original Shrewsbury |url=https://originalshrewsbury.co.uk/local-area/wyle-cop |access-date=2018-06-14 |website=originalshrewsbury.co.uk |language=en}} Four in five jobs in the town are in the [[service industry]]. Within this sector, the largest employers are the [[Business administration|administration]] and [[Distribution (business)|distribution]] sectors, which includes retail, food and accommodation.{{Cite web |title=Shrewsbury Town |url=http://www.safetypartnership.org.uk/v2/downloads/4.2%20ShrewsburyTown.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081217115152/http://www.safetypartnership.org.uk/v2/downloads/4.2%20ShrewsburyTown.pdf |archive-date=17 December 2008 |access-date=17 January 2008 |website=Safety Partnership}} [[File:The Parade Shopping Centre, St Mary's Place, Shrewsbury - geograph.org.uk - 117039.jpg|upright|thumb|[[The Parade Shopping Centre]] is housed in the former premises of the [[Royal Salop Infirmary]].]] Shrewsbury has two shopping centres. [[Darwin Shopping Centre|The Darwin]] shopping centre houses many [[high street]] retailers such as [[Marks & Spencer]], [[H&M]], [[JD Sports]] and [[Primark]].{{Cite web |title=Darwin and Pride Hill Shopping Centres {{!}} Original Shrewsbury |url=https://originalshrewsbury.co.uk/local-area/darwin-pride-hill-shopping-centres |access-date=2018-06-14 |website=originalshrewsbury.co.uk |language=en}} [[The Parade Shopping Centre]] is a second centre exclusively housing independent retailers.{{Cite web |date=2018-09-07 |title=Phil Gillam: On Parade at a favourite Shrewsbury spot |url=https://www.shropshirestar.com/news/voices/opinions/phil-gillam/2018/09/07/phil-gillam-on-parade-at-a-favourite-shrewsbury-spot/ |access-date=2025-05-13 |website=Shropshirestar.com |language=en}} Additionally, the town features the [[Shrewsbury Market Hall]], an indoor market with a variety of independent traders. The market has been named "Britain’s Favourite Market" in 2018, 2023, 2024, and 2025 by the National Association of British Market Authorities (NABMA).{{Cite web |last=NABMA |date=2024-01-25 |title=Celebrating the UK's Best Markets as Great British Market Award Winners are Revealed |url=https://nabma.com/celebrating-the-uks-best-markets-as-great-british-market-award-winners-are-revealed/ |access-date=2025-05-13 |website=NABMA |language=en-GB}} There are two retail warehouse clusters: at [[Meole Brace|Meole Brace Retail Park]] to the south and at [[Harlescott|Sundorne Retail Park]] to the north. Major supermarkets in the town are the [[Tesco]] Extra at Harlescott, [[Morrisons]] on Whitchurch Road, [[Asda]] on Old Potts Way and [[Sainsbury's]] at Meole Brace. [[File:High Street, Shrewsbury.JPG|thumb|High Street, facing the top of Wyle Cop, in 2012]] The [[Tourism|visitor economy]] of Shrewsbury and Atcham was worth about £115 million in 2001, with about 2,500 people employed directly in the visitor industry and 3,400 indirectly. There were about 3.1 million visitors – both day visitors and staying visitors – to the borough in 2001, with 88% being day visitors and 12% being staying visitors; staying visitors accounted for 42% of spending.{{Cite web |title=A Visitor Economy Strategy and Action Plan for Shrewsbury & Atcham |url=http://shrewsbury.gov.uk/public/business/towncentreissues/execsummary+for+publication.doc |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060927090441/http://www.shrewsbury.gov.uk/public/business/towncentreissues/execsummary+for+publication.doc |archive-date=27 September 2006 |access-date=21 March 2008 |website=Shrewsbury & Atcham Borough Council |df=dmy-all}} Shrewsbury's position of being the only sizeable town for a large area, especially to the west in [[Mid-Wales]], allows it to attract a large retail base beyond that of its resident population. This is not only evident in the retail sector, but also in the [[healthcare]] sector, where the [[Royal Shrewsbury Hospital]] has the only [[Accident and Emergency|A&E]] department westwards until [[Aberystwyth]], about {{convert|75|mi}} away.{{Cite news |date=10 July 2006 |title=Hospital's cash plans are delayed |work=BBC News |url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/wales/mid/5165812.stm |url-status=live |access-date=23 February 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060713214820/http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/wales/mid/5165812.stm |archive-date=13 July 2006 |df=dmy-all}} Businesses in Shrewsbury voted in favour of a Business Improvement District in late 2013 and Shrewsbury BID started operating in April 2014. Shrewsbury BID delivers on a five-year business plan of projects, which include major destination marketing campaigns, significant cost savings for businesses and strategic work ensuring the best possible town centre environment in which business can flourish. The company is governed by a board of directors and employed three staff full-time in 2017.{{Cite web |title=Shrewsbury BID |url=http://www.shrewsburybid.co.uk |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170509123407/http://www.shrewsburybid.co.uk/ |archive-date=9 May 2017 |df=dmy-all}} In terms of social and [[poverty|economic deprivation]], according to the Overall Index of Multiple Deprivation of 2004, one Super Output Area (SOA) in the town is in the bottom 15% of all areas nationally. This area is in the ward of [[Harlescott]].{{Cite web |title=Index of multiple deprivation – overall results |url=http://www.shropshire.gov.uk/factsfigures.nsf/open/EB9BEA10E543F61780256ED7003B0ACC |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081121121618/http://www.shropshire.gov.uk/factsfigures.nsf/open/EB9BEA10E543F61780256ED7003B0ACC |archive-date=21 November 2008 |access-date=17 January 2008 |website=Shropshire County Council |df=dmy-all}} A further four SOAs fall into the bottom 30% nationally, these being in the wards of Monkmoor, [[Sundorne]], [[Battlefield, Shropshire|Battlefield]] and [[Heathgates]] and Meole Brace. The most affluent areas of the town are generally to the south and west, around the grounds of [[Shrewsbury School]] and the [[Copthorne, Shropshire|Copthorne]] area.{{Citation needed|date=February 2024}} ==Culture== === Literary and performance heritage === [[File:Shoe makers arbour Shrewsbury.jpg|thumb|upright|A surviving 1679 arbour, that of the Shoemakers Guild]] Prior to the [[Reformation]], there are accounts of major festivals in [[Kingsland, Shropshire|Kingsland]]:
In ancient times, while the Romish religion prevailed, all the companies united once a year in celebrating the day of Corpus Christi, with great pomp and splendour. At the reformation this ceremony was commuted for another, held on the second Monday after Trinity Sunday, which is still continued, though with less pomp and circumstance than formerly. The Companies form themselves into processions, headed severally by men on horseback in gaudy apparel, called kings, probably as representatives of the monarchs who granted their charters* They move in marshalled array to Kingsland, where they are met by the mayor and corporation and the day is spent in festivity.{{Cite book |last=Nightingale |first=J. |url=https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/1/18/The_Beauties_of_England_and_Wales%2C_or%2C_Delineations%2C_topographical%2C_historical%2C_and_descriptive%2C_of_each_county_%28IA_beautiesofenglan1301brit%29.pdf |title=The Beauties of England and Wales, or, Delineations, topographical, historical, and descriptive, of each county |year=1819 |volume=13 |location=[[London]]}}
The town's Quarry Park has been the site of cultural activity since before the Reformation: a bank there, cut in the form of an [[amphitheatre]], was used by the [[friar]]s of the adjacent [[convent]], who performed the ancient religious [[mystery play]]s or miracle plays; this continued in the mid-16th century when the plays of [[Thomas Ashton (schoolmaster)|Thomas Ashton]]'s Shrewsbury School attracted royal attention.{{Cite web |title=Ashton Road – Shrewsbury Local History |url=https://shrewsburylocalhistory.org.uk/street-names/ashton-road |access-date=2023-07-08 |language=en-US}} On several occasions the school put on pageants for the visiting Council of Wales and the Marches. In 1581, the Lord President, Sir [[Henry Sidney]], leaving the town by [[barge]], was greeted by several scholars on an island downstream of the [[Shrewsbury Castle|castle]] dressed as green [[nymph]]s with willow branches tied to their heads reciting verses across the water.{{Cite book |last=Champion, Bill. |title=Everyday life in Tudor Shrewsbury |date=1994 |publisher=Shropshire Books |isbn=0-903802-60-0 |location=[Shropshire] |pages=40 |oclc=32893450}} In the later [[Renaissance]] period, the land at Kingsland was devoted to elaborate performances, with grand arbours being built by the various town guilds.{{Cite web |title=Shoemakers' Arbour in The Dingle, Shrewsbury - 1270557 {{!}} Historic England |url=https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1270557 |access-date=2023-03-11 |website=historicengland.org.uk |language=en}} Some of the arbours survive, such as that for the Shoemakers Guild.{{Cite web |title=Shoemakers' Arbour in The Dingle, Shrewsbury - 1270557 {{!}} Historic England |url=https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1270557 |access-date=2023-07-17 |website=historicengland.org.uk |language=en}} [[File:Henry IV, Part 1 Quarto 3.pdf|thumb|Quarto edition of ''Henry IV, Part 1'']] [[William Shakespeare]] set the last two acts of his play, ''Henry IV, Part 1'', written around 1596, near the town.{{Cite book |last1=Dunton-Downer |first1=Leslie |title=Essential Shakespeare |last2=Riding |first2=Alan |date=2004 |publisher=Dorling Kindersley |isbn=978-1-4093-4625-8 |edition=2014 |location=London |pages=116–122}} It has been suggested, placing reliance on a record of a performance by his company, the [[King's Men (playing company)|King's Men]] in the town between 1603 and 1605, and supposed familiarity with the landscape; that Shakespeare performed in the town and knew the area.{{Cite web |date=15 April 2016 |title=When Shakespeare played Shrewsbury: Evidence points to Bard's appearance in county town |url=https://www.shropshirestar.com/entertainment/2016/04/15/when-shakespeare-played-shrewsbury-evidence-points-to-bards-appearance-in-county-town/ |access-date=2023-03-11 |website=Shropshirestar.com |language=en}} Edward I's 13th century engagement with the town, and the execution of Welsh Prince Dafydd ap Gruffydd, was dramatized in [[George Peele]]'s Elizabethan play '''[[The Famous Chronicle of King Edward the First]]''' (c.1592).{{Cite book |last=Peele |first=George |url=http://elizabethandrama.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/10/Edward-I-Script.pdf |title=The famous chronicle of King Edward the First. 1593 |date=1593 |others=Internet Archive}} The playwright [[George Farquhar]]'s 1706 play ''The Recruiting Officer'' is set in the town.{{Cite web |date=16 September 2008 |title=Shrewsbury |url=http://www3.shropshire-cc.gov.uk/shrewsbu.htm |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121110202743/http://www3.shropshire-cc.gov.uk/shrewsbu.htm |archive-date=10 November 2012 |website=Literary Heritage West Midlands |publisher=Shropshire Council |df=dmy-all}} [[File:John Weaver Orpheus and Eurydice 1718.jpg|upright|thumb|John Weaver's 1718 production of ''Orpheus and Eurydice'']] Known as the father of English ballet,{{Cite web |title=Dance Festival in Celebration of 'Father of English Ballet' John Weaver |url=https://www.myshrewsbury.co.uk/blog/dance-festival-in-celebration-of-father-of-english-ballet-john-weaver/ |access-date=2023-03-11 |website=Myshrewsbury.co.uk |language=en}} as well as the originator of pantomime,{{Cite web |title=John Weaver |url=https://www.oxfordreference.com/display/10.1093/oi/authority.20110803121502615 |access-date=2023-03-11 |website=Oxford Reference |language=en}} [[John Weaver (dancer)|John Weaver]], developed his art in Shrewsbury. A second generation dancing master in the town,{{Cite book |title=Dictionary of National Biography, Volume 60 |publisher=Smith, Elder and Co., London |year=1885–1900 |editor-last=Lee |editor-first=Sidney |page=91}}Article by William George Dimock Fletcher. he also wrote on the philosophy, theology, statecraft and biology embedded in his era's understating of dance, which he located in a wider understanding of his culture as representing a component of [[Ptolemy|Ptolemaic]] [[harmony]] and an earnest part of the statecraft of his time.{{Cite journal |last=Taylor |first=Nancy |date=November 2001 |title=John Weaver and the Origins of English Pantomime: A Neoclassical Theory and Practice for Uniting Dance and Theatre |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/theatre-survey/article/abs/john-weaver-and-the-origins-of-english-pantomime-a-neoclassical-theory-and-practice-for-uniting-dance-and-theatre/51E38DC25AE95FF38B5890A6A2668B27 |journal=Theatre Survey |language=en |volume=42 |issue=2 |pages=191–214 |doi=10.1017/S0040557401000102 |issn=1475-4533 |s2cid=143360948|url-access=subscription }} ===In modern popular culture=== Pioneering early 18th-century travel writers [[Daniel Defoe]] and [[Celia Fiennes]] wrote about their visits to Shrewsbury in ''[[A Tour thro' the Whole Island of Great Britain]]''{{cite web |title=Roads of East Shropshire Through Time |url=https://www.amberley-books.com/roads-of-east-shropshire-through-time.html |website=Amberley publishing |access-date=6 August 2023}} and ''Through England on a Side Saddle in the Time of William and Mary''{{cite web |last1=Fiennes |first1=Celia |title=Through England on a Side Saddle in the Time of William and Mary |url=https://www.visionofbritain.org.uk/travellers/Fiennes/26 |website=Vision of Britain |access-date=6 August 2023}} respectively. In the 19th century, [[Charles Dickens]] made three visits to the town. The first, in 1838, was while he was travelling to Wales. On this occasion he stayed at the Lion Hotel. In 1852 he again visited, this time as part of a theatrical tour, staging benefit performances to raise money for the [[Guild of Literature and Art]]. His final visit, in 1858, was as part of a nationwide reading tour. Once again he stayed at the Lion.{{cite web |title=Charles Dickens and Shrewsbury |url=https://www.thecircumlocutionoffice.com/trail/shrewsbury/ |website=The circumlocution office |date=29 December 2015 |access-date=6 August 2023}} The town appears in the ''[[Brother Cadfael]]'' novels by [[Ellis Peters]]. The novels take Shrewsbury Abbey for their setting and have made medieval Shrewsbury familiar to a wide readership.{{Cite web |title=Brother Cadfael |url=http://user.chollian.net/~beringar/e-cad.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071215072718/http://user.chollian.net/~beringar/e-cad.htm |archive-date=15 December 2007 |access-date=23 February 2008 |website=user.chollian.net/~beringar}} Shrewsbury was used as the setting for the 1984 television film ''[[A Christmas Carol (1984 film)|A Christmas Carol]]'', which filmed many of its interior and exterior shots in and around the town. [[File:Evolution Explored Shrewsbury.jpg|thumb|The Magnum Photos ''Evolution Explored'' exhibition in The Square]] In early 2017, Shrewsbury BID, The Hive and GRAIN Photography Hub organised an outdoor [[Magnum Photos]] exhibition.{{Cite web |title=Evolution Explored {{!}} A Magnum Photos Exhibition |url=https://originalshrewsbury.co.uk/evolution-explored |df=dmy-all |access-date=14 June 2018 |archive-date=14 June 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180614144325/https://originalshrewsbury.co.uk/evolution-explored |url-status=dead }} Inspired by Shrewsbury's links to Charles Darwin, this exhibition considered the theme of evolution through the eyes of international photographers. The 10-week exhibition was free to the public and staged at St Mary's Churchyard and The Square. In 2022, the BBC production of ''[[Great Expectations (2023 TV series)|Great Expectations]]'' with [[Olivia Colman]] and [[Tom Hardy]] was filmed in the town.{{Cite web |last=Hill |first=Lauren |date=24 May 2022 |title=Filming of Great Expectations under way in Shrewsbury starring Olivia Colman and Tom Hardy |url=https://www.shropshirestar.com/news/local-hubs/shrewsbury/2022/05/24/filming-of-great-expectations-under-way-in-shrewsbury-starring-olivia-coleman-and-tom-hardy/ |access-date=2023-03-11 |website=Shropshirestar.com |language=en}} The same year, episodes of [[The Apprentice (British TV series)|''The Apprentice'']] and ''[[Celebrity Hunted]]'' were filmed in Shrewsbury. The prison was used for the BBC TV series [[Time (2021 TV series)|''Time'']] as well appearing in the ITV remake of [[The Ipcress File (TV series)|''The Ipcress File'']].{{cite web |title=Shrewsbury in TV and Film |url=https://originalshrewsbury.co.uk/blog/shrewsbury-in-tv-and-film |website=Original Shrewsbury |access-date=31 August 2023}} ===Contemporary performance=== Theatre Severn is the town's main performing arts complex, it is situated in Frankwell next to the Welsh Bridge on the bank of the River Severn. The theatre includes two performance spaces, the 635 seat Main Auditorium and a smaller studio space, the Walker Theatre, which can accommodate 250 seating or 500 standing. The venue includes a full sized dance studio, function rooms and a restaurant.{{Cite web |title=Theatre Severn {{!}} Original Shrewsbury |url=https://originalshrewsbury.co.uk/visit/theatre-severn |access-date=2018-06-14 |website=originalshrewsbury.co.uk |language=en}} The new complex replaced the old theatre, the Music Hall, which has been refurbished and expanded in preparation for its current use as home to [[Shrewsbury Museum and Art Gallery]], opened 2014.{{Cite web |title=Shrewsbury Museum and Art Gallery {{!}} Original Shrewsbury |url=https://originalshrewsbury.co.uk/visit/shrewsbury-museum-art-gallery |access-date=2018-06-14 |website=originalshrewsbury.co.uk |language=en}} == Royal visits == The following royal visits have been made to Shrewsbury in modern times: * [[Princess Victoria of Saxe-Coburg-Saalfeld|The Duchess of Kent]] and [[Queen Victoria|Princess Victoria]] visited in 1832. * The [[Prince George, Duke of Cambridge|Duke of Cambridge]] visited in 1886 when he inspected the [[Shropshire Yeomanry]] on the racecourse.{{cite book|last=Gladstone|first=E.W.|year=1953|title=The Shropshire Yeomanry 1795-1945, the History of a Volunteer Cavalry Regiment|publisher=The Whitethorn Press, Manchester|pages=111–114}} * [[Princess Louise, Duchess of Argyll|Princess Louise]], visited in 1898.{{Cite web |title=PRINCESS- LOUISE AT SHREWSBURY. '-{{!}}1898-01-20{{!}}Evening Express - Welsh Newspapers |url=https://newspapers.library.wales/view/3273211/3273215/79/lorne |access-date=2020-03-26 |website=newspapers.library.wales |language=en}} * The [[Duke of Teck]] (later Marquess of Cambridge) visited the town in 1911.{{Cite web |last=Shrewsbury School |title=Moments in our History |url=https://www.shrewsbury.org.uk/wiki/moments-in-our-history}} * [[George V]] visited the town in 1914.{{Cite web |title=Watch The King's Visit to the Royal Agricultural Show, Shrewsbury |url=https://player.bfi.org.uk/free/film/watch-the-kings-visit-to-the-royal-agricultural-show-shrewsbury-1914-online |access-date=2020-03-26 |website=BFI Player |language=en}} * In 1925 [[Princess Helena Victoria]] visited the town. * 1925 saw a shopping visit to Shrewsbury by [[Mary of Teck|Queen Mary]] who arrived in [[Yorton]]. * In 1929 the [[Sultan of Zanzibar]] and the [[Sultan of Oman]] |url=https://volunteeringshropshiresheritage.wordpress.com/2013/11/15/20th-century-royal-visitors-to-shrewsbury/ |access-date=2020-03-26 |website=volunteeringshropshiresheritage |language=en}} * As |website=Shropshirestar.com |language=en}} ==Festivals and events== [[File:Shrewsbury Flower Show 2013.jpg|thumb|The Shropshire Horticultural Society organises the town's annual flower show in August.]] The town is home to the 'longest running flower show in the world'. The annual [[Shrewsbury Flower Show]] is a two-day event, which takes place in mid-August, has been running for more than 125 years.{{Cite web |title=Shrewsbury Flower Show {{!}} Original Shrewsbury |url=https://originalshrewsbury.co.uk/see-do/events/shrewsbury-flower-show |access-date=2018-06-14 |website=originalshrewsbury.co.uk |language=en}} The event attracts around 100,000 visitors each year and offers a multitude of events, exhibitions and gardens, with a fireworks display at the end of each day. [[File:Musicians at Shrewsbury Folk Festival.jpg|thumb|The [[Shrewsbury Folk Festival]] is held at the West Mid Showground.]] The [[Shrewsbury Folk Festival]] has been held in Shrewsbury since 2006. Held annually over the August bank holiday, the event is very popular, with people travelling from across the UK to attend.{{Cite web |title=Shrewsbury Folk Festival {{!}} Original Shrewsbury |url=https://originalshrewsbury.co.uk/see-do/events/shrewsbury-folk-festival |access-date=2018-06-14 |website=originalshrewsbury.co.uk |language=en}} The Shrewsbury Arts Trail is focused on showcasing contemporary art and includes sculptures, exhibitions, workshops and events. 2024' theme is "Time" and features work by renowned artists alongside local artists.{{Cite web |title=Home {{!}} Shrewsbury Arts Trail |url=https://www.shrewsburyartstrail.com/ |access-date=2024-07-13 |website=Shrewsbury Arts Trai |language=en}} The town celebrates its links to Darwin with an annual Darwin Festival in February. The two and a half week multi-media event celebrates the town as the 'Origin of Independent Thinking' with activities including lectures, dance performances and live music.{{cite web |title=Darwin Shrewsbury Festival |url=https://originalshrewsbury.co.uk/events/darwin-shrewsbury-festival |website=Original Shrewsbury |access-date=27 August 2023}} [[File:Art_Exhibition_in_Shrewsbury_Museum_and_Art_Gallery,_image_includes_Jacob_Chandler's_illustrations_of_the_Dancing_Figures_in_'As_You_Like_It'.jpg|thumb|Art Exhibition in Shrewsbury Museum and Art Gallery]] Other events held in spring and summer include the Shrewsbury Bookfest, Shrewsbury Regatta, Cycle Grand Prix, Shrewsbury Carnival, Food Festival, Dragon Boat Race and the Coracle World Championships.{{Cite web |title=Events in Shrewsbury |url=http://www.originalshrewsbury.co.uk/see-do/events |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170509054917/http://www.originalshrewsbury.co.uk/see-do/events |archive-date=9 May 2017 |access-date=24 May 2017 |df=dmy-all}} Since 2016, Shrewsbury International Comedy Festival has been held over the third weekend of July in multiple venues across town.{{cite web |title=About |url=https://sicfest.co.uk/sample-page/ |website=Scifest |access-date=11 August 2023}} Comics Salopia (formerly the Cartoon Festival) was a large biannual festival of the comics arts, attracting over a quarter of a million visitors. In format and scope it aimed to emulate on a smaller scale, the [[Angoulême International Comics Festival]] in France. In June 2023, it was announced that after making substantial losses in 2022, it would not be continued.{{cite news |title=British comics festival Comics Salopia calls it a day |url=https://www.comicsbeat.com/british-comics-festival-comics-salopia-calls-it-a-day/ |newspaper=The Beat |date=20 June 2023 |access-date=11 August 2023 |last1=Simons |first1=Dean }} ==Museums and attractions== [[File:The Music Hall, Shrewsbury 01.jpg|thumb|upright|[[Shrewsbury Museum and Art Gallery]]]] The [[Shrewsbury Museum and Art Gallery]] is in the town square, occupying the former music hall and the 13th-century Vaughan's mansion and is part of Shropshire Museums.{{cite web |title=Shrewsbury Museum & Art Gallery |url=https://www.shropshiremuseums.org.uk/smag/ |website=Shropshire Museums |access-date=9 July 2023 |archive-date=30 May 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240530165944/https://www.shropshiremuseums.org.uk/smag/ |url-status=dead }} The [[Old Market Hall, Shrewsbury|Old Market Hall]] cinema opened in 2004 in the prominent Tudor market hall positioned in The Square. The independent cinema features daily screens of films from around the world along with a cafe and bar.{{Cite web |title=Old Market Hall {{!}} Original Shrewsbury |url=https://originalshrewsbury.co.uk/visit/old-market-hall |access-date=2018-06-14 |website=originalshrewsbury.co.uk |language=en}} Further museums in the town include the Shropshire Regimental Museum, renamed in 2019 as Soldiers of Shropshire Museum,{{Cite web |title=About Us |url=https://www.soldiersofshropshire.co.uk/about-us/ |access-date=5 July 2021 |publisher=Soldiers of Shropshire |archive-date=11 July 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210711140540/https://www.soldiersofshropshire.co.uk/about-us/ |url-status=dead }} based at Shrewsbury Castle, and the restored 19th-century steam-powered [[Coleham Pumping Station]],{{Cite web |title=Shrewsbury Museums |url=http://www.shrewsburymuseums.com/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060503032147/http://www.shrewsburymuseums.com/ |archive-date=3 May 2006 |access-date=18 September 2007 |publisher=Shrewsbury Museum Service |df=dmy-all}} which opens for tours on specific days each year. There are various private galleries and art shops around the town, including the Gateway Education and Arts Centre.{{Cite web |title=The Gateway {{!}} Original Shrewsbury |url=https://originalshrewsbury.co.uk/visit/gateway |access-date=2018-06-14 |website=originalshrewsbury.co.uk |language=en}} The [[National Trust]] owns the last remaining [[Town Walls Tower]] which dates from the 14th century. It is now available to rent as a one bedroom holiday cottage.{{Cite web |title=Attingham Park Estate: Town Walls |url=http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/attingham-park-estate-town-walls-tower/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130807082002/http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/attingham-park-estate-town-walls-tower/ |archive-date=7 August 2013 |publisher=[[National Trust]] |df=dmy-all}} [[File:Cross watercolor.jpg|thumb|upright|The Golden Cross]] The town has some very old [[public house]]s and [[coaching inn]]s: * The [[Golden Cross, Shrewsbury|Golden Cross]] is reputed to be the oldest licensed public house in Shrewsbury and records show that it was used as an inn as far back as 1428; its original name was the Sextry, because it began as the [[sacristy]] of Old St Chad's Church.{{Cite web |title=Shrewsbury's oldest pub |url=http://www.goldencrosshotel.co.uk/alternate.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080302165416/http://www.goldencrosshotel.co.uk/alternate.html |archive-date=2 March 2008 |access-date=23 February 2008 |publisher=GoldenCrossHotel.co.uk |df=dmy-all}} * The [[King's Head, Shrewsbury|King's Head]] in Mardol contains a 14th-century wall painting,{{Cite web |title=The King's Head |url=https://originalshrewsbury.co.uk/business-directory/kings-head |access-date=2023-07-28 |website=Original Shrewsbury |language=en-GB}} and its timbers have been dated to {{circa}}1404.{{Cite web |title=The King's Head, Shrewsbury, Shropshire {{!}} Educational Images {{!}} Historic England |url=https://historicengland.org.uk/services-skills/education/educational-images/the-kings-head-shrewsbury-7834 |access-date=2023-07-28 |website=historicengland.org.uk |language=en}} * The Dun Cow in Abbey Foregate dates to the 16th century.{{Cite web |title=The Dun Cow Public House, Shrewsbury - 1246447 {{!}} Historic England |url=https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1246447 |access-date=2023-07-28 |website=historicengland.org.uk |language=en}} ==Media== Two newspapers are published for Shrewsbury – the local edition of the county's ''[[Shropshire Star]]'' and the more traditional ''[[Shrewsbury Chronicle]]'', which is one of the oldest weekly newspapers in the country, having produced its first edition in 1772.{{cite news |title=The Shrewsbury Chronicle, 1772-1922 |url=http://archive.spectator.co.uk/article/16th-december-1922/26/the-shrewsbury-chronicle-1772-1922 |access-date=23 October 2018 |work=The Spectator |date=19 December 1922 |quote=We congratulate that good old country paper, the Shrewsbury Chronicle, on completing its hundred and fiftieth year. It is a few weeks younger than the Morning Post, having first appeared on November 28rd,1772, as the Shrewsbury Chronicle; or, Wood's British Commercial Pamphlet. Thomas Wood,- the publisher, had had experience of a Birmingham weekly before he went to Shrewsbury.}} The forerunner of ''[[Private Eye]]'' was a school magazine edited by [[Richard Ingrams]], [[Willie Rushton]], [[Christopher Booker]] and [[Paul Foot (journalist)|Paul Foot]] at [[Shrewsbury School]] in the mid-1950s.{{Cite web |title=From Private Eye to Public Nose |url=http://www.shrewsbury.org.uk/index.cfm?fuseaction=features.content&cmid=264 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090314003620/http://www.shrewsbury.org.uk/index.cfm?fuseaction=features.content&cmid=264 |archive-date=14 March 2009 |access-date=26 April 2010 |website=Shrewsbury School website |df=dmy-all}} Local news and television programmes are provided by [[BBC West Midlands]] and [[ITV Central]]. Television signals are received from the [[The Wrekin transmitting station|Wrekin]] TV transmitter.{{cite web|url=https://ukfree.tv/transmitters/tv/The_Wrekin|title=Full Freeview on the The[sic] Wrekin (Telford and Wrekin, England) transmitter|date=1 May 2004|website=UK Free TV|access-date=25 September 2023}} There are three radio stations that specifically serve either the Shrewsbury area or encompass it as part of a Shropshire-wide broadcast. They are [[Hits Radio Black Country & Shropshire]];{{Cite web |title=Free Radio Shropshire & Black Country |url=http://www.freeradio.co.uk/shropshire/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120821115903/http://www.freeradio.co.uk/shropshire/ |archive-date=21 August 2012 |access-date=27 March 2012 |df=dmy-all}} [[BBC Radio Shropshire]], which is based in Shrewsbury;{{Cite web |title=BBC Radio Shropshire |url=http://www.bbc.co.uk/shropshire/local_radio/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080106132306/http://www.bbc.co.uk/shropshire/local_radio/ |archive-date=6 January 2008 |access-date=23 February 2008 |df=dmy-all}} and, as of September 2020, [[Greatest Hits Radio Black Country & Shropshire]], which previously broadcast from the Shropshire Star building in Telford.{{Cite web |title=106.5 & 107.1 The Severn |url=http://www.thesevern.co.uk |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080103191301/http://www.thesevern.co.uk/ |archive-date=3 January 2008 |access-date=23 February 2008 |df=dmy-all}} In 2009 an online independent media company, Shropshire Live, launched covering Shrewsbury and Shropshire.{{Cite web |title=shropshirelive.com |url=http://www.shropshirelive.com |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110108032944/http://www.shropshirelive.com/ |archive-date=8 January 2011 |df=dmy-all}} ==Food== [[File:Shrewsbury Market Hall Interior.jpg|thumb|The interior of [[Shrewsbury Market Hall]], which hosts a variety of cafés and restaurants.]] [[Shrewsbury cake]]s (or biscuits) are typically crisp and brittle creations that may incorporate fruit. They can be small in size for serving several at a time, or large for serving as a dessert in their own right. Traditionally they have a distinct hint of lemon.{{Cite web |title=Shrewsbury Biscuits {{!}} Original Shrewsbury |url=https://originalshrewsbury.co.uk/shrewsbury-biscuits |access-date=2018-06-14 |website=originalshrewsbury.co.uk |language=en}} The playwright [[William Congreve]] mentioned Shrewsbury cakes in his play ''[[The Way of the World]]'' in 1700 as a simile{{Cite web |last=Congreve |first=William |year=1700 |title=The Way of the World |url=http://www.fullbooks.com/The-Way-of-the-World2.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100604061522/http://www.fullbooks.com/The-Way-of-the-World2.html |archive-date=4 June 2010 |access-date=21 June 2009 |publisher=Full Books |df=dmy-all}} (Witwoud – "Why, brother Wilfull of Salop, you may be as short as a Shrewsbury cake, if you please. But I tell you 'tis not modish to know relations in town"). The recipe is also included in several early cookbooks including ''The Compleat Cook of 1658''.{{Cite web |title=Shrewsbury Cake Recipes |url=http://www.theoldecookerybook.com/~theopden/wiki/index.php/Shrewsbury_cake_recipes |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://archive.today/20081231150504/http://www.theoldecookerybook.com/~theopden/wiki/index.php/Shrewsbury_cake_recipes |archive-date=31 December 2008 |access-date=21 June 2009 |website=The Olde Cookery Book |df=dmy-all}} A final reference to the cakes can be seen to this day as the subject of a plaque affixed to a building close to Shrewsbury's town library by the junction of Castle Street and School Gardens. The aforementioned plaque marks the spot where the Shrewsbury Cake's recipe is said to have been pioneered in 1760 by Mr Pailin; a further quote, drawn from [[Richard Harris Barham]]'s ''Ingoldby Legends'', reads: {{cquote| Oh! Pailin. Prince of Cake Compounders The mouth liquifies at the very name. }} Shrewsbury is the origin of a popular [[Simnel cake]] recipe. Different towns had their own recipes and shapes of the Simnel cake. [[Bury, Greater Manchester|Bury]], [[Devizes]] and Shrewsbury produced large numbers to their own recipes, but it is the Bury version that became most well known.{{cite web |title=Bury Simnel Cake |url=https://www.foodsofengland.info/burysimnelcake.html |website=Foods of England |access-date=21 April 2025}} The town is alleged to be the origin of [[Shrewsbury sauce]], made from Worcester sauce, red wine and mustard, thickened with flour, which is typically served with lamb. Only known from the 1960s when it appeared in the J. Salmon County Series Cookbooks.{{cite web |title=Shrewsbury Sauce |url=https://www.foodsofengland.info/shrewsburysauce.html |website=Foods of England |access-date=21 April 2025}} [[File:DSC00406 (cropped).jpg|thumb|[[Ditherington Flax Mill]]]] Beer brewed in Shrewsbury was celebrated as early as about 1400 when the bard [[Iolo Goch]] praised the supply of "Crwg Amwythig" dispensed at the [[Sycharth]] palace of [[Owain Glyndŵr]].{{Cite book |last=Pidgeon |first=Henry |url=https://archive.org/details/memorialsshrews01pidggoog |title=Memorials of Shrewsbury |publisher=J. H. Leake |year=1851 |page=[https://archive.org/details/memorialsshrews01pidggoog/page/n282 261]}} In 1900 there were eight breweries in the town, chief among them being Southam's and Trouncer's, which had their own [[malting]]s and owned many local public houses, as well as five other maltsters,{{Cite book |title=Kelly's Directory of Shropshire |publisher=Kelly's |year=1900 |pages=333, 391}} but the conventional brewing industry gradually closed after takeovers in the 1960s. The last maltings, at Ditherington, closed in 1987.{{Cite web |title=Shrewsbury Flaxmill Maltings Story (see Creating a Master Plan for the future) |url=http://www.flaxmill-maltings.co.uk/shrewsbury-flaxmill-maltings-story |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181222082023/http://www.flaxmill-maltings.co.uk/shrewsbury-flaxmill-maltings-story |archive-date=22 December 2018 |access-date=21 December 2018 |website=Friends of the Flaxmill-Maltings}} Completed in 1797, these maltings, known as the [[Ditherington Flax Mill]] from its original purpose, was the world's first iron-framed building and commonly regarded as "the grandfather of the skyscraper". Its importance was recognised in the 1950s, resulting in it becoming a Grade I [[listed building]].W. G. Rimmer, 'Castle Foregate Flax Mill, Shrewsbury' ''Transactions of Shropshire Archaeological Society'' LVI (1957–60), 49ff.{{Cite web |title='Father of the skyscraper' rescued for the nation |url=http://www.english-heritage.org.uk/server/show/ConWebDoc.4839 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090116041015/http://www.english-heritage.org.uk/server/show/ConWebDoc.4839 |archive-date=16 January 2009 |publisher=[[English Heritage]]}} After the biggest heritage project ever undertaken by [[Historic England]], the building was restored and opened as a museum in 2022.{{Cite news |last=Batten |first=Rhiannon |date=2022-10-20 |title=Steam trains, shipwrecks and Peter Pan's garden: 10 great UK family days out for half-term and autumn |language=en-GB |work=The Guardian |url=https://www.theguardian.com/travel/2022/oct/20/steam-trains-shipwrecks-and-peter-pans-garden-10-great-uk-family-days-out-for-half-term-and-autumn |access-date=2023-07-23 |issn=0261-3077}} A real ale brewery, The Salopian Brewery, was established in the town in 1995.{{Cite web |title=Salopian Brewing Company Ltd |url=http://www.quaffale.org.uk/php/brewery/489 |access-date=9 December 2017 |website=Quaffale.org.uk}} It was based in the Old Dairy on Mytton Oak Road before relocating in 2014 to [[Hadnall]] a few miles north of the town.{{Cite web |title=:: Welcome to Salopian Breweries |url=http://www.salopianbrewery.co.uk/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171002002932/http://www.salopianbrewery.co.uk/ |archive-date=2 October 2017 |access-date=9 December 2017 |publisher=Salopian Brewery |df=dmy-all}} ==Architecture== [[File:Fish Street, Shrewsbury - geograph.org.uk - 4492536.jpg|thumb|Fish Street and Grope Lane, Shrewsbury]] The historic town centre still retains its medieval street pattern and many narrow passages. Some of the passages, especially those that pass through buildings from one street to the next, are called "[[wikt:shut#Etymology 2|shuts]]" (the word deriving from "to shoot through" from one street to another).Scott-Davies, Allan; Sears, R.S., ''Shuts and Passages of Shrewsbury'', Shropshire Books, June 1986. {{ISBN|978-0-903802-34-5}} Many specialist shops, traditional pubs and local restaurants can be found in the hidden corners, squares and lanes of Shrewsbury. Many of the [[street name]]s have remained unchanged for centuries and there are some more unusual names, such as Longden Coleham, Dogpole, [[Mardol (street)|Mardol]], Frankwell, Roushill, [[Grope Lane]], Gullet Passage, Murivance, the Dana, Portobello, Bear Steps, Shoplatch and Bellstone.{{Cite web |title=Shropshire Information |url=http://www.fatbadgers.co.uk/Tourism/shrinfo.htm |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080202102909/http://www.fatbadgers.co.uk/Tourism/shrinfo.htm |archive-date=2 February 2008 |access-date=23 February 2008 |publisher=FatBadgers.co.uk |df=dmy-all}} The [[Shrewsbury Library|public library]], in the pre-1882 [[Shrewsbury School]] building,{{Cite web |title=Shrewsbury School history |url=http://www.shrewsbury.org.uk/index.cfm?fuseaction=features.content&cmid=124 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090314003503/http://www.shrewsbury.org.uk/index.cfm?fuseaction=features.content&cmid=124 |archive-date=14 March 2009 |access-date=11 May 2009 |website=shrewsbury.org.uk |df=dmy-all}} is on Castle Street. Above the main entrance are two statues bearing the Greek inscriptions "''Philomathes''" and "''Polymathes''". These portray the virtues "Lover of learning" and "Much learning" to convey the lesson that it is good to gain knowledge through a love of learning.{{Cite web|title=Shrewsbury - Philomath and Polymath|url=https://statues.vanderkrogt.net/object.php?webpage=ST&record=gbwm011|access-date=2020-07-16|website=statues.vanderkrogt.net}} In the centre of the town lies [[The Quarry (park)|The Quarry]]. This {{convert|29|acre|ha}}{{Cite web |title=The Quarry Park {{!}} Original Shrewsbury |url=https://originalshrewsbury.co.uk/visit/quarry-park |access-date=2018-06-14 |website=originalshrewsbury.co.uk |language=en}} riverside park attracts thousands of people throughout the year and is enjoyed as a place of recreation. Shrewsbury has traditionally been known as the "Town of Flowers", a slogan incorporated into many of the signs on entrance to the town via major roads, although this was replaced in 2007 with "The birthplace of Charles Darwin". [[File:Shrewsbury Column.jpg|upright|thumb|[[Lord Hill's Column]]]] The [[British Army]]'s [[Light Infantry]] has been associated with Shrewsbury since the 17th century when the first regiments were formed and many more regiments have been raised at Shrewsbury before being deployed all over the world from the [[American Revolutionary War]] to the conflicts in [[Iraq]] and [[Afghanistan]]. Today, after several major reorganisations, the Light Infantry now forms part of the regiment known simply as [[the Rifles]]. Shrewsbury's [[Copthorne Barracks]], spiritual home of the Light Division, ultimately housed the Headquarters of the British Army's [[143rd Infantry Brigade (United Kingdom)|143 (West Midlands) Brigade]] before it moved in 2014, while that of the [[British 5th Infantry Division|5th Division]] disbanded in April 2012 as part of the reorganisation of the Army's [[Support Command (United Kingdom)|Support Command]].{{Cite web |title=The Kings Shropshire Light Infantry (53rd and 85th foot) |url=http://www.army.mod.uk/lightinfantry/history_traditions/county_regiments/ksli.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060728214305/http://www.army.mod.uk/lightinfantry/history_traditions/county_regiments/ksli.htm |archive-date=28 July 2006 |access-date=4 March 2008 |publisher=Army.mod.uk}} Copthorne Barracks was ultimately closed and the site sold in 2018 for residential redevelopment.{{cite news|title=Hard to recognise barracks now|work=Shropshire Star|date=21 January 2019|page=1}} Under this, the acquired buildings were demolished apart from part of the 19th century 'Keep' which was retained for conversion to apartments. The development has been named Copthorne Keep.{{cite news|title=Diggers move in at historic military base|work=Shropshire Star|date=21 January 2019|page=2}} Another notable feature of the town is [[Lord Hill's Column]], sited outside the Shirehall. At {{convert|133|ft|6|in|m|1|abbr=on}} it is the tallest Doric column in England.{{Cite web |title=About The Column |url=https://friendsoflordhillscolumn.co.uk/about/ |access-date=15 February 2022 |website=Friends of Lord Hill's Column}} It was erected as a monument to [[Rowland Hill, 1st Viscount Hill|Rowland Hill]] commander of [[II Corps (United Kingdom)|II Corps]] at [[Battle of Waterloo|Waterloo]] and the man who led the charge against the [[Imperial Guard (Napoleon I)|Imperial Guard]] towards the end of the battle.{{Cite web |title=Photo Gallery |url=http://www.shrewsbury.gov.uk/public/leisure/gallery/default.htm |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071107040530/http://www.shrewsbury.gov.uk/public/leisure/gallery/default.htm |archive-date=7 November 2007 |access-date=2 January 2008 |website=Shrewsbury and Atcham Borough Council |df=dmy-all}} ''[[The Quantum Leap]]'' is an abstract sculpture unveiled in the town centre in 2009 to mark the bicentenary of the birth of Shrewsbury biologist [[Charles Darwin]].{{Cite news|url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/local/shropshire/hi/people_and_places/arts_and_culture/newsid_8103000/8103529.stm|title=Shrewsbury's Quantum Leap built|date=2009-06-22|access-date=2009-10-21|publisher=[[BBC News]]}} Shrewsbury's town centre is almost entirely encircled by the River Severn and there are [[List of crossings of the River Severn|nine bridges]] across the river. In addition, there are several that cross the [[Rea Brook]]. Working downstream, they are in order: *Frankwell Bridge, a modern pedestrian footbridge which spans the River Severn between Frankwell and the town centre. {{multiple image | width = 120 | image1 = Shrewsbury bridge 01956.jpg | alt1 = | image2 = Welsh Bridge, Shrewsbury, 27 May 2021 from Frankwell Footbridge.jpg | alt2 = | footer = | align = | direction = | total_width = | caption1 = The medieval St George's Bridge, {{circa|1776}} | caption2 = The current Welsh Bridge }} *The [[Welsh Bridge]], which was built in 1793-95 to replace the medieval [[St George's Bridge]]; featured in [[Thomas Pennant]]'s ''A Tour through Wales'' published in 1781. The old bridge was sketched by [[J. M. W. Turner]] in 1794 as the basis for a later water colour painting.{{Cite web |last=Tate |title='Shrewsbury: The Old Welsh Bridge', Joseph Mallord William Turner, 1794 |url=https://www.tate.org.uk/art/artworks/turner-shrewsbury-the-old-welsh-bridge-d00330 |access-date=2023-07-20 |website=Tate |language=en-GB}} *Further along from the Welsh Bridge is the [[Porthill Bridge]], a pedestrian suspension bridge running between the Quarry and Porthill, built in 1922.{{Cite news |date=13 July 2012 |title=Article of the bridge reopening in 2012 from local newspaper. |work=[[Shropshire Star]] |url=http://www.shropshirestar.com/news/2012/07/13/repaired-shrewsbury-bridge-open-for-business/ |access-date=4 May 2014}}{{Cite news |date=20 June 2012 |title=BBC News article of the bridge reopening |work=BBC News |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-england-shropshire-18518275 |access-date=4 May 2014}} [[File:Kingsland BridgeCB.jpg|thumb|[[Kingsland Bridge]], the town's only toll bridge]] *The next bridge along the river is [[Kingsland Bridge]], a privately owned [[toll bridge]]. *The subsequent bridge is the [[Greyfriars Bridge]], a pedestrian bridge between Coleham and the town centre. [[File:English Bridge Shrewsbury.jpg|thumb|The [[English Bridge]]]] *Following the Greyfriars Bridge is the [[English Bridge]], historically called ''Stone Bridge'', which was rebuilt in the 1920s. The bridge was also sketched by Turner.{{cite web |title=Shrewsbury: The Town seen from the River with the New English Bridge in the Foreground |url=https://www.tate.org.uk/art/artworks/turner-shrewsbury-the-town-seen-from-the-river-with-the-new-english-bridge-in-the-d00331 |website=Tate Gallery |access-date=26 September 2023}} *Beyond it is the [[Shrewsbury railway station|railway station]], which is partly built over the river. *After the station is [[Castle Walk Footbridge]], another modern pedestrian footbridge.{{Cite web |title=A Short History of Shrewsbury |url=http://www.localhistories.org/shrewsbury.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080219123422/http://www.localhistories.org/shrewsbury.html |archive-date=19 February 2008 |access-date=3 February 2008 |website=localhistories.org |df=dmy-all}}{{Cite web |title=Severn Bridges {{!}} Original Shrewsbury |url=https://originalshrewsbury.co.uk/see-do/severn-bridges |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180614171604/https://originalshrewsbury.co.uk/see-do/severn-bridges |archive-date=14 June 2018 |access-date=2018-06-14 |website=originalshrewsbury.co.uk |language=en}} *The last bridge to cross the river within the Shrewsbury bypass area is the [[A5112]] Telford Way, which has separate lanes for vehicles, bicycles and pedestrians. [[A. E. Housman]] wrote of the area in ''[[A Shropshire Lad]]'', which mentions the bridges of the town in ''part XXVIII: The Welsh Marches''.{{Cite web |title=Complete Housman |url=http://www.chiark.greenend.org.uk/~martinh/poems/complete_housman.html#ASLxxviii |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080113204350/http://www.chiark.greenend.org.uk/~martinh/poems/complete_housman.html |archive-date=13 January 2008 |access-date=17 March 2008 |website=greenend.org.uk/~martinh |df=dmy-all}} {{cquote| High the vanes of Shrewsbury gleam Islanded in Severn stream; The bridges from the steepled crest, Cross the water east and west. }} ==Transport== ===Railway=== [[File:Shrewsbury station.JPG|thumb|The main station building]] [[Shrewsbury railway station]] is served by two [[train operating companies]]: * [[Transport for Wales Rail]] operates services running north to {{stnlink|Wrexham General}}, {{stnlink|Crewe}}, {{stnlink|Chester}} and {{rws|Manchester Piccadilly}}; southbound trains go to {{stnlink|Hereford}}, {{stnlink|Cardiff Central}} and {{stnlink|Swansea}}; and westbound to {{stnlink|Aberystwyth}}{{Cite web |title=Timetables |work=Transport for Wales |date=10 December 2023 |access-date=14 April 2024 |url= https://tfw.wales/service-status/timetables |quote=}} * [[West Midlands Trains]] run services to {{stnlink|Birmingham New Street}}, via [[Telford Central railway station|Telford]] and {{stnlink|Wolverhampton}}{{Cite web |title=Train timetables and schedules |work=West Midlands Railway |date=10 December 2023 |access-date=14 April 2024 |url= https://www.westmidlandsrailway.co.uk/travel-information/journey-planning/timetables |quote=}} The main railway station building was built in a [[mock Tudor]] architectural style; it includes a clock tower, imitation Tudor chimneys and carved heads in the frames of every window and is [[Grade II listed]].{{NHLE|grade=II|desc=Shrewsbury Station|num=1246546|date=13 May 1969}} There is a small [[British Transport Police]] station within the building. The station is known as the ''Gateway to Wales''.{{Cite web |title=Travel Information {{!}} Original Shrewsbury |url=http://www.originalshrewsbury.co.uk/see-do/travel-information |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170522160008/http://www.originalshrewsbury.co.uk/see-do/travel-information |archive-date=22 May 2017 |df=dmy-all}} {{rws|Shrewsbury Abbey}} was the terminus of the [[Shropshire and Montgomeryshire Railway]], which connected Shrewsbury with [[Llanymynech]]. {{rws|Shrewsbury West}} was the railway's other station in the town. The line and the stations closed in 1960.{{cite book |first=Eric S. |last=Tonks |title=The Shropshire and Montgomeryshire Railway |publisher=The Industrial Society |orig-date=1949 |date=1972 |isbn=9780901096098 |pages=11–12}} {{rws|Abbey Foregate}} was built by the [[Shrewsbury and Birmingham Railway]] and closed in 1912.{{cite book|author=R.V.J. Butt |title= The Directory of Railway Stations |publisher=Patrick Stephens Ltd.|page=11 |year=1995}} {{ISBN|1-85260-508-1}} ===Buses=== [[File:The quick way into Shrewsbury (geograph 7641484) (cropped).jpg|thumb|An Arriva [[park & ride]] bus at the Oxon site in November 2023]] Bus services in the town are operated primarily by [[Arriva Midlands]]; routes are centred around [[Shrewsbury bus station]], adjacent to the [[Darwin Shopping Centre]], and is a short walk from the railway station. Arriva also operate county services both independently and on behalf of [[Shropshire Council]]. Key routes connect the town with Telford, [[Market Drayton]] and [[Newport, Shropshire|Newport]].{{Cite web |title=Coach & Bus Services |work=Bus Times |date=2024 |access-date=14 April 2024 |url= https://bustimes.org/localities/shrewsbury |quote=}} There are other bus companies operating around the Shrewsbury area, including Boultons of Shropshire, [[Minsterley Motors]]{{cite web |title=Bus Routes And Timetables |url=https://www.minsterleymotors.co.uk/BusRoutesAndTimetables.php |website=Minsterley Motors |access-date=27 August 2023}} and [[Tanat Valley Coaches]] with the latter operating services across the Welsh border from nearby towns including [[Llanfyllin]] and [[Montgomery, Powys|Montgomery]].{{cite web |title=Public services |url=https://www.tanat.co.uk/public-services |website=Tanat Valley Coaches |access-date=27 August 2023}} Shrewsbury has a [[park & ride]] bus scheme in operation, with three car parks on the edge of town; these are at Harlescott (to the north, colour-coded blue), Oxon (to the west, colour-coded pink) and Meole Brace (to the south, colour-coded green).{{cite web |title=Park and Ride |url=https://shropshire.maps.arcgis.com/apps/Minimalist/index.html?appid=91f42605da964c8dabfcdecee4083d7c¢er=349163,312650,27700&level=4 |website=Shropshire Council |access-date=27 August 2023}} ===Road=== [[File:ShrewsburyMap.jpg|thumb|left|A map of Shrewsbury showing suburbs, surrounding villages, rivers (blue), roads (red) and rail routes (green)]] Shrewsbury has been an important centre for road traffic. In 1815, [[Thomas Telford]] designed a new coaching route from London to [[Holyhead]] in order to improve communications with [[Ireland]]. He routed the new road via Shrewsbury, which opened in 1830. The road is now the [[A5 road (Great Britain)|A5]].{{Cite book |last1=M. G. Lay |url=https://archive.org/details/waysofworldhisto00laym |title=Ways of the World: A History of the World's Roads and of the Vehicles That Used Them |last2=James E. Vance, Jr. |publisher=Rutgers University Press |year=1992 |isbn=978-0-813-52691-1 |page=[https://archive.org/details/waysofworldhisto00laym/page/109 109] |url-access=registration}} The road connects the town north-west to [[Oswestry]] and east towards Telford, where it joins the [[M54 motorway|M54]]. The A5 once ran through the town centre, until a [[Bypass route|bypass]] was built in the 1930s. Subsequently, in 1992, a {{convert|17|mi|km|adj=on}} [[dual carriageway]] was completed at a cost of £79 million to the south of the town and was made to form part of the A5 route. This dual carriageway was built further out of the town to act as a substantial link to Telford, as well as a bypass for the town.{{Cite web |title=Pre-Motorway New Roads |url=http://newroads.speedlimit.org.uk/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080218232557/http://newroads.speedlimit.org.uk/ |archive-date=18 February 2008 |access-date=23 February 2008 |website=speedlimit.org.uk |df=dmy-all}} The [[A49 road|A49]] goes to Shrewsbury, joining the A5 at the south of the town, coming from [[Ludlow]] and [[Leominster]]. At this point, the road merges with the A5 for {{convert|3|mi}}, before separating again to the east of the town. From there it runs north, passing Sundorne, then [[Battlefield, Shropshire|Battlefield]], before heading out towards [[Whitchurch, Shropshire|Whitchurch]]. At Battlefield, the [[A53 road|A53]] route begins and heads north-east towards [[Shawbury]] and [[Market Drayton]], then onwards towards [[Newcastle-under-Lyme]] and [[Stoke-on-Trent]]. The [[A458]] ([[Mallwyd]]-[[Quinton, Birmingham|Quinton]]) runs through the town centre, entering in the west and leaving to the south-east. The [[A528]] begins in the town centre and heads north, heading for [[Ellesmere, Shropshire|Ellesmere]]. The [[A488]] begins just west of the town centre in Frankwell and heads out to [[Bishop's Castle]], [[Clun]] and [[Knighton, Powys|Knighton]] crossing the border in the southwest of Shropshire. Major roads within the town include the [[A5112]], A5191 and A5064. The A5191 goes north–south via the town centre, while the A5112 runs north–south to the east of the town centre. The A5064 is a short, {{convert|1|mi|km|spell=in}} stretch of road to the south-east of the town centre, called ''London Road''. Additionally, the [[A5124]], the most recent bypass, was completed in 1998 and runs across the northern edge of the town at Battlefield (connecting the A49/A53 to the A528), though it did exist before as Harlescott Lane (which has since become unclassified). Construction of a major new artery, referred to as the ''[[Shrewsbury North West Relief Road|North West Relief Road]]'' (NWRR), was granted central government funding in April 2019. Together with the existing A5 and A49 by-passes, the Battlefield Link Road (A5124) and the Oxon Link Road; this will result in the completion of the [[ring road]] around the outskirts of the town. Construction is expected to be completed by 2026.{{cite web |title=Key Dates |url=https://www.shropshire.gov.uk/roads-and-highways/shrewsbury-north-west-relief-road/key-dates/ |website=Shropshire Council |access-date=27 August 2023}} The NWRR will involve the construction of a new bridge over the River Severn, upstream from the town centre.[https://www.shropshirestar.com/news/local-hubs/shrewsbury/2019/01/22/nwrr-wins-government-funding-bid/ Shropshire Star] NWRR wins government funding bid (22 January 2019) ===Cycling=== Shrewsbury has a comprehensive network of on-road and traffic-free cycle routes.{{Cite web |title=Cycle routes |url=http://www.cycleshrewsbury.co.uk/cycle-routes |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090516055117/http://www.cycleshrewsbury.co.uk/cycle-routes |archive-date=16 May 2009 |access-date=25 July 2017 |publisher=Cycle Shrewsbury |df=dmy-all}} In 2008, the town was awarded Cycling Town status by [[Cycling England]];{{Cite web |title=[archived content] Cycling England |url=http://www.dft.gov.uk/cyclingengland/cycling-cities-towns/ |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090519000604/http://www.dft.gov.uk/cyclingengland/cycling-cities-towns/ |archive-date=19 May 2009}} as a result, it benefited from £1.8 million of grant funding from the [[Department for Transport]] between 2008 and 2011. The funding was used to make improvements to the cycle network in Shrewsbury and to provide cycle training, information and advice to people to help encourage them to cycle to school and work.{{Cite web |title=cycle shrewsbury |url=http://www.cycleshrewsbury.co.uk/about |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090515163822/http://www.cycleshrewsbury.co.uk/about |archive-date=15 May 2009 |access-date=27 April 2018 |website=Cycleshrewsbury.co.uk |df=dmy-all}} ==Education== [[File:The entrance to the original (1630) Shrewsbury school - in greek = if you love learning you will become learned - panoramio.jpg|thumb|upright|Shrewsbury Library, Castle Gates; formerly Shrewsbury School]] Prior to the [[English Reformation|reformation]], Shrewsbury Abbey and the [[Collegiate church|Collegiate Churches]] of [[St Mary's Church, Shrewsbury|St Mary]] (established by [[Edgar the Peaceful|King Edgar]] in the 10th century) and [[St Chad's Church, Shrewsbury|St Chad]] (established in the 13th) were providing education in the town.{{citation needed|date=August 2023}} Remains of the college of St Chad can be traced in the land adjoining the south-western extremity of the church on the old site, with portions of the wall traceable to a considerable distance in the neighbouring gardens.{{better source needed|date=August 2023|reason=This source is over 150 years old, are the remains still traceable?}} These were closed by the dissolutions. There is mention of a grammar school at Shrewsbury in a court case of 1439.{{Cite book |last=Champion, Bill. |title=Everyday life in Tudor Shrewsbury |date=1994 |publisher=Shropshire Books |isbn=0-903802-60-0 |location=[Shropshire] |pages=38 |oclc=32893450}} An effort was made to found a university in the 1600s during the [[Commonwealth of England|Commonwealth]] which followed the execution of [[Charles I of England|Charles I]]. [[Richard Baxter]], a puritan minister from Shropshire, suggested the establishment of a university for Wales at Shrewsbury in the belief that he could obtain the support of [[Cromwell]] and Parliament for the scheme.{{Cite book |last=Carr, A. M. |title=Shrewsbury Library : its history and restoration. |date=1983 |publisher=Shropshire Libraries |others=Fullman, T. |isbn=0-903802-26-0 |location=[Shrewsbury] |oclc=12478648}} ===Independent sector === [[File:School Boathouse Shrewsbury (20960693446).jpg|thumb|[[Shrewsbury School]]'s main building on the site it moved to in 1882 was built {{circa}} 1765]] [[Shrewsbury School]] is a [[Public school (UK)|public school]], on a large site in Kingsland, just south of the town centre overlooking the loop of the Severn. The school was located in the town centre between 1552 and 1882. The buildings it formerly occupied then are now occupied by the main county library on Castle Street.{{Cite web |title=History of Shrewsbury School |url=http://www.shrewsbury.org.uk/index.cfm?fuseaction=features.content&cmid=124 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090314003503/http://www.shrewsbury.org.uk/index.cfm?fuseaction=features.content&cmid=124 |archive-date=14 March 2009 |access-date=2 March 2008 |publisher=Shrewsbury School |df=dmy-all}} Opposite it on the other side of the river is [[Shrewsbury High School (England)|Shrewsbury High School]], an independent girls' day school.{{cite web |title=Our History |url=https://shrewsburyhigh.gdst.net/explore/our-community/our-history/ |website=Shrewsbury High School |access-date=26 September 2023}} [[Prestfelde School]] is an [[Preparatory school (UK)|independent preparatory school]], on London Road, close to the [[Lord Hill's Column]]. As part of the [[Woodard Schools]] group, it is affiliated to the largest group of [[Church of England]] schools in the country. Whilst originally a school for boys it started accepting girls between the ages of three and thirteen. The school is set in {{convert|30|acre|ha}} of grounds on the outskirts of the town.{{Cite web |title=Prestfelde Preparatory School Home Page |url=http://www.prestfelde.co.uk/home.php?menu=2 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070630003513/http://www.prestfelde.co.uk/home.php?menu=2 |archive-date=30 June 2007 |access-date=2 March 2008 |publisher=Prestfelde Preparatory School |df=dmy-all}} The town's other long-established boys' preparatory school is Kingsland Grange, on Old Roman Road in Kingsland. In 2007, it merged with the junior department of Shrewsbury Girls' High School, sharing the two sites with some classes remaining single sex, but others switching to a [[co-educational]] format.{{Cite web |title=Shrewsbury High Prep at Kingsland Grange |url=http://www.indschools.co.uk/cgi-bin/woda/is97direct_linksall.pl/Show?_id=shrewsburyhighprepschoolatkingslandgrangesy39ah&sort=TIME |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110721061651/http://www.indschools.co.uk/cgi-bin/woda/is97direct_linksall.pl/Show?_id=shrewsburyhighprepschoolatkingslandgrangesy39ah&sort=TIME |archive-date=21 July 2011 |access-date=21 February 2009 |publisher=Independent Schools Directory |df=dmy-all}} === State sector === [[File:Shrewsbury VI form College.JPG|thumb|The Main Grade II listed building of [[Shrewsbury Sixth Form College]], built circa 1910]] The majority of the town's pupils attend one of the several comprehensive schools. [[The Priory School (Shrewsbury)|The Priory School]], formerly a [[grammar school]] for girls;{{Cite news |title=League tables: Secondary Schools in Shropshire |publisher=BBC.co.uk |url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/shared/bsp/hi/education/07/school_tables/secondary_schools/html/893_4368.stm |access-date=26 February 2008}} [[Meole Brace School]], The Grange School, Sundorne School and [[Belvidere School, Shrewsbury|Belvidere School]]. In 2016, The Grange and Sundorne schools were amalgamated to form [[Shrewsbury Academy]]. The school has two campuses; however, it is planned in the next few years for all pupils to move to the Corndon Crescent site of the former Sundorne School.{{cite web |title=Shrewsbury schools merger formally approved |url=https://www.shropshirestar.com/news/education/2015/07/01/shrewsbury-schools-merger-formally-approved/ |website=Shropshire Star |date=July 2015 |access-date=1 September 2023}} [[The Wakeman School]], which was geographically the closest school to the town centre 'loop', next to the [[English Bridge]], was previously the Shrewsbury Technical School and was attended by the First World War poet [[Wilfred Owen]]. It closed as part of reorganisation in July 2013.{{Cite web |date=15 June 2013 |title=Shropshire Star |url=http://www.shropshirestar.com/news/2012/1-/13/wakeman-school-memories-sought-as-closure-looms/ |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://archive.today/20130615174250/http://www.shropshirestar.com/news/2012/1-/13/wakeman-school-memories-sought-as-closure-looms/ |archive-date=15 June 2013}} The site is now utilised by the Shrewsbury Colleges Group.{{cite news |title=Shrewsbury Sixth Form College to take over Wakeman School site |url=https://www.shropshirestar.com/news/education/2013/02/21/shrewsbury-sixth-form-college-to-take-over-wakeman-school-site/ |access-date=9 June 2020 |publisher=[[Shropshire Star]] |date=21 February 2013}} Further education is provided by [[Shrewsbury Sixth Form College]], previously [[The Priory Grammar School for Boys, Shrewsbury|the Priory School for Boys]],{{Cite web |title=Shrewsbury Sixth Form College |url=http://www.ssfc.ac.uk |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170804133413/http://www.ssfc.ac.uk/ |archive-date=4 August 2017 |access-date=25 July 2017 |publisher=Ssfc.ac.uk |df=dmy-all}} ranked 17th in the top 20 of sixth form colleges nationally by the ''Sunday Times'' newspaper in November 2012,{{Cite web |date=21 November 2012 |title=Joy as Shrewsbury Sixth Form College lands top-20 ranking in UK |url=https://www.shropshirestar.com/news/2012/11/21/joy-as-shrewsbury-sixth-form-college-lands-top-20-ranking-in-uk/ |access-date=5 January 2022 |website=[[Shropshire Star]]}} and [[Shrewsbury College]], which handles primarily vocational courses. In 2016, the two establishments were merged into the Shrewsbury Colleges Group.{{cite web |title=About us |url=https://www.scg.ac.uk/about-us/governance-and-leadership/the-shrewsbury-colleges-group |website=Shrewsbury Colleges Group |access-date=28 August 2023}} === University === [[University Centre Shrewsbury]] has been offering postgraduate courses since autumn 2014 and undergraduate courses from autumn 2015. It was established by the [[University of Chester]] and [[Shropshire Council]]. The main campus is located in the renovated Guildhall.{{cite web |title=Our Site and Facilities |url=https://www1.chester.ac.uk/university-centre-shrewsbury/our-sites-and-facilities |website=University of Chester |date=5 May 2021 |access-date=28 August 2023}} ==Religious sites== [[File:The old St Chad's - geograph.org.uk - 687195.jpg|thumb|Ruins of Old St Chad's]] [[File:Fish Street, Shrewsbury.JPG|thumb|upright|The spire of St Alkmund's Church and the tower of St Julian's Church]] There are two Anglo-Saxon foundations of [[collegiate church]]es: that of [[St Chad's Church, Shrewsbury|St Chad]], since resited after the collapse of the original church and rebuilt in 1792 and [[St Mary's Church, Shrewsbury|St Mary]], replaced by what is described as the most complete medieval church in Shrewsbury, dating back to the 12th century.{{cite web |title=St Mary the Virgin, Shrewsbury |url=https://www.visitchurches.org.uk/visit/church-listing/st-mary-shrewsbury.html |website=Churches Consevation Trust |access-date=27 September 2023}} The Norman [[Shrewsbury Abbey]] was founded in 1083{{Cite web |title=History of Shrewsbury Abbey |url=http://www.shrewsburyabbey.com/left_menu/abbeyhistory.htm |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080621123816/http://www.shrewsburyabbey.com/left_menu/abbeyhistory.htm |archive-date=21 June 2008 |access-date=17 March 2008 |website=ShrewsburyAbbey.com |df=dmy-all}} and its nave survived as a parish church following [[Dissolution of the monasteries|the dissolution]]. [[File:Shrewsbury Methodism 02.jpg|thumb|John Wesley first preached here.]] According to legend, the spire of St Alkmund's Church was damaged by the Devil in 1553 and climbed four times by a drunken steeplejack in 1621.{{Cite book |last=Ash |first=Russell |title=Folklore, Myths and Legends of Britain |date=1973 |publisher=Reader's Digest Association Limited |isbn=9780340165973 |page=328}} There are a number of other [[Anglican]] churches in Shrewsbury: Shrewsbury All Saints in Castlefields, The Church of the Holy Spirit in Harlescott, Holy Trinity, St George of Cappadocia, St Giles, Greenfields United Church and St Peter in Monkmoor.{{Cite web |last=[[Archbishops' Council]] |title=Shrewsbury |url=http://www.acny.org.uk/result.php?query=shrewsbury&type=place |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://archive.today/20120719222312/http://www.acny.org.uk/result.php?query=shrewsbury&type=place |archive-date=19 July 2012 |access-date=17 March 2008 |website=A Church Near You |df=dmy-all}} and the [[United Reformed Church]] are also represented, alongside newer church groups including [[Elim Pentecostal]]{{Cite web |title=Rivers Way – An Elim Church
