Shrewsbury Evangelical Church met in the former Anglican parish church of St Julian, which was previously a craft centre, at the Wyle Cop end of Fish Street,{{Cite web |title=Shrewsbury Evangelical Church |url=http://www.shrewsburyevangelicalchurch.org |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090114075021/http://www.shrewsburyevangelicalchurch.org/ |archive-date=14 January 2009 |access-date=27 December 2008 |website=shrewsburyevangelicalchurch.org |df=dmy-all}} later moving into the Springfield estate in the eastern suburbs{{Cite web |title=Shrewsbury Evangelical Church |url=https://www.shrewsburyevangelicalchurch.org/ |access-date=5 July 2021}} meeting at the Mereside Community Centre.{{cite web |title=Location & Contact |url=https://www.shrewsburyevangelicalchurch.org/contact/ |website=Shrewsbury Evangelical Church |access-date=12 January 2025}} One of the houses in Fish Street, facing St Alkmund's Church, was the site of [[John Wesley]]'s first preaching in Shrewsbury; a wall plaque records the date as 16 March 1761. The Grade II listed [[Shrewsbury Unitarian Church]] was founded in 1662 according to the inscription above the main door. The current building was built between 1839 and 1840.{{NHLE|grade=II|desc=Unitarian Church|num=1254520|date=17 November 1995}} Shrewsbury has a Roman Catholic [[Shrewsbury Cathedral|Cathedral]], by the Town Walls.{{Cite web |title=Shrewsbury Cathedral Home Page |url=http://www.shrewsburycathedral.org/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080605233103/http://www.shrewsburycathedral.org/ |archive-date=5 June 2008 |access-date=17 March 2008 |website=ShrewsburyCathedral.org |df=dmy-all}} Designed by [[Edward Pugin]] after the death of his father, [[Augustus Pugin|Augustus]], it was consecrated in 1856.''History of the Cathedral'', [http://www.dioceseofshrewsbury.org/about-us/cathedral/welcome Diocese of Shrewsbury] There are two other parishes, in Harlescott and Monkmoor, within the [[Roman Catholic]] [[Diocese of Shrewsbury]]. Shrewsbury's [[Greek Orthodox]] Church, a former Anglican church building, is at Dove Close off Oteley Road to the south. The site of which had been used as a place of worship for some four thousand years. The building, dating from the 13th century, was purchased by the Orthodox church in the 1990s after being disused for services since the 1950s and restored, as the Church of the 318 Holy Fathers, with funds from English Heritage.{{cite web |title=Our Sacred Site |url=https://shrewsburyorthodox.com/about-us/our-sacred-site/ |website=Greek Orthodox Church Shrewsbury |access-date=12 January 2025}} Regular Sunday services are now conducted at St Julian's Centre, which is privately owned, owing to the need for a larger venue{{cite news |title=Shrewsbury town centre church set to host Christian celebration with hundreds expected |url=https://www.shropshirestar.com/news/local-hubs/shrewsbury/2024/04/30/town-centre-church-set-to-host-christian-celebration/ |access-date=12 January 2025 |work=Shropshire Star |date=30 April 2024}} although weekday services continue at the Church of the 318 Holy Fathers.{{cite web |title=Church of the 318 Holy Fathers |url=https://shrewsburyorthodox.com/find-us/church-of-the-318-holy-fathers/ |website=Greek Orthodox Church Shrewsbury |access-date=12 January 2025}} Shrewsbury's first known dedicated non-Christian place of worship, a [[Muslim]] prayer centre, was approved in 2013. It is in the Column Lodge, the former registry office in Preston Street. Before then, the local Muslim community had been hosted by the United Reformed Church on English Bridge.{{Cite news |date=21 June 2013 |title=Shrewsbury Muslim prayer centre plans approved |work=[[Shropshire Star]] |publisher=[[MNA Media]] |url=http://www.shropshirestar.com/news/2013/06/21/decision-due-on-shrewsbury-muslim-prayer-centre/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130622065006/http://www.shropshirestar.com/news/2013/06/21/decision-due-on-shrewsbury-muslim-prayer-centre/ |archive-date=22 June 2013 |df=dmy-all}} ===Community and charity projects=== Many community projects in Shrewsbury are based in, or have been started by local churches, including the Isaiah 58 project, which is the primary work amongst homeless people in the town, whilst 'Churches Together in Shrewsbury' works to help homeless people through the Ark project.{{Cite web |title=Churches Together in Shrewsbury – The Shrewsbury Ark |url=http://www.shrewsburychurches.org/ark.htm |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080706131803/http://www.shrewsburychurches.org/ark.htm |archive-date=6 July 2008 |access-date=17 March 2008 |website=ShrewsburyChurches.org |df=dmy-all}}{{Cite web |title=Isaiah 58 Project |url=http://www.shrop.net/isaiah58project/ |url-status=usurped |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080229032453/http://www.shrop.net/isaiah58project/ |archive-date=29 February 2008 |access-date=17 March 2008 |website=shrop.net}} Shrewsbury [[Food Bank]], based at Barnabas Community Church Centre and part of 'Food Bank PLUS,' provides a wide range of social action initiatives including 'Money Advice' (a confidential, not for profit debt, benefits and financial help service) and Eclipse Child Bereavement, which works with local schools to help children who have experienced losses to overcome their situation. Also run by Barnabas are projects including '360 Journey to Work,' which help people gain skills in applying for jobs including basics like CV writing. 'Cage football' is an initiative that is lent out to local community groups, youth clubs and other churches.{{Cite web |title=Community |url=http://www.barnabascommunitychurch.com/community.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180828060815/http://barnabascommunitychurch.com/community.html |archive-date=28 August 2018 |access-date=9 January 2019 |website=Barnabas Community Church Shrewsbury |df=dmy-all}} ==Sport== === Football === [[File:STFC - New Meadow (Aerial).jpg|thumb|[[New Meadow]] stadium, home of [[Shrewsbury Town]]]] The town has a claim on the emergence of the formally codified game of [[association football]] via Shrewsbury School which published a set of ten rules in about 1856, agreed with [[Eton College|Eton]], [[Harrow School|Harrow]] and [[Rugby School|Rugby]] schools and [[Cambridge University]] This predated the [[Football Association]]'s initial rule book by seven years.{{Cite web |date=2013-02-16 |title=We played by our own set of rules |url=https://www.shropshirestar.com/news/2013/02/16/we-played-by-our-own-set-of-rules/ |access-date=2023-07-20 |website=Shropshirestar.com |language=en}} Shrewsbury is home to a professional football club, [[Shrewsbury Town]]. As of March 2026, they compete in {{English football updater|ShrewsbT}} and since 2007 has played their home games at [[New Meadow]] – from 1910 to 2007 the club played at the [[Gay Meadow]] stadium. The town is also home to a semi-professional [[Association football|football]] club, [[Haughmond F.C.|Haughmond]], who take their name from the nearby [[Haughmond Hill]]. They currently compete in the {{English football updater|Haughmon}} and play their home games at the Shrewsbury Sports Village, in Sundorne.{{cite web |title=Home |url=https://www.pitchero.com/clubs/haughmondfootballclub |website=Haughmond Football Club |access-date=30 August 2023}} === Rowing === [[File:Rowing at Shrewsbury - geograph.org.uk - 1195498.jpg|thumb|An [[Eight (rowing)|eight]] rowing on the Severn in Shrewsbury]] The River Severn in the town is used for rowing by both the [[Pengwern Boat Club]],{{Cite web |title=Pengwern Boat Club website |url=http://www.pengwernbc.co.uk |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080509195912/http://www.pengwernbc.co.uk/ |archive-date=9 May 2008 |access-date=20 March 2008 |website=PengwernBC |df=dmy-all}} founded in 1871 and using an ancient name for the town,{{cite web |title=Pengwern Boat Club |url=http://www.pengwernbc.co.uk/#!about/c15v1 |access-date=2016-05-22 |website=Pengwern Boat Club}} and the Royal [[Shrewsbury School]] Boat Club (RSSBC), founded in 1866.{{cite web |title=School Rowing |url=https://www.shrewsbury.org.uk/page/rowing-rssbc |website=Shrewsbury School}}{{Cite web |title=Rowing |url=http://www.shrewsbury.org.uk/index.cfm?fuseaction=sport.content&cmid=75 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080111015236/http://www.shrewsbury.org.uk/index.cfm?fuseaction=sport.content&cmid=75 |archive-date=11 January 2008 |access-date=4 March 2008 |website=Shrewsbury School |df=dmy-all}} The Pengwern brick and timber club house was built in 1881 and is a Grade II listed building.{{Cite web |title=Pengwern Boat House at Sj 4852 1220 - Shrewsbury - Shropshire - England {{!}} British Listed Buildings |url=http://www.britishlistedbuildings.co.uk/en-457388-pengwern-boat-house-at-sj-4852-1220-shre#.V0G6pvkrJqw |access-date=2016-05-22 |website=Britishlistedbuildings.co.uk}} The club house was expanded around 2013.{{Cite web |title=Shrewsbury's Pengwern Boat Club club floats an expansion bid « Shropshire Star |url=http://www.shropshirestar.com/news/2013/09/03/shrewsburys-pengwern-boat-club-club-floats-an-expansion-bid/ |access-date=2016-05-22 |website=Shropshirestar.com|date=3 September 2013 }} More recently, the two clubs have been joined by students of [[Harper Adams University]], [[University Centre Shrewsbury]] and crews from other local schools. There is an annual rowing regatta in the town in May. It is one of the oldest events in the rowing calendar, having first been held in 1871.{{Cite web |title=Pictures: Thousands enjoy Shrewsbury Regatta « Shropshire Star |url=http://www.shropshirestar.com/entertainment/2016/05/09/pictures-thousands-enjoy-shrewsbury-regatta/ |access-date=2016-05-22 |website=Shropshirestar.com|date=9 May 2016 }}{{Cite web |date=8 October 1849 |title=The Shrewsbury Regatta ... will take place on Monday August 27th 1849 1st race at 2 O'clock for 8 oar boats ... etc. (List of events follows) Course ... An excellent Brass Band will be in attendance ... |url=http://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/details/r/02b14694-6c21-4422-afac-38ad4c572f2f |via=National Archive of the UK}} A [[Head race|head of the river race]] was run annually between 1936 and the 1990s.{{Cite web |date=2016-03-10 |title=The History of Pengwern BC – And the Friendship Between Two Rowing Historians |url=https://heartheboatsing.com/2016/03/10/the-history-of-pengwern-bc-and-the-friendship-between-two-rowing-historians/ |access-date=2023-07-20 |website=Hear The Boat Sing |language=en-GB}} === Rugby === There is a local [[Rugby union|rugby]] club, Shrewsbury Rugby Club.{{Cite web |title=Rugby Clubs in Shropshire |url=http://www.shropshire.gov.uk/sports.nsf/open/7BA9BAFA99E9B372802572A60034D952 |access-date=16 January 2008 |website=Shropshire County Council}}{{dead link|date=March 2016|bot=medic}}{{cbignore|bot=medic}} ===Motor sports=== The local motorsports heritage includes the [[Loton Park Hillclimb]] and [[Hawkstone Park Motocross Circuit]] near Shrewsbury. [[Shrewsbury Motocross Club]] has staged [[motocross]] events in the area for over 30 years.{{Cite web |title=History of SMXC |url=http://www.shrop.net/shrewsburymxc/history-of-smxc/ |url-status=usurped |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070714114837/http://www.shrop.net/shrewsburymxc/history-of-smxc/ |archive-date=14 July 2007 |access-date=4 March 2008 |website=Shrop.net}} === Other sports === Shrewsbury Sports Village is a sports centre in the Sundorne district of the town, aimed at providing a wide range of sports facilities for townspeople.{{Cite web |title=Shrewsbury Sports Village |url=http://www.shrewsbury.gov.uk/public/sport/facilities/shrewsburysportsvillage/default.htm |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080218031407/http://www.shrewsbury.gov.uk/public/sport/facilities/shrewsburysportsvillage/default.htm |archive-date=18 February 2008 |access-date=4 March 2008 |publisher=Shrewsbury and Atcham council |df=dmy-all}} There are a number of golf facilities, including Meole Brace Municipal Golf Course, in the area. Shrewsbury holds its own annual Sprint Triathlon, which takes place each September at the West Midlands Country Showground, organised by SYTri (Shrewsbury Triathlon Club) which is affiliated to the British Triathlon Federation.{{cite web |title=Shrewsbury Sprint Tri, Quad, Aquathlon and Aquabike |url=https://www.sytri.org/races/shrewsbury-sprint-tri-and-quad/ |website=Sytri |access-date=1 September 2023}} A free weekly [[parkrun]] takes place in the Quarry.{{cite web |title=Shrewsbury parkrun |url=https://www.parkrun.org.uk/shrewsbury/ |website=Parkrun |access-date=1 September 2023}} ==Notable Salopians== {{For|alumni of Shrewsbury School|List of Old Salopians}} There have been a number of notable Salopians, including [[Charles Darwin]], the biologist and [[evolutionary theorist]].{{Cite EB1911|wstitle=Darwin, Charles Robert|volume=7|last=Poulton|first=Edward Bagnall|author-link=Edward Bagnall Poulton|pages=840–843|short=1}} Darwin, one of the most important thinkers of the 19th century,{{Cite web |title=Charles Darwin – Great Minds, Great Thinkers |url=http://www.edinformatics.com/great_thinkers/darwin.htm |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080413155115/http://www.edinformatics.com/great_thinkers/darwin.htm |archive-date=13 April 2008 |access-date=16 March 2008 |publisher=EDinformatics |df=dmy-all}} was born in Shrewsbury on 12 February 1809 at the Mount House, baptised at St Chad's Church and educated at [[Shrewsbury School]]. The town's river and proximity to the countryside inspired his interest in the natural world, while its abundant ice-age boulders sparked his interest in geology.{{Cite web |title=The Bellstone, Shrewsbury {{!}} Original Shrewsbury |url=https://originalshrewsbury.co.uk/bellstone-shrewsbury |access-date=2018-06-14 |website=originalshrewsbury.co.uk |language=en}} Classicist [[Mary Beard]], (born 1955) Cambridge professor and television presenter, was educated in Shrewsbury where her father was a prominent architect.{{Cite web |last=Laity |first=Paul |date=2007-11-10 |title=A life in writing: Mary Beard, Britain's best-known classicist |url=https://www.theguardian.com/books/2007/nov/10/featuresreviews.guardianreview19 |access-date=2018-06-14 |website=[[The Guardian]]}} [[File:Wilfred Owen 2.png|thumb|upright|[[Wilfred Owen]]]] Shrewsbury has been home to many contributors to literature. [[Thomas Churchyard]] ({{Circa|1523}}–1604) son of a farmer, was an author of autobiographical or semi-autobiographical verse collections.{{Cite EB1911|wstitle=Churchyard, Thomas|volume=6|page=348|short=1}} In the early years of the 18th century, the Irish dramatist [[George Farquhar]], (1677–1707) resided in the town while serving as a recruiting officer for the Army. He drew on this experience in writing the comedy ''[[The Recruiting Officer]]''. The romantic novelist [[Mary Webb]], (1881–1927) lived in and around outer Shrewsbury and was buried there upon her death. Before the [[First World War]], the poet [[Wilfred Owen]], (1893–1918) lived in the town and there is a memorial to Owen at Shrewsbury Abbey.{{Cite web |last=Thompson |first=Harvey |date=2 December 1998 |title=The war poet Wilfred Owen 80 years on |url=http://www.wsws.org/arts/1998/dec1998/owen-d02.shtml |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080111065950/http://www.wsws.org/arts/1998/dec1998/owen-d02.shtml |archive-date=11 January 2008 |access-date=15 January 2008 |website=World Socialist Web Site}} Comedian [[George Robey]], (1869–1954) lived in the town, near [[Lord Hill's Column]], before and during the [[Second World War]].{{Cite book |title=A Town At War, Shrewsbury 1939–45 |page=37}}It notes "...Shrewsbury [had its resident comedian] with the legendary [[George Robey]], (then in his seventies) living near the Column." The contemporary poet, [[Jemma L. King]] is from Shrewsbury.{{cite news |title=Poet Jemma King shortlisted for Dylan Thomas Prize |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-wales-north-west-wales-26547312 |work=BBC News |date=12 March 2014 |access-date=25 June 2025}} [[File:Clive of India statue.jpg|thumb|Statue of [[Robert Clive, 1st Baron Clive|Robert Clive]]]] Politicians with connections with the town include [[Sir William Pulteney, 5th Baronet]], (1729–1805) once Britain's richest man, he was MP for Shrewsbury from 1768 to 1805.{{Cite web |last=Johnstone |first=Jeffrey |title=Sir William Johnstone Pulteney and The Scottish Origins of Western New York |url=http://www.crookedlakereview.com/articles/101_135/132summer2004/132johnstone.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071028101841/http://www.crookedlakereview.com/articles/101_135/132summer2004/132johnstone.html |archive-date=28 October 2007 |access-date=16 January 2008 |website=The Crooked Lake Review |df=dmy-all}} He lived in apartments at Shrewsbury Castle. [[Robert Clive]], (1725–1774), was MP for Shrewsbury and also the mayor.{{Cite web |title=Robert Clive: Tearaway to empire builder |url=http://www.bbc.co.uk/shropshire/content/articles/2005/03/29/robert_clive_feature.shtml |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080111202200/http://www.bbc.co.uk/shropshire/content/articles/2005/03/29/robert_clive_feature.shtml |archive-date=11 January 2008 |access-date=16 January 2008 |website=BBC.co.uk |df=dmy-all}}{{Cite EB1911|wstitle=Clive, Robert Clive, Baron|volume=6|pages=532–536|short=1}} [[Leo Blair]], (1923–2012) the father of former Prime Minister [[Tony Blair]], (born 1953) was a resident of the town.{{Cite news |date=20 May 2000 |title=Leo Blair: What's in a name |work=BBC News |url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/uk/756633.stm |url-status=live |access-date=17 March 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060512213607/http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/uk/756633.stm |archive-date=12 May 2006 |df=dmy-all}} [[Ian Hunter (singer)|Ian Hunter]], (born 1939) the lead singer of the 1970s pop group [[Mott the Hoople]], was a resident of 23a Swan Hill in the town centre and wrote a song of the same name.{{Cite web |title=Ian Hunter |url=http://everything2.com/node/1170116 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080503213653/http://everything2.com/node/1170116 |archive-date=3 May 2008 |access-date=17 March 2008 |website=Everything2.com |df=dmy-all}} The 1980s pop group ''[[T'Pau (band)|T'Pau]]'' was formed in the town and the band's vocalist [[Carol Decker]], (born 1957) has lived in the town, along with other members of the band.{{Cite web |title=For Crying Out Loud! (T'Pau interviews) |url=http://www.tpau.org/ints/recmir87.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080513142412/http://www.tpau.org/ints/recmir87.html |archive-date=13 May 2008 |access-date=17 March 2008 |website=T'Pau.org |df=dmy-all}} Notable music historian and composer [[Charles Burney]], (1726–1814) was born and educated in the town.{{Cite EB1911|wstitle=Burney, Charles|volume=4|pages=853–854|short=1}} [[Lange (musician)|Lange]], (born 1974), a DJ and dance music producer, was born in Shrewsbury.{{Cite web |title=Langa (AKA Firewall) |url=http://supra.armadamusic.nl/artists/lange-aka-firewall/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071222191410/http://supra.armadamusic.nl/artists/lange-aka-firewall/ |archive-date=22 December 2007 |access-date=17 March 2008 |publisher=Armada Music}} Sporting Salopians include four [[FA Cup Final]] winning players who took part in the first decade of the Cup's history and were born in or lived in Shrewsbury: [[John Hawley Edwards]], (1850–1893), [[Henry Wace (footballer)|Henry Wace]], (1853–1947) and [[John Wylie (footballer, born 1854)|John Wylie]], (1854–1924) of the [[Wanderers F.C.|Wanderers]] and [[Clopton Lloyd-Jones]], (1858–1918) of [[Clapham Rovers]].{{Cite book |last=Warsop |first=Keith |title=The Early F.A.
